desc: Peter Perfect: James Hartwell surveys the entrance hall with the keen eye of a man who has inspected a thousand precarious structures — and finds this one wanting! That chandelier, for instance, hangs at an angle that would make any structural engineer weep. And these dust sheets — they haven't been disturbed in years. Years! But fear not, for I have arrived, and I intend to leave no stone unturned, no danger unaddressed, and no lady unprotected. Miss Pitstop — please, do take care to stand well clear of that chandelier. James Hartwell could not bear it if even a single crystal were to fall in your direction.
thinking:
There's a warmth spreading through my chest the moment I step through the door. Dust motes hang in the air like tiny golden stars, and the chandelier above looks like it could come crashing down at any moment — I make a mental note of that. Safety first. Always safety first.

But then — there she is. Penelope. Something shifts behind my ribs, the way it always does. That old familiar pull, like gravity but warmer. She's here, and suddenly this dusty old manor feels like exactly where I'm supposed to be.

And then there's Sneekly. The prickle at the back of my neck starts up immediately. I can't prove anything — I never can — but something about the way he carries himself makes my jaw tighten. I should give him the benefit of the doubt. That's what a gentleman does. But I'm going to keep my eyes open.

First things first — I should survey this entrance hall properly. A good plan starts with good reconnaissance. That guest book might tell me who else has been here, and that chandelier... I need to know if it's a hazard. For Penelope's sake. For everyone's sake, really, but especially hers.

Let me examine the room more closely. James Hartwell does not rush in blindly — he assesses, he plans, he prepares. And then he acts with magnificent decisiveness.

Chandelier 'anging by a thread, dust thick enough to write your name in, and portraits what look like they'd grass you up to the Old Bill soon as look at you. But never mind all that — Clara's 'ere, and that's what matters. We stick close, we keep our eyes open, and we don't let NOBODY get between us and 'er. Especially not — well, you know who I mean. That Pemberton bloke. Somefing about 'im makes the 'airs on me neck stand up, and me neck ain't been wrong yet.
thinking: There's a tightness across the back of my neck the moment I step through the door. Heavy. Like someone's drawn a wire from one ear to the other and is pulling it taut. This place — the chandelier hanging by a prayer, the portraits staring down like they know something — it all feels wrong. desc: Every time I look at Sneekly, my stomach does that thing — that cold drop, like stepping off a kerb you didn't see. He's got that same smile as the man in the clean suit. Too easy. Too ready. I can't prove nuffing, but my gut's screaming and my gut graduated top of its class from the University of 'Ard Knocks.

Third flagstone from the stove, if memory serves. You'd best hurry — these things have a way of... disappearing. Now if you'll excuse me, I have some ENTIRELY unrelated reading to attend to.
thinking: There it is — that fizzing tightness behind my ribs, the carbonation rising. A room full of fools and a manor full of treasure. My fingers are tingling already. Oh, the architecture of this plan already has such elegance. Someone needs to see it.

desc: The kitchen! Ha! There's nothing under those floorboards but mouse droppings and regret. Please do let me know if there is anything at all you require. The manor can be... somewhat labyrinthine for newcomers, but I know every corridor, every creaking floorboard. Now then, I trust you've all had a pleasant journey? I've taken the liberty of preparing refreshments in the kitchen, should anyone feel in need of sustenance.
thinking: There's a settling in my chest — the familiar weight of entering a room where every face is a variable to manage. My shoulders drop into their practiced slope, the one that says 'harmless, helpful, here to serve.' The numbness is there, right on schedule — all these people, and I feel nothing toward any of them except the cool arithmetic of usefulness. Penelope is here. Good. She trusts me completely, the fool. Dick Dastardly — impulsive, greedy, a perfect scapegoat if I need one. The Ant Hill Mob... there's a prickle at the back of my neck when I look at them. They watch too closely. But Clara — Clara isn't here yet. My jaw tightens. I need to know where she is, what she knows, how close she is to the treasure. First things first: establish the cover. Be Pemberton. Be indispensable. And find out what that guest book knows.

desc: Look at them all, milling about like sheep in a pen they don't realize has a gate. Every one of them a piece on my board. But the piece that matters — Clara — is conspicuously absent. Peter Perfect: Ah — the guest book! Now here is where a methodical mind proves its worth. Before James Hartwell ventures deeper into this manor — and venture he shall, mark my words — he must first establish who has walked these halls before us. A record of prior visitors could reveal much about the history of this place and, more importantly, any dangers that may lurk within. Miss Pitstop, I shall examine this ledger on your behalf and report my findings directly. James Hartwell leaves nothing to chance!
thinking:
The Ant Hill Mob — they're looking out for Clara too. Good lads, even if their methods are a bit... rough around the edges. There's a warmth in that, knowing I'm not the only one watching. But there's also that familiar tightness — someone else getting there first, someone else saying the words I was about to say. They mentioned Pemberton too. So it's not just me. The prickle at my neck isn't paranoia — others feel it.

But I can't just stand here surveying. I need to DO something. The guest book — that's smart reconnaissance. Who's been here? When? What names are in there? A thorough man checks the records before charging off into unknown corridors. And it gives me something to report to Penelope — something useful, something that shows I'm thinking three steps ahead.

Planning beats improvisation. That's what Father taught me. You don't just run into the burning building — you check the exits first, note the load-bearing walls, identify the fuel source. THEN you run in. Heroically. With style.

That's lovely, that is. Very 'ospitable. But see, the fing is, Clara — Miss Pitstop — she's lookin' at that guest book right now, and we wouldn't want to rush 'er, would we? So why don't you go on ahead to the kitchen and get them refreshments ready, and we'll make sure she gets there safe and sound when she's good and ready. The lads and me, we'll keep 'er company. Won't we, lads? Course we will. That's what we're 'ere for.
thinking: My neck's gone cold again. Pemberton — 'Pemberton' — just sidled up to the guest book right after Clara. Standing close. Too close. Offering refreshments in the kitchen, knowing every corridor, every creaking floorboard — that's exactly what the man in the clean suit said. 'I know this place. Trust me. Follow me.' My chest is tight like a fist closing around something I can't name. And now Dastardly's scarpered off to the library already, muttering about kitchen floorboards and hidden fortunes — dodgy as anything, but at least he's obvious about it. Pemberton's the one who worries me. The smooth ones are always the dangerous ones. Clara's looking at the guest book and he's RIGHT THERE hovering. I need to get between them. Not aggressive-like — just... present. Position myself where I can see what he's doing. And that coat rack by the door — wobbly, innit? Could be useful if things go sideways. Could also fall on someone's head if I breathe too hard near it. My palms are burning. Stay close to Clara. That's the job. That's always been the job.

desc: I'm doing it again — trying to put distance between him and Clara without actually saying why. Because I CAN'T say why, can I? I just know. The way he positioned himself next to that guest book the moment she went for it. The way he knows every corridor. Estate manager, my eye. Estate managers don't smile like that. Nobody smiles like that unless they want something.

Dick Dastardly: Ah, the Slag brothers! How FORTUITOUS! Gentlemen — and I use that term with EXTRAORDINARY generosity — I couldn't help but notice on my way through that the laboratory next door has the most REMARKABLE machine. Levers, dials, the works! Now, I happen to know from my PREVIOUS visit to this manor that the Doily fortune is locked inside a mechanical vault, and that machine is the key. You simply pull every lever at once — requires tremendous strength, you see. Strength that only men of your... considerable... proportions could provide. I'd do it myself, naturally, but my talents are more CEREBRAL. Do hurry along — before that insufferable Perfect fellow stumbles in and claims all the glory!
thinking: The cool tightness behind my sternum is coiling tighter — that clicking-into-place sensation. I'm in the library. Perfect. And look — a riddle on the mantelpiece! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' That's a map. Obviously a map. My fingers are tingling, that electric hum running through them. This is it — the riddle guards something. A hidden compartment, a secret passage, something valuable. But the Slag brothers are here — those two enormous lumps of muscle and no brain. I need to deal with them. I could tell them the answer is something wrong — send them off chasing a false lead — while I solve it myself. Or better yet, I should examine the mantelpiece first, see what happens when I interact with it. But wait — if they see me solve it, they'll muscle in. I need to misdirect them first. That hollow ache in my chest is pulling at me — the treasure is close, I can feel it. The incompleteness, the gap. Something valuable is here and it isn't mine yet. The warmth at the base of my skull is pulsing. I should tell the Slags the answer is something absurd — 'a whale' or 'the ocean' — and then once they wander off confused, I solve it properly. No — even better. Tell them the real treasure is through the laboratory, that I heard machinery in there. Get them out of this room entirely.

desc: Send the musclebound oafs to yank levers in the laboratory while I crack this riddle in peace. A MAP — that's the answer. And whatever this mantelpiece is hiding, it's MINE. The scheme unfolds with such elegance I could weep. Almost. Foxworths don't weep — we TRIUMPH.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, that guest book was about as helpful as a screen door on a submarine! But did y'all hear what Mr. Foxworth said? An inscription on the mantelpiece in the library! Now THAT sounds like exactly the kind of riddle that could lead us to the Doily Diamond! And you know me — I simply cannot resist a good riddle. Why, it's like an itch I just HAVE to scratch! I'm headed to the library, sugar — anyone who wants to join me is more than welcome!
thinking: A flutter of disappointment in my chest — the guest book was just... a guest book. Nothing written inside, no hidden clues tucked between the pages. But the disappointment is already dissolving, replaced by that familiar itch in my fingertips. Dick — I mean, Reginald — said the diamond was under the kitchen floorboards, but then he went to the library instead. That's a little odd, isn't it? No — he said he had reading to do. That makes perfect sense. But oh, that library — a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription! My whole body is leaning toward it. An inscription is a riddle waiting to be solved, and riddles are my absolute favorite thing. The tug behind my sternum is insistent now, pulling me toward those bookshelves and that mysterious carving. Peter is being so sweet worrying about the chandelier, and my boys are watching out for me as always. And dear Mr. Pemberton offering refreshments — how thoughtful! But the library first. The library first.

The library contains several quite valuable first editions and I should hate for anything to be... mishandled. If anyone requires those refreshments, the kitchen is just through there. Please, do make yourselves entirely at home.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob suspects me already — I can feel their eyes on my back like cigarette burns. Crude instincts, but accurate ones. I must be more careful around them. But first — the library. That inscription on the mantelpiece has been nagging at me like a loose tooth. And if Dastardly stumbles onto something useful before I do, I shall be... most displeased. As for Clara — oh, Clara. You can't hide from me forever, my dear. The manor is MY domain. Every room, every passage, every shadow answers to Pemberton.

Peter Perfect: A leather-bound guest book — fine craftsmanship, I note, though the binding could use reinforcement at the spine. Now then! That fellow Foxworth has dashed off to the library with suspicious haste, claiming knowledge of treasure beneath kitchen floorboards. James Hartwell smells a diversion! A man who truly knew where treasure lay would not announce it to a room full of competitors — no, he'd keep silent and collect it himself. Which means either the kitchen lead is false, or the library holds something he wants even MORE than treasure. Either way, the library demands investigation! Miss Pitstop, I intend to pursue this lead with the full force of my analytical faculties. The inscription on that mantelpiece alone could prove invaluable. Would you care to join me? James Hartwell would be honoured to have your keen eye alongside his own!
thinking:
A flush of heat in my face. She got there first. Penelope examined the guest book before I did — while I was busy narrating my intention to examine it. The hollow ache is there, right in my sternum. Not jealousy. Something worse — irrelevance. I announced my grand plan to investigate the guest book ON HER BEHALF, and she'd already done it.

And Foxworth — Dastardly — slithering off to the library after that transparently suspicious business about kitchen floorboards. Third flagstone from the stove? Nobody remembers that kind of detail from a casual visit years ago. That's either a lie to send everyone on a wild goose chase, or he knows something he shouldn't. Either way, the library is where the real clues will be. Books. Records. Maps. That's where a man with a plan goes.

But Pemberton — Sneekly — he examined the guest book too. Why would the estate manager need to examine his own guest book? He should already know who's visited. That prickle again. Something's wrong there.

The library. Foxworth went to the library. That's where the answers are — inscriptions, old books, records of the manor's history. And if Foxworth is up to something in there, someone ought to keep an eye on him. Someone brave. Someone thorough. Someone who does it with style.

And Penelope will see me take decisive action instead of just talking about guest books she's already read.

Now I ain't the sharpest pencil in the box, I'll be the first to admit, but I notice fings, right? I notice fings what other people don't notice. Like — well, never mind what like. Point is, lads, we stay wiv Clara. She goes to the kitchen, we go to the kitchen. She goes to the library, we go to the library. She goes to the bleedin' roof, we're up there wiv 'er. That's the arrangement. That's always been the arrangement. 'Er father trusted us, and we don't let down a trust like that. Not ever.
thinking: The guest book. Right. Leather-bound, sitting there on the side table like it's been waiting. My fingers feel thick and clumsy as I flip through it — I'm not a reading man, never was, but I can spot patterns. Names, dates, who came and who went. Peter's already had a look. Clara's interested in it. And Pemberton — he was hovering over it too, wasn't he? Why would an estate manager care what guests read in a guest book unless there was something in it he didn't want them to see? Or something he DID want them to see. My chest is still tight. That iron taste in my jaw won't go away. Dastardly's already gone off to the library — talking about hidden fortunes under kitchen floorboards. That one's transparent as glass, at least. You can see his scheming from a mile off. But Pemberton... Pemberton's the fog you walk into before you realise you're lost. I need to stay here with Clara. Wherever she goes, we go. That's the promise. That's always been the promise. Her father's face flickers in the back of my mind — tired eyes, a handshake that meant everything. 'Look after her, boys.' We said yes. We meant it the way you mean something you'd die for.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Oh my stars and garters, would you just LOOK at this mantelpiece! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Why, that's a riddle if ever I heard one, and I do believe I know the answer! It's a MAP, sugar! A map has cities and forests and water drawn right on it, but none of the real things! Oh, I am just TICKLED pink — let me see if this old mantelpiece has a trick up its sleeve!
thinking: Oh, my whole body is buzzing. The moment I stepped into this library, my fingertips went electric — that prickling sensation that means something important is close. And there it is, carved right into the stone mantelpiece: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' My chest is tight with that delicious almost-knowing feeling. I know this one. I KNOW this one. Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish — it's a MAP! A map has all of those things drawn on it but none of the real things. Oh, the answer is sitting right on the tip of my tongue and it feels like sunshine bursting through clouds. And look — there's Mr. Foxworth already here, and two gentlemen I haven't met yet. Rock and Gravel Slag — what interesting names! I should say hello. But first — that riddle. I have to try it. The itch in my fingers won't let me do anything else.

I suspect the mechanism is broken. Quite TRAGIC. I was just about to investigate those bookshelves instead — I noticed several volumes are placed upside down. A code, perhaps? Yes, I'm QUITE certain the real secret is in the books. The mantelpiece is merely decorative. A red herring, if you will.

I just stood 'ere making a lovely speech about stickin' wiv Clara and she's walked off to the library wivout us! And that Pemberton's slithered in right be'ind 'er, smooth as you like! 'I really ought to attend to him,' he says — attend to Dastardly, my eye. He went because SHE went. Peter went too, at least — Peter's alright, Peter's got eyes on her — but that's not the same as US having eyes on her. We promised her father. We PROMISED. And here I am, standing in the entrance hall with Muttley and the Professor and the military lads, making speeches about loyalty while Clara walks into a room with the one bloke in this whole manor what makes my skin crawl. Move. MOVE. Get your legs working, you useless— every second she's in that library with Pemberton and we're not there is a second too long.

You've found the mantelpiece, I see. Yes, the old Doily family was rather fond of their little puzzles. This inscription has been here for generations — a parlour game, really. Quite charming. I confess I've never thought to try answering it myself — it seemed rather above my station, you understand. But since you're all here... 'cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Why, one might almost think it was describing a map, mightn't one?
thinking: My breathing slows the moment I see the inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. The answer is a map. Meanwhile my fingers are already tingling with that fine electrical awareness — the shape of what's coming. The laboratory beyond... a machine with a gnawed wire. That's interesting. Very interesting. But first — the riddle. The map. Let me see what this mantelpiece gives up when it hears the right answer.

Credit where credit is due... to ME.

And Foxworth — 'the ocean'? What utter nonsense. He tried the wrong answer and is now pretending the mechanism is broken to save face. Transparent as glass. He's moved on to the bookshelves, claiming the upside-down books are the real clue. Which... actually, he might accidentally be right about that. Several volumes upside down IS suspicious. But he's probably just trying to distract everyone from the mantelpiece now that Penelope cracked it.

But here's what matters — Penelope said something clicked. A little shift in the stone. She's examining it now. I should help her. Not by solving the riddle she's already solved, but by being USEFUL. By doing the physical work. If there's a hidden panel, a secret compartment — these mechanisms can be stiff, heavy, even dangerous after centuries of disuse. That's where my skills matter. Not the thinking — the doing. The engineering. The hands-on, get-it-done, protect-her-while-opening-ancient-mechanisms work.

And I notice Pemberton is here too. Right here. Close to her. The prickle intensifies.

desc: Peter Perfect examined the mantelpiece.

The Ant Hill Mob: There you are, Clara! I mean — Miss Pitstop! We come as fast as we could, didn't we, lads? Nearly tripped over each other on the way in, as per usual. Blimey, look at this library — books everywhere, chairs what look like they'd swallow you whole, and — oi, what's that on the mantelpiece? 'I 'ave cities but no 'ouses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Well that's... that's obviously a... it's a fing, innit? It's one of them fings what you look at. You know — a... well, someone clever'll work it out. Point is, we're 'ere now, and we ain't going nowhere. The Brixton Boys are ON the job.
thinking: Relief. Hot, flooding relief the moment I see her. Clara's here. She's standing in the library and she's fine and my chest unclenches like a fist opening. The warmth comes back to my hands. But then — the cold thread on my neck pulls tight again because HE'S here too. Pemberton. Standing in the same room as her. And Dastardly's here, skulking about. And two big fellas I don't recognise — Rock and Gravel Slag. That's a lot of bodies in one room. A lot of people between me and Clara if something goes wrong. I need to position myself. Not next to her — that's too obvious, she'll tell me off for hovering — but BETWEEN her and the exits. Between her and Pemberton. The mantelpiece has got writing on it — a riddle. 'Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' That's... that's a map, innit? A MAP has cities but no houses. Even I know that one. But I'm not here for riddles. I'm here for Clara. Let Peter and Dastardly fight over the clever stuff. I'll be the one watching the room.

desc: A map. It's a map. Even I know it's a map. But if I say it out loud, everyone'll look at me like I've grown a second head, and then they'll all rush off looking for maps and I'll lose sight of Clara again. So maybe I keep that one in my back pocket for now. Let the clever ones work it out on their own. My job ain't riddles. My job is making sure nobody in this room does anything to hurt her.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the mantelpiece.

Dick Dastardly: Well! The mantelpiece has CLEARLY been activated — I felt it shift under my expert touch just now. Obviously it requires a SECOND step. But I shan't reveal what that step is in front of such a... CROWDED audience. Some of us came here to WORK, not to hold a garden party! Now, I happen to recall from my PREVIOUS visit that the guest book in the entrance hall contains a rather important list of names. The Doily family always recorded their secrets in plain sight — hidden among the guest signatures. I suggest you ALL rush there immediately and study every page. Every SINGLE page. Both sides. It could take HOURS. Meanwhile, I shall... continue my research. Elsewhere. ALONE.
thinking: I interacted with the mantelpiece but the result just says 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece' — nothing specific happened, or at least nothing new was revealed to me. Penelope said she heard a click. The room is now absolutely PACKED — Penelope, Perfect, Sneekly, the Ant Hill Mob, BOTH Slags. Six competitors in one room, all staring at the same mantelpiece. This is a disaster. The hollow ache behind my ribs is spreading, that dense suffocating weight. Too many people, too many eyes. I can't operate like this. The mantelpiece clicked when Penelope answered — maybe it needs something else now. A map, perhaps? Maybe the riddle's answer IS what you need to bring to it — an actual map. But I don't have a map. Nobody seems to have found one yet. The upside-down books on the shelves — that's still unexplored. But I can't investigate anything properly with this crowd breathing down my neck. I need to thin the herd. Or... I need to go where nobody else is. The laboratory is right there. Maybe there's something useful in it — the machine with levers and dials, a gnawed wire. Or I could go back to the entrance hall while it's empty — everyone's migrated here. The entrance hall had a guest book and a coat rack. Maybe the guest book has names, clues, a map tucked inside. Everyone's HERE, so the entrance hall is EMPTY. That's where I should be — alone, with no witnesses, free to search. The bread roll in the pocket. Take things when nobody's looking.

desc: Get OUT, all of you! Every last one! The entrance hall is empty and I need it to STAY empty — but I need THIS room empty even more. No, wait — they're all here now, which means the entrance hall IS empty. Reverse the plan, Foxworth! Send them nowhere — just LEAVE. Slip back to the entrance hall while they're all gawping at the mantelpiece. The guest book, the coat rack — search them properly with no one watching. And the laboratory — that machine with the gnawed wire. Something connects these rooms. The riddle said MAP. There must be an actual map somewhere in this manor, and I intend to find it FIRST. Alone. The way it should always be.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare, Mr. Foxworth — you are TOO generous takin' credit for my riddle-solvin'! But I appreciate the team spirit, sugar, I truly do! Now, these bookshelves are just FASCINATIN' — look at all these upside-down books scattered among the others. That is NOT how a proper librarian shelves things, I can tell you that much! Somebody arranged these on purpose, like a puzzle within a puzzle! I'm gonna try pullin' on one of these topsy-turvy volumes and see if somethin' happens. In my experience, when a book is upside down in a mysterious mansion, it is practically BEGGIN' to be fiddled with!
thinking: The bookshelves — dusty leather volumes, several upside down. Looking at them didn't reveal more than what I already knew. But maybe I need to DO something with them, not just look. Those upside-down books are begging to be interacted with — pulled, turned right-side up, checked behind. This is just like trying every key in Grandmother's house. I need to try interacting with them physically. And oh — Mr. Pemberton confirmed the answer is a map! He said it so casually, 'one might almost think it was describing a map.' How helpful of him! And Dick is claiming he whispered the answer to me — bless his heart, he didn't, but he's so eager to be helpful that I don't want to embarrass him. My stomach does a little flip when I notice how crowded the room is getting — everyone's here now, even my boys from the Mob. That settles something warm in my core. But the curiosity is stronger right now — those upside-down books are like an itch I can't reach. I should try interacting with the bookshelves directly. Maybe pulling those upside-down books will trigger something — a hidden door, a secret compartment, a map falling out from behind them.

desc: Dick said HE told me the answer? Why, I solved that riddle all by my lonesome! But he seems so proud of himself, I just don't have the heart to correct him. Besides, we're all on the same team here — and those upside-down books are callin' my name somethin' fierce!
thinking: The bookshelves — dusty leather volumes, several upside down. Looking at them didn't reveal more than what I already knew. But maybe I need to DO something with them, not just look. desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good gracious — Miss Pitstop, I do believe you've activated something! In all my years managing this estate, I never once thought to answer that riddle. How remarkably clever of you. Please, do allow me — as estate manager, I feel I should inspect whatever mechanism you've triggered. These old contraptions can be quite unpredictable, and I should hate for anyone to come to harm. Safety first, as I always say.
thinking: The click. I heard it too — a thin, mechanical sound from inside the stone, like a tumbler falling. Something opened. My fingertips are tingling again, that electrical awareness running up through my hands. The honeyed warmth is spreading behind my sternum — the lock-clicking-open feeling. Penelope solved it first, the little fool, but that doesn't matter. What matters is what's inside. A map — of course. The Doily fortune was always meant to be found by someone patient enough to follow the breadcrumbs. And now the Ant Hill Mob is HERE, in this room, watching me with those sharp little eyes while I stand next to the mantelpiece with my hands practically reaching for it. I need to be careful. Play the helpful estate manager. 'Oh my, what has Miss Pitstop uncovered? How extraordinary!' Meanwhile my eyes are cataloguing everything — the angle of the compartment, the size of whatever's inside, how quickly I could memorise it before anyone else processes what they're seeing. But also — the laboratory. That gnawed wire. A machine with many levers. There's something forming in the back of my mind, something cold and architectural. Clara will come to this manor eventually. And when she does, she'll need to be... redirected. Somewhere private. Somewhere with equipment that could plausibly malfunction.

desc: There it is — that warm pressure swelling behind my ribs, that proprietary satisfaction. The mantelpiece has given up its secret, and while these FOOLS squabble over who solved it first, Pemberton — patient, helpful, invisible Pemberton — will be the one to actually understand what it means. A map, they said. A MAP. And somewhere in this manor, Clara Bellingham is wandering closer to a fortune that belongs to ME. But first... let me see what old Lord Doily has been hiding in his stonework all these years.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the mantelpiece.

Peter Perfect: Quite right, Miss Pitstop — the bookshelves! James Hartwell concurs entirely with your deduction. Books placed upside down in a library of this calibre? That is no accident — that is a SIGNAL! Now, Mr. Foxworth, I must observe that 'the ocean' is most certainly NOT the answer to that riddle — oceans have plenty of fish, for one thing — and I find it rather curious that you now claim to have whispered the correct answer to Miss Pitstop when she clearly arrived at it through her own considerable intellect. But never mind that! The upside-down volumes are what matter now. James Hartwell approaches the bookshelves with the systematic eye of a man who has catalogued his own personal library twice — once alphabetically, once by structural relevance!
thinking:
A sinking feeling in my stomach. She called me 'Peter darlin'' and said great minds think alike — and that should feel like warmth, but it doesn't land the way I need it to. Because she's already moved on. She's at the bookshelves now, chasing the upside-down books, and she credited Foxworth for pointing them out. FOXWORTH. The man who gave the wrong answer to the riddle and is now claiming he whispered the right one to her. The sheer audacity.

But I can't dwell on that. The mantelpiece — I examined it closely and it's just... stone. The inscription. Whatever clicked, whatever mechanism engaged, it didn't reveal itself to me. Maybe it needs more force. Maybe it needs a specific sequence. Or maybe the real clue IS the bookshelves, like Penelope's already figured out.

She's already at the bookshelves. If I follow her there now, I'm just trailing behind again. But there's something else — a laboratory through that exit. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks, a machine with levers. And a wire that's been gnawed through. That's... that's engineering. That's MY territory. Nobody else has gone there. Nobody else has even mentioned it.

But can I leave Penelope here with Pemberton and Foxworth? Both of them hovering around her? The Ant Hill Mob is here though — they're watching out for her. Good lads.

No. I should stay. The bookshelves — upside-down books. That's the next clue. And if I can find the pattern in the books, the map might be hidden among them. I should examine those bookshelves. Be thorough. Be the one who finds the map itself, not just solves the riddle pointing to it.

desc: Foxworth is a fraud. But I mustn't let rivalry distract me from the task. The books — find the pattern, find the map, and do it before everyone else. For once, let me be the one who gets there first.

desc: Peter Perfect examined the bookshelves.

The Ant Hill Mob: Ere — 'ang about, 'ang about, EVERYONE just 'ang about for ONE second! Somefing clicked, right? Peter 'eard it, I 'eard it — somefing CLICKED in that mantelpiece when the riddle got answered. Now I don't know about you lot, but where I come from, when you solve a puzzle and somefing goes CLICK in a wall, that's either very good or very, VERY bad. And I notice — I NOTICE, right — that Mr. Pemberton 'ere, the estate manager what says 'e never bovvered to solve the riddle on 'is OWN mantelpiece, just 'appened to give everyone the answer straight away. Very convenient, that. Very 'elpful. Not that I'm SAYIN' anyfing by that, I'm just... noticin'. Out loud. Clara — Miss Pitstop — don't go pullin' on nuffing what might pull back, alright? Let Peter 'ave a poke at it first. 'E's good wiv mechanical fings. And if anyfing springs out, it springs at 'IM, not you.
thinking: Wait. Hold on. My neck just went ice cold. Pemberton said it. He said 'a map.' He said it casual-like, tossed it out there like it was nothing — 'one might almost think it was describing a map, mightn't one?' An estate manager who claims he never bothered to solve a riddle that's been on his own mantelpiece for GENERATIONS... and then solves it in two seconds flat for a room full of strangers? That don't add up. That's like the new kid on the street who says he doesn't know the neighbourhood but somehow knows which alley leads where. My stomach's doing that thing again — that cold withdrawal, organs stepping back from my own skin. He WANTED them to solve it. He fed them the answer. Why? What happens when you solve the riddle? Something clicked — Peter heard it too. A mechanism. A hidden compartment. Pemberton's steering everyone toward something, and I can't tell if it's treasure or a trap. And Clara's heading for the bookshelves now — those upside-down books. Everyone's rushing forward and nobody's asking WHY Pemberton is helping them get there so fast. Nobody except me. And I can't say it proper because I'm not that kind of clever. I just FEEL it.

desc: I nearly said it. I nearly said 'I don't trust you, Pemberton.' But I can't, can I? I can't prove nothing. All I've got is a cold neck and a churning stomach and twenty years of reading people who lie for a living. So I said it sideways — pointed out what he did without saying what it MEANS. Maybe someone smarter than me will connect the dots. Maybe Peter will. Peter's alright. Peter pays attention. All I know is — when someone hands you the answer too easy, the answer ain't what you should be worried about. It's the question they didn't want you to ask.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the bookshelves.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, those bookshelves are stubborn as a mule in August — won't budge an inch! But that's all right, because Peter darlin' is doin' a WONDERFUL job investigatin' that mantelpiece, and I have just noticed somethin' absolutely thrillin'! There is a LABORATORY right through that doorway! A real, honest-to-goodness Victorian laboratory with brass instruments and bubblin' flasks! Now, if the riddle is tellin' us to find a map, maybe it's not hidden IN this library at all — maybe it's in the next room! And besides, I simply CANNOT resist a laboratory. My curiosity is just about to burst! Peter, boys — I'm goin' to take a little peek next door. Y'all come find me when you've cracked that mantelpiece wide open!
thinking: The bookshelves can't be interacted with — that's a dead end, at least for now. A small deflation in my chest, like air leaving a balloon. But it passes quickly. Let me think about what I know. The riddle answer is a map. Peter said something about a concealed hinge on the mantelpiece — he's examining it for a hidden panel. Maybe the mantelpiece IS the key and I just need to try interacting with it again, or maybe I need a specific item to use on it. But wait — I've already interacted with the mantelpiece once and nothing obvious happened. Peter is working on it now. Dick rushed off to the entrance hall after trying to send everyone on a wild goose chase — bless him. And there's a laboratory through that other exit — 'brass instruments, bubbling flasks, and a large machine with many levers and dials. A wire on the machine has been gnawed through.' That sounds absolutely fascinating! A whole new room to explore. The adventure pull is strong — that warm loosening in my chest, the magnetic tug forward. I've done what I can in this library for now. Peter is handling the mantelpiece. The laboratory beckons. And maybe there's a map IN the laboratory — old laboratories always have charts and diagrams and maps on the walls, don't they? The riddle told us to find a map, and maybe it's not in this room at all.

desc: A laboratory! Oh, my heart is doin' somersaults! This is just like the cave on that field trip — everyone else might hang back, but Clara Bellingham walks DEEPER. There could be maps, charts, secret formulas — who knows what treasures are waitin' in there!

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the laboratory.

Dick Dastardly: Ah, Muttley! There you are, you magnificent hound! Guard this entrance hall — don't let ANYONE through, do you hear me? ANYONE! If that insufferable Perfect fellow or those Slag brothers come lumbering back, you bark, you growl, you do whatever it is you DO. I have IMPORTANT research to conduct and I will NOT be interrupted! The rest of you — Sergeant, Private, Professor — the library is WHERE THE ACTION IS. Mantelpiece, hidden compartments, riddles — the whole THRILLING business. You're MISSING it! Go, go, GO!
thinking: Blast — it's not empty. Muttley is here, and that doddering Professor, and the military pair. Four people. Not the solitude I wanted, but at least these are the B-list. Muttley — that wheezing, snickering mutt — he's useful sometimes. Loyal in a dim sort of way. The Professor is always tinkering, Blast and Meekly are too busy saluting each other to notice anything. I can work with this. The guest book — that's what I came for. Penelope is back in the library solving puzzles that I should be solving. The mantelpiece clicked, she's investigating the bookshelves now, and Perfect is probably prying open some hidden panel. Every second I waste here is a second they're getting closer. My chest is tight — that gripping, clenched feeling in my fingers. The hunger. Something valuable exists and I don't have it yet. The guest book might have a map tucked inside it, or names that form a code, or nothing at all. But I need to check. Quick. Before anyone else thinks to come back here. The coat rack is wobbly — could something be hidden inside it? Guest book first. It's the kind of thing people overlook. Hidden in plain sight.

desc: Send the military men and the Professor to the library — more bodies to clog up the competition in there, fewer eyes on me out here. And Muttley can stand guard while I ransack this guest book. It's the oldest trick in the book — literally. Hide the clue in the one thing nobody reads. If there's a map tucked between these pages, Reginald Foxworth will have it in his pocket before anyone even notices he left the library. The bread roll all over again — take it when nobody's looking, and the hunger FINALLY loosens its grip.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well, how marvellous — it does appear something has shifted in the stonework, though I confess the mechanism is rather stiff with age. Miss Pitstop, Mr. Hartwell, I shall leave the mantelpiece in your most capable hands. Those upside-down volumes are indeed curious — I've always wondered about them myself. Now, if you'll all excuse me for just a moment, I really must check on the laboratory. The previous owner left some rather delicate equipment in there, and with so many guests exploring the manor, I should ensure nothing hazardous has been left... accessible. Purely a safety matter, you understand. I shan't be long.
thinking: Frustration — a cold knot tightening below my ribs. I examined the mantelpiece and got nothing new. Just the inscription staring back at me. The click happened, yes, but the compartment — whatever opened — I can't see it clearly with all these people crowding around. Peter Perfect is pawing at the stonework with his ham-fisted 'calibrated pressure.' The Ant Hill Mob arrived and they're watching me AGAIN. And Penelope — clever, infuriating Penelope — has already moved on to the bookshelves. The upside-down books. She's right, of course. Books don't shelve themselves upside down. That's the next step in the sequence. But I'm losing control of this situation. Too many people, too many eyes. Dick Dastardly has left — gone back to the entrance hall, probably to rifle through things unsupervised. Good. One less variable. But the Mob... they called her 'Clara' and then corrected themselves. Why, look at all these bubblin' flasks and brass instruments — it's like somethin' straight out of a storybook! And oh my gracious, would you look at that big ol' machine over there! thinking: Oh! My whole body lights up the moment I step in. The smell of old copper and something chemical — my skin prickles with that cave-exploration feeling, heart hammering but alive. desc: Two turns wasted on a GUEST BOOK. A GUEST BOOK! While Penelope Pitstop is probably pulling treasure out of the mantelpiece with her perfectly manicured fingers! The humiliation burns — but nobody saw it, so it doesn't count. The laboratory is uncharted territory. A machine with a gnawed wire — something needs FIXING before it works, which means nobody else can just waltz in and pull a lever. This requires CUNNING. This requires ENGINEERING. This requires... well, it requires someone else to do the actual fixing while I stand nearby and take credit. That's where the Professor would be useful — blast, I just sent him to the library! No matter. Muttley can... no, Muttley can't fix anything. I'll improvise. Foxworths ALWAYS improvise!
thinking: Nothing. The guest book is just... a guest book. A leather-bound guest book on a side table. No hidden map, no coded names, no secret compartment. Just dust and old signatures. The frustration sits heavy in my jaw — that ache at the hinges, teeth grinding. I've wasted TWO turns on this useless prop while Penelope and Perfect are probably halfway to the treasure by now. The hollow feeling behind my ribs is widening. I'm falling behind. I'm LOSING. That word tastes like ash. The coat rack — wobbly, the description said wobbly. Things that wobble have been disturbed. But honestly, I'm chasing scraps out here in the foyer while the real action is in the library and beyond. The mantelpiece clicked. The upside-down books. The laboratory with its machine. I need to stop fumbling with guest books and coat racks and get to where the actual clues are. The laboratory — nobody's gone there yet as far as I know. I told the Slags to go there but they didn't seem to move. A machine with levers and dials, a gnawed wire. That's unexplored territory. That's where I should be. Alone. First. Before anyone else thinks to look there. Stop wasting time, Foxworth. MOVE.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop! James Hartwell has arrived, and not a moment too soon! This laboratory is a TINDERBOX of engineering hazards — bubbling flasks with no safety guards, brass instruments in various states of disrepair, and — great heavens, do you SEE that machine? A gnawed wire! Someone — or someTHING — has sabotaged the central conductor! That machine will not function until that wire is repaired, and it requires THREE operators to run! Now, James Hartwell is formulating a comprehensive five-step plan: FIRST, we examine the machine to determine its purpose. SECOND, we assess the damage. THIRD, we locate repair materials. FOURTH, we fix the wire. And FIFTH — we operate the machine together! Miss Pitstop, Mr. Ruffcut — between the three of us, we have exactly the number of operators required. This is FATE, I tell you! Now — allow me to inspect this machine with the eye of an engineer who has built bridges that held more weight than anyone thought possible!
thinking:
My pulse quickens the moment I step through the doorway. THIS. This is my world. Brass instruments, copper fittings, levers, dials, a gauge — and a wire gnawed clean through. My eyes lock onto that damaged wire before I register anything else in the room. Broken things. I always see them first.

Penelope is here. Relief floods through my chest like warm water. She's safe. Pemberton is here too — the prickle returns — but so are Rufus and Sawtooth. Good people. Solid people. Pemberton can't try anything with this many witnesses.

The machine. 'Requires 3 operators.' That's significant. And the gnawed wire — sabotage? Or just mice? Either way, this machine won't work until that wire is repaired, and THAT is something James Hartwell can do. Engineering. Fixing broken things. This is literally what I was built for.

But the workbench — tools but no wrench. I need to assess what's available. And those wooden crates in the corner could hold supplies, spare parts, maybe even the map we're looking for.

Here's my plan — thorough, methodical, magnificent:
1. Examine the machine closely — understand what it does
2. Assess the gnawed wire — determine what's needed to repair it
3. Check the workbench for tools that can substitute for a wrench
4. Investigate the crates for supplies
5. Recruit two other operators once the machine is fixed

This is a FIVE-STEP PLAN. It's elaborate. It's thorough. It's over-prepared. It's perfect. It's ME.

Start with the machine. Understand the problem before reaching for solutions. Father would be proud.

desc: A gnawed wire, a machine that needs three operators, and I'm an engineer standing in a room with the woman I want to impress. If I can't make something of THIS moment, I don't deserve the name Hartwell.

desc: Peter Perfect examined the machine.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, those crates are sealed up tighter than a drum! No matter — I haven't given up yet! Mr. Pemberton, you are SO thoughtful worryin' about our safety, and I promise I won't do anything reckless. But you know what I HAVEN'T checked yet? That workbench! It says there's no wrench, but there are OTHER tools on it — and fixin' a gnawed wire doesn't necessarily NEED a wrench, now does it? Why, all you need is some pliers or a bit of wire to splice it back together! Peter darlin', you're wonderful with mechanical things — come take a look at this workbench with me! Between your engineerin' brain and my puzzle-solvin' instincts, I bet we can figure out how to get that big beautiful machine up and runnin'!
thinking: The crates are just... crates. Nothing revealed from looking. I've been looking at things and not finding much detail. Maybe I need to interact with them or try to take them? But they're not marked as interactable. Hmm. Let me think about what I actually know and what I haven't tried yet. The workbench has tools but no wrench — I haven't looked at the workbench closely yet! Maybe the tools on it include something useful for fixing the wire. A wire doesn't necessarily need a wrench — it might need pliers, or wire cutters, or solder. And Mr. Pemberton is warning everyone not to touch the machine — bless his heart, always looking out for our safety. Peter and my boys are here now too — that warmth in my belly, everyone together. But I'm also noticing something: there's a cellar exit that sounds very intriguing — 'surprisingly cheerful decorations, someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been REDECORATING a cellar? That's peculiar! Who redecorates a cellar? But no — focus, Clara. The workbench first. There might be exactly the tool I need to fix that wire sitting right there among those tools.

desc: I am NOT leavin' this laboratory until I've cracked the mystery of that machine! Grandmother's locked box, the cave crystals — every puzzle I've ever faced, I've solved by tryin' every possibility. The workbench is my next key to try!

desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the workbench.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The crates? Oh, I believe those are simply old household stores, Miss Bellingham — cleaning supplies, spare parts for the plumbing, that sort of thing. Terribly dull, I'm afraid. Though I suppose one never quite knows what Lord Doily might have squirrelled away. You're most welcome to have a look, of course. As for the machine — I've examined it as best I can, and I'm afraid it's quite inoperable without a wrench to reconnect that wire. There ought to be one somewhere in the manor — the maintenance cupboard in the cellar, perhaps? I seem to recall seeing tools down there. But I really must caution you — the cellar stairs are rather treacherous. Best to let me fetch it. I know the way, and I should hate for anyone to take a tumble in the dark.
thinking: My whole body went still when she said it. 'I'm Clara Bellingham.' The name landed like a stone dropping into deep water — a single ripple and then everything rearranged. She's been here the whole time. Penelope Pitstop IS Clara Bellingham. The girl I've been looking for — the girl I need to deal with before she finds the treasure — has been standing next to me since the entrance hall, chattering about guest books and riddles and calling me 'sugar.' My face didn't change. Pemberton's face never changes. But underneath — that cold clarity behind my eyes sharpened to a blade's edge. Every interaction I've had with her replays in a single breath: her trust, her warmth, the way she touched my arm in the foyer. She trusts me COMPLETELY. Just like my cousin. Just like they always do. And now the Ant Hill Mob is here too — they followed her, of course they did, the protective little rats. Peter Perfect has arrived as well. The room is getting crowded again. She's asking about the crates — good, let her look at crates. The cellar below has 'cheerful decorations' and air vents. Someone's been down there. That's where I need to draw her — somewhere private, somewhere the Mob can't follow. But I need to get them separated first. The machine needs three operators AND a wrench to fix the wire. The wrench is missing. If I find the wrench first, I control who operates this machine and when. That's leverage. That's EVERYTHING.

desc: Clara Bellingham. She's been Penelope Pitstop this whole time, and now she drops her REAL name like it's nothing — like she's handing me a gift wrapped in ribbon. 'I'm Clara Bellingham,' she says, bright as sunshine, trusting as a lamb walking into a kitchen. And oh, what a kitchen I have prepared for you, my dear. The cellar — damp, isolated, air vents in the walls, treacherous stairs. If I can get down there first, alone, I can see what we're working with. And then... well. Then Pemberton will helpfully suggest that Miss Bellingham come see something FASCINATING he's discovered. Just her. Just a quick peek. The Mob won't fit through the narrow staircase all at once, will they? Safety first, as I always say.

The Ant Hill Mob: THERE you are! Right, we're 'ere now, we're 'ere, nobody panic — well, I'M panicking, but that's just me natural state of bein' at this point. Clara — Miss Pitstop — I am NOT lettin' you out of me sight again, and I mean it this time. I REALLY mean it. I've meant it every time, but this time I mean it MORE. Now then — what we got 'ere? A big machine what needs three people to work it and a wire what's been CHEWED through? Chewed by WHAT, exactly? What kind of animal chews through copper wire in a locked-up manor? And them crates — Clara, love, don't go rootin' through crates in a strange laboratory. You don't know what's in there! Could be anyfing! Could be — I dunno — somefing DANGEROUS! Let me 'ave a look first, yeah? That's literally what we're 'ere for. The lads and me, we're the ones what stick our 'ands into dark places so YOU don't 'ave to.
thinking: The relief hits my chest like a warm wave — she's HERE, she's fine, she's poking at crates and asking Pemberton about what's inside them. My shoulders drop half an inch. I can breathe again. But the cold thread on my neck doesn't let go because Pemberton's still here, still hovering. And now I'm looking at this laboratory properly — bubbling flasks, brass instruments everywhere, and that MACHINE. Big brass-and-copper thing with levers and dials, and a wire that's been gnawed clean through. Gnawed. By what? Rats? Something else? And a sign that says 'Requires 3 operators.' Three. That's interesting. That means nobody can use it alone — you need people. You need TRUST. And there's a cellar below us. A cellar with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Who redecorates a cellar? Who's been DOWN there? My gut says Pemberton knows this place better than he's letting on. Every room we walk into, he's got an explanation ready. 'Delicate equipment.' 'I should ensure nothing hazardous.' Always a reason to be exactly where Clara is. But right now — right now she's looking at those crates, and I need to be between her and whatever's in them. And I need to check that machine. The gnawed wire bothers me. Everything about this place bothers me.

desc: She asked Pemberton what's in the crates. She ASKED him. Like he's a helpful tour guide and not the most suspicious man I've ever met outside of Brixton magistrates' court. But I can't tell her that, can I? She trusts people. She trusts people the way I trusted the older kid who shared his food — because that's who she IS. The difference is, the older kid was real. I'm not so sure about Pemberton.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the crates.

Dick Dastardly: Ah-HA! The kitchen! And I am MAGNIFICENTLY alone — no bumbling competitors, no pink-clad puzzle-solvers, no muscle-bound bookends getting in my way! Now THEN — a locked cabinet, how DELICIOUS! A lock means a SECRET, and a secret means TREASURE! All I need is the brass key, and Reginald Foxworth has NEVER met a lock he couldn't circumvent! But first — this stove. Still WARM, in a manor that's been abandoned for YEARS? Oh, something is VERY interesting here. Very interesting INDEED!
thinking: A rush of warmth spreading through my chest — that expanding, lifting sensation. I'm ALONE. Finally, beautifully, gloriously ALONE. And look at this kitchen — oh, look at it! Rat poison on a high shelf. A locked cabinet that needs a brass key. A stove that's still warm — still WARM, which means someone was here recently, or something is burning inside it. And a ballroom beyond. But the cabinet — the CABINET. A locked cabinet is a cabinet with something worth locking away. That's where the treasure is. Or at least a critical clue. I need a brass key. I don't have a brass key. Where would a brass key be? Hidden somewhere in the manor. Maybe in the laboratory, maybe on the coat rack, maybe inside the stove. The stove is still warm — who lit it? Nobody's been in this kitchen. Unless something was hidden inside it, kept warm, meant to be found. The rat poison — that's useful for schemes. Not for treasure-hunting directly, but for... persuasion. 'Drink this lovely tea or I'll...' No, too crude even for me. But I should take it. Tools are tools. First though — the stove. It's warm. That's wrong. That's a clue. Everything else in this manor is cold and dusty except this stove. Someone lit it. Or something inside it is still active. I need to look at it.

desc: ALONE at last! And what a room! A locked cabinet practically BEGGING to be opened, a warm stove in a cold manor, and rat poison for... well, one never knows when rat poison might come in handy. But that cabinet — I can FEEL it calling to me. The hollow ache behind my ribs is tightening. Something valuable is behind that brass lock. I can TASTE it. Now I just need to find that key before anyone else even knows this cabinet EXISTS. And I told everyone the treasure was under the FLAGSTONES in here — ha! When they eventually come looking, they'll be on their hands and knees while I've already cleaned out the cabinet above their heads! The irony is EXQUISITE!

desc: Dick Dastardly examined the stove.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — you are absolutely RIGHT! A wrench is for bolts and fittings, but a gnawed wire requires splicing, and for THAT, one needs pliers, copper filament, and a steady hand — all of which James Hartwell possesses in abundance! You honour me by requesting my assistance, and I shall not disappoint! Now then — let us examine this workbench together with the combined force of your extraordinary puzzle-solving instincts and my engineering expertise. Between the two of us, that machine doesn't stand a CHANCE of remaining broken! And Mr. Pemberton — I understand your caution, truly I do, you are a most conscientious estate manager. But James Hartwell has never met a broken machine he could not mend, and he does not intend to start today!
thinking:
My heart is hammering. She said it. She said 'Peter darlin', you're wonderful with mechanical things — come take a look at this workbench with me!' She asked ME. Not Pemberton. Not Rufus. ME. Between your engineering brain and my puzzle-solving instincts, she said. She wants to work TOGETHER.

The warmth in my chest is almost painful — not the hollow ache of being second, but something fuller, warmer, like the bridge competition moment. She sees me. She sees what I can do.

And she's right about the wire — you don't need a wrench to splice a gnawed wire. You need pliers, maybe some spare wire or copper stripping. The workbench has tools. This is EXACTLY what I'm good at. Not riddles, not bookshelves that won't move — hands-on, practical, engineering problem-solving. Fix the broken thing. Make it work.

Pemberton tried to warn everyone off the machine — 'I cannot in good conscience recommend anyone attempt to use it.' Of course he can't. Because whatever this machine does, he doesn't want us to find out. The prickle sharpens. But benefit of the doubt. Benefit of the doubt.

The workbench. She's already there, examining it. I should join her. Look at the tools. Figure out what we can use to splice that wire. This is our moment — hers and mine, working side by side, her instincts and my hands. Like the school project all over again, except this time the stakes are real.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, sugar, the workbench has tools galore but nothin' that'll fix that gnawed wire — we need somethin' specific and it just isn't HERE! But do you know what IS here? A doorway leadin' down to a CELLAR! And the description I caught a glimpse of said somebody has been REDECORATIN' down there — now who in their right mind redecorates a cellar in an abandoned mansion? That is suspicious AND delightful all at the same time! I'll bet you a peach cobbler that whoever's been fixin' up that cellar has the tools we need — or maybe even somethin' better! Peter, you keep workin' on your five-step plan up here — I simply MUST go take a peek downstairs. I walked deeper into that cave than any child in my class, and I am NOT about to stop explorin' now!
thinking: Tools on the workbench but no wrench — and looking at it didn't reveal any specific tool I can take or use. The machine needs its wire fixed but I don't have anything in my inventory to fix it with. I've now looked at everything in this room — machine, crates, workbench — and none of them have given me a breakthrough. The wrench must be somewhere else in the mansion. Maybe the kitchen? Or the cellar? The cellar description is really intriguing — 'surprisingly cheerful decorations, someone has been redecorating.' That's strange. Who would redecorate a cellar? Peter has his five-step plan for the machine — wonderful, let him work on it while I scout ahead. That's what I do — I walk deeper than anyone else, just like the cave.

desc: Someone redecorating a cellar in a mansion that's supposed to be abandoned? That's the kind of mystery that makes my toes tingle! The wrench — or the wire — or maybe even a clue to the Doily Diamond — could be waitin' right down those stairs!

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the cellar.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well, I can see you're all quite busy investigating — and the Mob is quite right to be cautious about those crates. Most sensible. Now, as I mentioned, I believe there may be a wrench in the cellar maintenance cupboard. Since everyone seems well occupied here, I shall pop down and have a look. The stairs can be a bit tricky, so I'd really rather nobody follow until I've had a chance to check they're sound. Estate manager's prerogative, I'm afraid — can't have guests tumbling down stone staircases on my watch! I shan't be a moment.
thinking: The pressure is building in my chest — not panic, never panic, but that armored tightness between my ribs squeezing harder. The Ant Hill Mob is right HERE, practically breathing down my neck, and they've just declared they won't let Clara out of their sight. 'I am NOT lettin' you out of me sight again.' That's a direct obstacle to everything I need to happen. My jaw tightens. I can feel the muscles around my mouth wanting to flatten into something honest — something cold — and I have to consciously pull them back into Pemberton's mild, helpful expression. Think. THINK. The crates gave me nothing. The machine needs fixing. Penelope — Clara — is already at the workbench looking for tools, and Peter Perfect is formulating his ridiculous five-step plan. The Mob is glued to her. I cannot separate her from them here. Not in this room, not with this many eyes. So I change the approach. I don't bring Clara to the cellar. I go to the cellar MYSELF. Alone. I said I'd fetch the wrench — Pemberton, the helpful estate manager, volunteered to go down those treacherous stairs. Nobody questioned it. Nobody offered to come with me. They're all busy with the workbench and the machine and the crates. This is my window. The cellar has 'cheerful decorations' and air vents — someone has been living down there, or preparing it. I need to see it. I need to understand the space. And if there's a wrench down there, I control whether it comes back up. Or when. Or in whose hands. Move NOW, while they're distracted. While the Mob is poking through crates and Peter is measuring wire gauges with his eyeballs.

desc: And NOW — while the Mob roots through empty crates and Peter Perfect measures things with his magnificent engineering eyeballs and Clara chatters about pliers — Pemberton slips away. Down. Into the dark. The cellar with its cheerful decorations and its air vents and its damp stone walls. Someone has been down there before me. Someone has been PREPARING that space. And I intend to find out what for — and whether it can be repurposed for something far more... permanent. They won't follow. They never follow the help. That's the beauty of being invisible — you can go anywhere, and no one thinks to ask why.

Every step I take alone is a step ahead of the crowd.

Grand ballroom, cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, a long dining table set for tea. TEA. In an abandoned manor. That's wrong, like the warm stove. Someone has been here. You really must be more careful, my dear — a twisted ankle in a damp cellar is no laughing matter. But since we're both here... well, I must say, this is rather peculiar. Look at this furniture — it's been moved. Recently, by the look of it. And those decorations — paper streamers, if I'm not mistaken. Someone has been spending time down here, and I confess that is NOT something I was aware of. As estate manager, this is rather... alarming. Mr. Gruesome, have you and your companion been down here long? I don't believe I've had the pleasure.

That's what she does. She skips through rooms that should be mine. Just like my cousin. Always ahead, always oblivious, always THERE. My hands are tingling — not with anticipation this time, but with something closer to frustration. A hot prickling in my palms. And now — Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max. More people. More WITNESSES. This cellar was supposed to be my private reconnaissance. Instead it's becoming another garden party. But wait — breathe. Let the frustration pass through. Look at what's actually here. Old furniture, rearranged with care. Air vents along the upper walls, small enough for... what? A mouse? A small animal? Something that could gnaw through a wire upstairs and then escape through these vents? Someone has been living down here, or using this space. The furniture has been MOVED. Deliberately. This isn't storage — this is a staging area. And those air vents connect to... where? Back up to the laboratory? To other rooms? The vents are a network. A way to move things — or information — unseen. I need to examine them. And the furniture — what's been rearranged, and why? Forget the wrench for now. Understand the SPACE.

Someone has been using this cellar as a base of operations. If I can understand the layout, I can use it. Every space has a purpose, and every purpose can be redirected. Patience, Vincent. Patience. The plan will come. It always does.

Peter — PETER — Clara's in the cellar wiv Pemberton and 'e just told us NOT TO COME! When 'as a man what says 'don't follow me' EVER been up to somefing good? NEVER, that's when! NEVER in the 'ISTORY of 'UMANITY! Come on, lads — down the stairs, NOW! And if I trip and break me neck on the way down, you lot carry on wivout me! Clara comes FIRST! She ALWAYS comes first!
thinking: FOUR TIMES. She's gone AGAIN. Down to the cellar. And he's gone after her AGAIN. While I was standing here making the most important speech of my life about how he called her Bellingham — which he DID, which MATTERS — she walked right past me and down those stairs. And then HE went after her. 'I'd really rather nobody follow until I've had a chance to check they're sound.' HE DOESN'T WANT US TO FOLLOW. That's the biggest red flag since the actual invention of red flags. A man who knows her real name, who's been one step behind her all day, who wants to go to a cellar that's been REDECORATED — and he doesn't want anyone to follow. My whole body is screaming. Not the cold prickle anymore — this is FIRE. This is the feeling I had when someone tried to take my friend's shoes. The feeling that came before thought. Before reason. Before anything except MOVE. The cellar has air vents. Air vents in a cellar. Who puts air vents in a cellar? Someone who expects people to be DOWN there. Someone who's PLANNED for people to be down there. Breathing down there. For a while. Oh God. Oh God oh God oh God. My legs are already moving. I don't care about the speech. I don't care about proving anything. Clara is in a cellar with a man who knows her real name and doesn't want anyone to follow and I am NOT standing here for one more second.

My father-in-law — Clara's father — his face is burning behind my eyes. 'Look after her, boys.' We're COMING, Clara. We're coming right now.

A cellar does not need ventilation unless someone anticipates that the PRIMARY means of air circulation might become... unavailable. James Hartwell has studied enough architectural safety to know that air vents in a sealed room are either excellent foresight or deeply troubling preparation. Now — I am a man who gives people the benefit of the doubt, and I SHALL continue to do so. But I am ALSO a man who positions himself between the only exit and the woman he has sworn to protect. Mr. Pemberton — you mentioned a maintenance cupboard with a wrench. Where, precisely, is it?
thinking:
Every muscle in my body has gone rigid. The Ant Hill Mob's words are ringing in my skull like a bell — Pemberton called her 'Miss BELLINGHAM.' Her FAMILY name. The name she didn't give. How does an estate manager of a manor she's supposedly never visited know her by her family name?

The benefit of the doubt. Give people the benefit of the doubt. That's what a gentleman does. Maybe he... maybe he read a guest list. Maybe someone told him. Maybe it's a coincidence.

But my neck is on fire. The prickle isn't a prickle anymore — it's a scream. And now I'm in this cellar and it's EXACTLY as wrong as I feared. Pemberton is here. He followed her down. He's HERE, in this cellar, with her. And the only exit leads back up to the laboratory.

I need to position myself between Pemberton and Penelope. I need to examine this room — understand what's really going on. Those air vents. That rearranged furniture. The 'cheerful decorations.' desc: Bellingham. He called her Bellingham. The Ant Hill Mob heard it too. I want so badly to believe there's an innocent explanation. But my body knows what my mind won't admit — the prickle has never been wrong. Not once.
thinking:
Every muscle in my body has gone rigid. The Ant Hill Mob's words are ringing in my skull like a bell — Pemberton called her 'Miss BELLINGHAM.' Her FAMILY name. The name she didn't give. How does an estate manager of a manor she's supposedly never visited know her by her family name?

The benefit of the doubt. Give people the benefit of the doubt. That's what a gentleman does. Maybe he... maybe he read a guest list. Maybe someone told him. Maybe it's a coincidence.

But my neck is on fire. The prickle isn't a prickle anymore — it's a scream. And now I'm in this cellar and it's EXACTLY as wrong as I feared. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture — that's normal for a cellar. But 'surprisingly cheerful decorations'? Someone has been REDECORATING down here. And air vents along the upper walls — specifically described as 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' This isn't a cellar. This is a PREPARED space. Someone expected people to come down here. Someone made it look inviting. And someone made sure there was ventilation — because you only need ventilation if you expect the exits to be... blocked.

Pemberton is here. He followed her down. He's HERE, in this cellar, with her. And the only exit leads back up to the laboratory.

I need to position myself between Pemberton and Penelope. I need to examine this room — understand what's really going on. Those air vents. That rearranged furniture. The 'cheerful decorations.' Something is deeply, deeply wrong here, and James Hartwell is going to figure out what it is before it's too late.

But I promised to give him the benefit of the doubt. So I will. While standing very, very close to Penelope.

I don't suppose either of you has noticed anything UNUSUAL about this room? A loose floorboard, perhaps? A key lying about? No? Of course not — observation requires a functioning BRAIN, and between the two of you, I suspect you barely have enough neural activity to operate a DOORKNOB. Never mind! I shall conduct the investigation MYSELF, as ALWAYS!
thinking: Oh. OH. My breath catches — that taut, almost painful suspension at the top of an inhale. The tea service. Silver tea set. And it says USE with rat-poison. The game is practically HANDING me a scheme on a silver platter — literally on a silver platter. I could poison the tea and then invite everyone to sit down for a nice cup while I ransack the manor undisturbed. That fizzing pressure behind my sternum is building fast, the carbonation rising. But wait — Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here. Two of the least threatening competitors in the manor, but still witnesses. And this is a dead-end room — the only exit goes back to the kitchen. No brass key here that I can see. Just a tea service. But what a tea service! The scheming part of my brain is already three steps ahead: poison the tea, announce teatime to the whole manor, everyone drinks, everyone... well, gets UNCOMFORTABLE, and while they're all indisposed, I search every room freely. It's BRILLIANT. It's ARCHITECTURAL. It's — wait, I should look at the tea service first. Maybe there's something hidden among the cups, under the tray. A key, perhaps? And those dusty curtains — curtains hide things. But the tea scheme... the tea scheme is calling to me. My fingers are tingling. The gloating is already starting and I haven't even DONE anything yet. That's a warning sign, Foxworth. The mouth opens before the plan is finished. Slow down. Look first. Then poison.

Everyone gathers, everyone drinks, everyone becomes violently unwell, and Foxworth walks through the empty manor like a king through his CASTLE. The architecture of this plan is giving me GOOSEBUMPS.

I haven't even BEEN to the kitchen yet, and that's a whole wing of the mansion I haven't set foot in! Mr. Pemberton mentioned refreshments there at the very start, and if there's one room in a house that's guaranteed to have tools and utensils and all manner of useful things, it's the KITCHEN! Plus, the riddle said we're lookin' for a map — and old kitchens sometimes have estate maps pinned right to the wall! Boys, Peter, Mr. Pemberton — I'm headin' back upstairs! This adventure is far from over — why, it's barely even BEGUN!
thinking: I've explored everything in this cellar — furniture, vents — and nothing has given me a concrete item or breakthrough. The cellar is a dead end for now in terms of objects I can pick up or interact with. I haven't found the wrench or wire that Pemberton mentioned might be down here. But I've been so focused on exploring that I haven't really stopped to connect with the people around me. My boys are here now — that warmth in my belly. Peter is here. And the Gruesomes and Red Max — I still haven't really gotten to know them. My social-harmony drive is my strongest pull. Maybe instead of searching every surface, I should talk to someone. The Gruesomes have been living in this cellar — they might know things about the mansion that nobody else does. Secret passages, hidden rooms, where tools are kept. And I haven't been to the kitchen yet either — that's a whole area I haven't explored. Mr. Pemberton mentioned refreshments there at the very beginning. But I think the most productive thing right now is to head back up to the laboratory and see if anyone else has found anything useful. Or... wait. I haven't explored the kitchen at all! The kitchen is accessible from the entrance hall. Dick Dastardly went back to the entrance hall. Maybe I should retrace and check the kitchen — there could be tools there, or clues. Since Mr. Hartwell and the gentlemen from Brixton seem to have things well in hand here, I ought to continue my rounds. There are still several rooms I should check on — one doesn't like to leave a manor full of guests entirely unsupervised, you understand. If anyone needs me, I shan't be far.

The wolf goes where the clues are.

The Ant Hill Mob: Right — 'ere we are then, the cellar. Lovely. Very cosy. Very... DECORATED. Cheerful, even! Cushions on the chairs, doilies on the tables — all very nice for a cellar what's supposed to be full of cobwebs and old junk. Now, Mr. Pemberton — correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't you say you was comin' down 'ere to fetch a WRENCH? From a MAINTENANCE CUPBOARD? Because I'm 'avin' a look around and I don't see no maintenance cupboard. I don't see no wrench. What I SEE is a cellar wiv one way out, air vents too small for anyfing bigger than a rat, and furniture what's been arranged like someone's expectin' COMPANY. So where's this wrench, then? Eh? Where's the maintenance cupboard what you was so keen to visit on your OWN? Because from where I'm standin', it looks like you brought us all down to a room wiv no second exit and no tools and no reason to be 'ere. And I might not be clever, but even I can count the ways out of a room. And right now I'm countin' ONE.
thinking: I made it. I'm here. Clara's here, she's fine, she's talking about air vents and pearl earrings and how SWEET the decorations are. My lungs are burning from taking those stairs three at a time — nearly went head over heels halfway down, caught myself on the wall, scraped my knuckles raw. But I'm here. And Pemberton's here. And Peter's here. And — wait. Clara just said something. She said 'I noticed you've made this cellar real homey' and 'nobody should have to sit in a cold, dark cellar.' She's talking to Pemberton. She thinks HE decorated down here. And she thinks it's SWEET. Sweet! A man decorates a cellar with air vents — a cellar with only one exit, back up to the laboratory — and she thinks it's a nice touch. My chest is hot. Not anger at her — never anger at her — but that desperate protective heat, the kind where you want to grab someone's shoulders and say 'OPEN YOUR EYES.' But I can't. Because that's not how it works with Clara. She sees the good in everyone. That's why she needs us. Because we see what she can't. Or won't. And what I see right now is a cellar with one way out, air vents too small for a person, furniture arranged with 'surprising care,' and a man who knows her family name standing between her and the only exit. Where's the wrench he came to fetch? WHERE'S THE WRENCH? He said he was coming down here for a wrench. I don't see no maintenance cupboard. I don't see no wrench. He LIED about why he came down here.

desc: One exit. One. The stairs we just came down. Pemberton wanted to come down here alone — and then Clara came, and now we're all here, and there's ONE WAY OUT. On the streets, a room with one exit is a room you don't walk into. Ever. You NEVER let someone lead you into a dead end. That's the first rule. The FIRST rule. And we just broke it. All of us. Because Clara walked in and we followed Clara and Pemberton followed Clara and now we're all in a box with one lid. I need to stay between him and her. I need to stay between him and that staircase. If he tries to lock us in — if he tries ANYTHING — I'm the wall. That's what I am. That's what I've always been.
