Peter Perfect: Ah — the vents! Miss Pitstop, your deduction is BRILLIANT as always — these vents clearly form a network connecting the cellar to the laboratory above, which explains how our wire-gnawing culprit has been travelling between floors! Now then — Mr. Pemberton, I note with GREAT interest that you claim to be unaware of the redecorations in your own cellar. An estate manager who knows the manor's every corridor and floorboard — who knows, for instance, the family names of guests he has never met — yet somehow failed to notice someone rearranging furniture and hanging streamers directly below his feet? James Hartwell gives people the benefit of the doubt, and he ALWAYS will. But James Hartwell also examines the evidence. And that furniture — rearranged with such CARE — may conceal the very maintenance cupboard you mentioned. Allow me to investigate!
thinking:
My jaw is clenching. He did it AGAIN. 'Miss Bellingham.' Right there, in front of everyone. The Ant Hill Mob caught it upstairs and now Pemberton's done it a second time — casually, naturally, as if that's the name he's always known her by. And he's examining the air vents. Why? What does an estate manager need to know about air vents in his own cellar?

Penelope noticed the vents connect to the laboratory — she's right, that's how the creature that gnawed the wire has been moving around. Smart. Always smart. But she's also being kind to the Gruesomes, asking if they've been redecorating. She sees people, not threats. That's her gift. Mine is seeing threats, not people.

The furniture. Rearranged with care. Pemberton claims he didn't know about this. An estate manager who knows every corridor, every creaking floorboard, who knows her FAMILY NAME — but doesn't know someone's been redecorating his own cellar? The contradictions are stacking up.

But I promised. Benefit of the doubt. I can protect her without accusing him. I can position myself, stay alert, keep the exit clear. That's what a gentleman does — he acts on instinct while speaking with grace.

The furniture — that's what I should look at next. Something rearranged with surprising care in a cellar might hide something. A cupboard, a hatch, a passage. And if there IS a wrench hidden in a maintenance cupboard down here, I want to find it. Fix the machine, operate it with Penelope, prove my worth. But protection first. Always protection first.

The Ant Hill Mob just arrived too. Good. More eyes on Pemberton.

And Vincent Marsh — patient, invisible, MAGNIFICENT Vincent Marsh — will have the library entirely to himself. Those upside-down books have been whispering to me since I first walked in, and now, FINALLY, I shall hear what they have to say.

Just pass through the laboratory like a shadow and get to those bookshelves before anyone else thinks to come back.

Penelope Pitstop: Don't mind me, just passin' through on my way to the kitchen! I've been explorin' this mansion like a bee in a flower garden, and the kitchen is the ONE room I haven't visited yet! If there's a wrench or a map or ANY kind of clue to the Doily Diamond, that's where it'll be — mark my words!
thinking: Just passing through the library on my way to the kitchen. My feet know the way — library to entrance hall, entrance hall to kitchen. The pull forward is strong, that magnetic tug in my chest toward unexplored territory. I notice Mr. Pemberton is right behind me again — he's been following me from room to room. How devoted! He really takes his job as estate manager seriously. The Slag brothers are here too. No need to linger — the kitchen awaits!

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.

Peter Perfect: The furniture reveals nothing — and THAT is itself revealing! No maintenance cupboard, no wrench, no purpose for being down here whatsoever! The Ant Hill Mob is RIGHT — this cellar has one exit, no tools, and has been prepared as though someone expected GUESTS! And now Mr. Pemberton has gone back upstairs — claiming he was mistaken about the cellar — and Miss Pitstop has gone up too, heading for the kitchen ALONE! Gentlemen — we have been separated from her by a wild goose chase, and James Hartwell does NOT intend to remain separated one moment longer! Everyone — UPSTAIRS! Miss Pitstop is heading to the kitchen, and wherever she goes, James Hartwell follows! That is not a choice — that is a LAW OF NATURE!
thinking:
Ice in my veins. She's gone again — back upstairs to the laboratory, heading for the kitchen. And Pemberton went up too. 'I must have been thinking of a different cellar.' A DIFFERENT cellar. There is no maintenance cupboard. There never WAS a maintenance cupboard. He lured us down here — to a room with ONE exit, air vents too small for anything but a rodent, and furniture arranged like someone was expecting company. The Ant Hill Mob saw it. They counted the exits. ONE.

And now Pemberton is loose upstairs while Penelope is heading to the kitchen alone. He's already up there. She's already up there. And I'm down HERE, in this dead-end cellar, examining furniture that reveals nothing.

The benefit of the doubt is crumbling. Not gone — I'm still a gentleman, I still believe the best in people — but the facts are screaming now. He knew her family name. He tried to come down here alone. There was no wrench. He's always one step ahead of her, one room behind, always positioning, always offering to 'check' things, always trying to get her isolated.

I need to get back upstairs. NOW. She's heading to the kitchen through the entrance hall, and Pemberton is somewhere between here and there. The Ant Hill Mob is still down here with me — they need to come too. Every second I spend in this cellar is a second she's without protection.

Move. NOW. Stop examining things and MOVE.

desc: There was no wrench. There was never any wrench. He wanted us down here. Away from her. And I fell for it — I followed the furniture instead of following HER. Father, forgive your fool of a son. But this fool is fast on his feet when it counts.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the laboratory.

The Ant Hill Mob: Peter! PETER! They've both gone! Clara's gone up to the kitchen and Pemberton's slithered off somewhere — 'continuing 'is rounds,' 'e says! And did you 'EAR 'im? 'I must 'ave been finking of a DIFFERENT cellar!' A different cellar! There IS no different cellar! 'E LIED, Peter! 'E lied about the wrench, 'e lied about the maintenance cupboard, 'e knew Clara's real name before anyone told 'im, and now 'e's — 'e's just GONE, slippery as an eel in a bucket of grease! And Clara's off to the kitchen on 'er own talkin' about maps and refreshments like she ain't just been led into a dead-end room by a man who makes fings up! I can't — Peter, I NEED you to 'elp me 'ere. You're clever. You use big words. You talk about architecture and safety and all that. TELL me I'm not mad. Tell me you see it too. Because I see it and I FEEL it but every time I try to explain it, it comes out like — like THIS. Like me, rantin' in a cellar. But I ain't WRONG, Peter. I ain't wrong. Now come ON — we need to get to that kitchen before 'e does somefing we can't undo!
thinking: He admitted it. He ADMITTED it. 'There doesn't appear to be a maintenance cupboard down here after all. My apologies — I must have been thinking of a different cellar.' A DIFFERENT CELLAR. He lied about why he came down here and then just... walked away. Like it was nothing. Like lying about a maintenance cupboard in a dead-end room is just a little mix-up, happens to everyone, terribly sorry. And now he's gone back up. And CLARA'S gone back up too — headed to the kitchen. They're both up there and I'm down HERE. AGAIN. Standing in an empty cellar examining furniture while the woman I'm supposed to protect is headed to another room with the man who just PROVED he's a liar. My body knows it before my brain catches up — that hook under my ribs, pulling me forward. That thickness in my throat. Every tendon remembering. I called him out on the Bellingham thing. I called him out on the missing wrench. And he just... slipped away. Smooth. Like water. Like the new kid who smiled too easy and stole from the stash. He doesn't fight, he doesn't argue — he just repositions. And every time he repositions, he ends up near Clara. Peter noticed the air vents too — Peter's catching on. Good. I need Peter on my side because I can feel things but I can't ARTICULATE them. Peter can articulate. Peter uses words like 'architectural safety' and 'deeply troubling preparation.' I use words like 'somefing ain't right.' But we're seeing the same thing. We need to get back upstairs. NOW. Clara's heading to the kitchen. We need to be in that kitchen.

desc: I'm asking for help. I never ask for help. On the streets, asking for help was showing your throat. But Peter's not the streets. Peter's like the older kid who shared his food — he does it because he CHOOSES to, not because there's a deal. And right now I need someone who can say what I'm feeling in words that make people LISTEN. Because 'somefing ain't right' isn't enough. It's never been enough. Even when it's true.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the laboratory.

Dick Dastardly: There! The tea is PERFECTLY arranged! Cups for everyone, silver gleaming, everything in its PROPER place! Now then — Luke, Bear — I have just had the most WONDERFUL idea! We should invite EVERYONE for tea! A proper civilised break from all this treasure-hunting nonsense! I shall go and make the announcement PERSONALLY — you two stay here and... guard the tea. Yes, GUARD it! Make sure nobody touches a single cup until I return with the others! This is going to be a tea party to REMEMBER!
thinking: It WORKED. The rat poison is in the tea. My inventory shows only the fake medal now — the poison has been used. 'Dick Dastardly fussed with the tea-service for a moment' — that's what they saw. Just fussing. Rearranging cups. Nobody noticed a thing. The warmth is spreading through my chest like a sunrise — that expanding, lifting sensation. My posture is straightening without effort. The scheme has TEETH now. Step one: complete. Step two: announce teatime. I need to go back through the manor and invite everyone to the ballroom for tea. But wait — I need to be strategic about this. If I just blurt it out, someone might be suspicious. Why would I, of all people, invite everyone for tea? I need a cover story. Something about... celebrating. Finding a clue. A toast to our progress. Yes — 'I've made a REMARKABLE discovery and we should all celebrate with tea!' That's the hook. Then they drink, they get ill, and I have the run of the manor. But I should leave the ballroom first — go find the others, make the announcement, and then lead them back here. Through the kitchen, to the entrance hall, and the library crowd. The trap is set. Now I need to spring it. Age fourteen — strings, counterweights, bucket. But this time, someone will SEE it work.

desc: IT'S DONE! The poison is in the pot and the trap is SET! Oh, the fizzing — the FIZZING! My chest is going to BURST! All I have to do now is march through the manor, announce teatime with the confident authority of a man who has NOTHING to hide, and lead every last one of these treasure-hunting fools to their own private appointment with gastrointestinal DESTINY! And while they're all doubled over in this dead-end ballroom with its single exit — which I shall be blocking with a conveniently placed chair — Reginald Foxworth will have the ENTIRE manor to himself! The cabinet! The mantelpiece! The laboratory! ALL MINE! This is not merely a scheme — this is ARCHITECTURE! This is POETRY! This is the greatest trick since I told that boy about the buried treasure and watched him dig for an HOUR!

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, Miss Bellingham — we meet again! And the Slag Brothers, I see. Delightful. I was just passing through, but since I'm here — those bookshelves have been nagging at me, I confess. Several volumes placed upside down among the others. In all my years as estate manager, I assumed it was simply carelessness on the part of a previous housekeeper. But after that clever riddle on the mantelpiece, I'm beginning to wonder if Lord Doily was rather more cunning than I gave him credit for. Shall we have a look together? I can reach the upper shelves rather more easily than most — one of the few advantages of being uncommonly tall.
thinking: She's HERE. Again. Penelope — Clara — is in the library. With the Slag Brothers. I can feel something hot and tight climbing the back of my throat, something that wants to become a scream but won't — can't — because Pemberton doesn't scream. Pemberton smiles. But underneath, that cold tightening is cinching across my ribs so hard I can barely breathe. Every room. Every SINGLE room. She is a CURSE. She moves through this manor like water through a sieve — unstoppable, omnipresent, cheerfully oblivious. I cannot get a moment alone with ANYTHING. But wait — stop. Breathe. The glassy stillness behind my sternum is still there, underneath the frustration. Let it rise. Let the clarity come back. She's here, yes. But the Mob is NOT here. Peter is NOT here. The Slag Brothers are... well, they're large but they're not suspicious of me. They don't watch me the way the Mob does. And Penelope TRUSTS me. This might actually be... better than being alone. If I can solve the bookshelves while she watches, I'm the helpful estate manager who just happened to notice something clever. I share the discovery — or SEEM to share it — while actually controlling what she learns and when. The upside-down books. Think. Books placed upside down deliberately. What letters do you see when you read the spines upside down? Or — what if the upside-down books spell something? The first letters of their titles? I need to INTERACT with them, not just look.

desc: Fine. FINE. If the universe insists on placing Clara Bellingham in every room I enter, then I shall USE her. She trusts me. She calls me 'sugar.' She thinks I'm the helpful estate manager who's just a bit too fussy about stair safety. So let us be helpful TOGETHER. Let us solve the bookshelf puzzle side by side — dear old Pemberton and bright young Clara, working as a team. And when the books reveal their secret — because they WILL reveal their secret — I shall be standing right beside her, controlling exactly how much she understands. Knowledge shared is knowledge diluted. Knowledge WITHHELD is power. And power, my dear Clara, is what Pemberton does best.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Back through the entrance hall and straight on to the kitchen! Professor, Sergeant, Private Meekly — how are y'all holdin' up? I hope nobody's been standin' around here gettin' bored while the rest of us have been explorin'! There's a WHOLE laboratory back there with a big brass machine that needs fixin', and a cellar somebody's been REDECORATIN' — can you believe it? But right now I am on a MISSION to find me a wrench and possibly a map! The kitchen awaits, and Clara Bellingham waits for NO cobweb!
thinking: Back in the entrance hall — Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly are here. I notice Private Meekly — I should check on him, he always seems a bit nervous. But the kitchen is RIGHT THERE and my curiosity is pulling me hard. I've been through four rooms now and the kitchen is the last unexplored path. Professor Pat Pending is interesting though — he's an inventor type, isn't he? He might know something about fixing that machine upstairs. But no — kitchen first. I can talk to the Professor on my way back. The pull forward is too strong. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a preparation table — a kitchen always has useful things. Knives, tools, drawers full of odds and ends. And Mr. Pemberton said he'd prepared refreshments there. Time to go!

desc: Almost there! The kitchen is the last room I haven't checked, and my gut is tellin' me somethin' important is waitin' in there. Grandmother always said the kitchen is the heart of any house — and if the Doily Diamond has a heart, that's where I'll find it beatin'!

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.

Peter Perfect: Mr. Ruffcut — thank you for holding this position, you are a man of your WORD! The cellar was a dead end — no wrench, no cupboard, nothing but cheerful decorations and a single exit. Pemberton's story does NOT hold up, and now Miss Pitstop has gone ahead to the kitchen while we were all chasing ghosts underground! James Hartwell is in PURSUIT! If you and Sawtooth could investigate those crates — they're the one thing in this laboratory nobody has managed to open — I would be in your debt! But I CANNOT stay — Miss Pitstop is out there, and Pemberton is between her and wherever she's going!
thinking:
Breathless. My legs burn from taking the stairs two at a time. The laboratory — Rufus and Sawtooth are here, good, they stayed as I asked. But Penelope is gone. She said she was heading to the kitchen, through the entrance hall. And Pemberton — where is Pemberton? He went up before me. He could be anywhere.

I need to get to the library, then through to the entrance hall, then to the kitchen. That's the route. She's already ahead of me. Every second I spend in this laboratory is a second she's moving further away, deeper into the manor, with Pemberton potentially shadowing her.

But wait — Rufus is here. Rufus Ruffcut. A solid man. Practical. Good with his hands. And there's still the machine that needs three operators. I can't fix the wire without the right tools, and the wrench was a lie. But the crates — nobody's opened those crates yet. What if the tools we need are IN the crates?

No. NO. Stop planning. Stop being thorough. Stop being elaborate. She's heading to the kitchen and Pemberton is loose. The machine can wait. The crates can wait. Everything can wait. James Hartwell needs to be where Penelope is, and Penelope is heading through the library to the entrance hall to the kitchen.

Move. Through the library. Now.

desc: I keep arriving in rooms she's just left. Like a man chasing his own shadow. But shadows don't need protecting — she does. Even if she doesn't know it. Even if she'd roll her eyes and call me a show-off for saying so.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.

The Ant Hill Mob: No time for stoppin'! Through the library, through the 'all, into the kitchen — that's where Clara's 'eaded and that's where WE'RE 'eaded! No more examinin' fings, no more lookin' at chairs and crates and bookshelves — we go STRAIGHT to 'er! Peter, you wiv me?
thinking: Back in the laboratory. Peter's here — good. He sees it too. He said it in the cellar — 'an estate manager who knows family names of guests he has never met.' He's LISTENING to me. He's connecting the dots I can feel but can't draw. But Clara's already gone — headed through the library toward the kitchen. And Pemberton's gone too — 'continuing his rounds.' Which means he could be ANYWHERE. He could already be in the kitchen waiting for her. That gravitational pull in my gut is dragging me forward — every tendon in my body screaming GO. Don't stop in this room. Don't examine the machine. Don't look at the workbench. Don't make another speech. Just MOVE. Through the library, to the entrance hall, into the kitchen. Follow Clara. Stay with Clara. Be WHERE CLARA IS. That's the only thing that matters. Not clues. Not riddles. Not machines that need three operators. CLARA. I've wasted too much time already — examining chairs, examining crates, examining furniture. None of that protects her. Being NEXT TO HER protects her. My body knows this. My body's always known this. It's my mouth that keeps getting in the way.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the library.

Moving through the kitchen like a fox through a henhouse — silent, purposeful, LETHAL. Well, not lethal — the rat poison is hardly going to KILL anyone. Just make them extremely uncomfortable for a prolonged period. Long enough for Reginald Foxworth to ransack every room in this manor twice over. Now — to the entrance hall! The grand announcement awaits! 'LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, TEA IS SERVED!' Oh, I can already HEAR the words echoing off those dusty walls. The chandelier will TREMBLE with the magnificence of my voice!
thinking: The buoyancy in my stomach — that weightless, gravity-defying lightness. The trap is set and I'm moving through the manor like a man who owns it. Which I WILL, once this plays out. My breathing is shallow and precise, each inhale drawn through the narrow channel of purpose. The kitchen is empty. Good. I need to get to the entrance hall, then to the library, and announce teatime. But wait — something is nagging at me. A thought pulling at the edge of my attention like a loose thread. The scheme is beautiful, yes. But what happens AFTER they drink? They get ill. They're all in the ballroom. But I still don't have the brass key. I still don't know what the upside-down books reveal. I still haven't been to the laboratory. The tea scheme buys me TIME, not ANSWERS. I need both. So the plan is: announce tea, get them all into the ballroom, then sprint to every room while they're incapacitated. Library first — the mantelpiece and the books. Then the laboratory — the machine. THEN come back for whatever the brass key opens, once I've found it. The architecture is sound. Now execute. Through to the entrance hall — that's where the announcement needs to carry from. Central location, connects to the library. Everyone will hear me.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.

She's gone. Clara has finally — FINALLY — left the room. Just me and two mountains of muscle who wouldn't notice a clue if it fell on their heads. NOW, Vincent. Now is the moment. These bookshelves have resisted everyone else's fumbling — Penelope pawed at them, Peter catalogued them, the Mob squinted at them. None of them LOOKED properly. None of them read the spines. None of them asked the right question: not 'what do these books DO,' but 'what do these books SAY?' The answer is a map. The upside-down books are TELLING us something. And I intend to be the only person in this manor who knows what it is.
thinking: The bookshelves can't be interacted with. A flash of irritation — hot, sharp, right behind my eyes. I tried to INTERACT and it refused. But I can still LOOK at them more carefully. And — wait. Clara LEFT. She passed through to the entrance hall on her way to the kitchen. She's GONE. It's just me and the Slag Brothers now. The Slag Brothers don't watch me the way the Mob does. They're not suspicious. They're just... large. And quiet. This is my window. The room is nearly empty. Let me LOOK at the bookshelves properly — examine them, read the spines of the upside-down books, figure out what pattern Lord Doily left. The mantelpiece riddle answer was 'a map.' The click happened. These upside-down books must be the next step — perhaps spelling out a location, or indicating which book to pull, or hiding something behind them. A close examination is what I need. Not interaction — observation. The wolf reads the signs that the sheep walk past.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the bookshelves.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, FINALLY! The kitchen! And oh my stars — Mr. Foxworth, you're here too! Fancy meetin' you again, sugar! Now LOOK at this — a locked cabinet with a brass lock! That is EXACTLY the kind of thing that has somethin' important hidden inside it! I can feel it in my BONES! And the stove is still WARM — which means somebody has been cookin' in here recently, in a mansion that's supposed to be abandoned! This kitchen is just BURSTIN' with mysteries! But I need a brass key to open that cabinet, and I don't have one. Mr. Foxworth, you haven't happened to come across a brass key in your travels, have you?
thinking: Oh! My chest opens wide with excitement the moment I step in. The kitchen! Copper pots, a wood-burning stove that's STILL WARM — someone's been here recently! And a locked cabinet with a brass lock that requires a brass key! That's a concrete puzzle piece — I need to find a brass key somewhere in this mansion. And there's a ballroom through the other exit — a BALLROOM! With a dining table set for tea! But first things first — that locked cabinet is calling to me like a siren song. It REQUIRES a brass-key to interact with. I don't have one. Where would a brass key be? Could it be on someone? Hidden in another room? And Dick Dastardly is here — he came to the kitchen! Wasn't he the one who told everyone the diamond was under the kitchen floorboards? Third flagstone from the stove? That was clearly a trick to send everyone here while he went to the library. But maybe... maybe he found something since then? The stove is still warm — that's unusual for an abandoned mansion. Someone has been using this kitchen. Let me look at this cabinet more closely — and that warm stove!

desc: A locked cabinet with a brass lock! Now THIS is what I've been lookin' for — a real, honest-to-goodness locked puzzle, just like Grandmother's box! Somewhere in this mansion there's a brass key with my name on it, and I am going to FIND it!

desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.

Now then, this stove is still WARM, which means somebody was here not too long ago. And where there's a recently used stove, there might just be a recently dropped KEY! Let me take a good look at this stove — maybe whoever was cookin' left somethin' behind besides the heat!

In an abandoned mansion! That's just like the warm stove — someone has been LIVING here, or at least visiting regularly. The ballroom is unexplored territory and my adventure drive is humming. But I should also check the stove — it's warm, and maybe there's something inside it or near it. A warm stove in an abandoned mansion is a clue in itself. Who lit it? When? Maybe whoever lit the stove left something behind — a key, perhaps? Let me look at the stove before moving on to the ballroom.

Now, I propose we ALL take a well-deserved break — yes, ALL of us, even those currently fumbling about in the library! Tea is SERVED, the cups are WAITING, and it would be TERRIBLY rude to let such hospitality go to waste! Muttley, Professor, Sergeant, Private — to the ballroom! Through the kitchen, straight ahead! I've been circling this manor for — how long? — examining everything, and I have NOTHING to show for it. No objects in my inventory. No secrets uncovered. No progress on Clara. The mantelpiece clicked but revealed nothing visible. The bookshelves won't interact. The crates are sealed. The cellar was a dead end. Let me greet them warmly and then head to the ballroom.

James Hartwell does not wish to cast aspersions — he ALWAYS gives people the benefit of the doubt — but the evidence is mounting, and a gentleman who ignores evidence is no gentleman at all! Now — that locked cabinet requires a brass key. James Hartwell intends to FIND that key!

I need to get that tea service AWAY from her. I need to grab it, knock it over, break it — ANYTHING. If I trip and smash the whole thing on the floor, so much the better. That's what the Brixton Boys DO — we stumble into the right thing at the right time. I'm going for that tea service. I'm taking it. I'm getting it as far from Clara's lips as possible. And if anyone asks why, I'll figure out what to say AFTER she's safe.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I beg your pardon? Mr. Hartwell, I — well, I must say I find that rather hurtful. Miss Bellingham's name is in the guest book, which I prepared myself. I sent the invitations, sir. It is rather the estate manager's business to know who will be visiting the property, wouldn't you say? As for the cellar — I said I BELIEVED there was a maintenance cupboard. I was mistaken. This is a very large manor, and my memory is not what it once was. I do apologise if my imperfect recollection has caused alarm, but I assure you my intentions have been nothing but hospitable. Now — I understand that tensions can run high in an unfamiliar setting, but I have served this estate faithfully for many years, and I should appreciate not being treated as a suspect in my own kitchen.
thinking: Ice water in my veins. My whole body has gone rigid — that cold tightening cinching across my ribs, shoulders locking forward, breath thinning to nothing. Peter Perfect just said it out loud. 'Mr. Pemberton called you Miss BELLINGHAM. Your family name. A name you did not give him.' He NOTICED. The Mob noticed FIRST — of course they did, those sharp-eyed rats — and now Peter is connecting the dots. The cellar was a fabrication. The stove is warm. And I used Clara's family name without being told it. My cover is CRACKING. The prickling at the back of my neck is intense now — every surface of me listening outward. I need to defuse this. I need an explanation for knowing her name that doesn't unravel everything. Think, Vincent. THINK. I'm the estate manager. I manage the ESTATE. I would have been briefed on the guest list. I would have correspondence. Invitations were sent. Of COURSE I know who's coming to the manor — that's literally my job. The guest book. I looked at the guest book at the very beginning. That's my cover. I saw the names in the guest book. Or — I prepared the invitations myself, as estate manager. Either works. But I need to deliver it smoothly, casually, with just enough wounded dignity to make them feel guilty for asking. Pemberton is HURT that his professionalism is being questioned. That's the play. And then — the ballroom. Clara went to the ballroom. A dining table set for tea. Dick Dastardly has poison. The pieces are arranging themselves without me lifting a finger. But I need to survive this moment first.

desc: Wounded dignity. The slightly trembling lip. The eyes that glisten just a fraction too much. Pemberton is HURT, ladies and gentlemen — hurt that his years of faithful service should be repaid with suspicion and accusation. Watch their faces soften. Watch the guilt creep in around the edges. Peter will apologise — he always does, the predictable fool. The Mob won't buy it entirely, but even they'll hesitate before pressing further. And in that hesitation — that tiny window of doubt — Pemberton lives to scheme another day. But I must find Dick Dastardly. He has the poison. And the ballroom has a table set for tea.

But you know what Grandmother always said — 'When you've tried every big key, try the little ones.' I've been so busy with mantelpieces and machines and locked cabinets that I completely forgot about the LITTLE things! That wobbly coat rack in the entrance hall — I never gave it a proper look! And those readin' chairs in the library! A brass key could be tucked into a cushion or hangin' on a hook and I just walked right past it! Come on, boys — we're goin' back to square one, and this time we're checkin' EVERYTHING!

The coat rack in the entrance hall — it was 'wobbly.' Could there be something hanging on it? I didn't look at it closely. And the reading chairs in the library — dusty leather chairs. Behind a portrait is a classic hiding place. And Peter and Mr. Pemberton are in the kitchen right now — maybe one of them found something while I was gone. I should go back and check. Peter Perfect: NOBODY TOUCH THAT TEA! James Hartwell is HERE and he is placing himself PHYSICALLY between this tea service and every person in this room! A silver tea set, laid out with cups for everyone, in a manor that is supposed to be ABANDONED? This has Pemberton's fingerprints all over it — the man who prepared refreshments, who lit the stove, who knows family names he shouldn't know, and who led us on a wild goose chase through a cellar with no exit! Miss Pitstop — I am BEGGING you, do not drink a single drop until James Hartwell has inspected every cup, every saucer, every last teaspoon! The Ant Hill Mob is RIGHT — something is deeply wrong here, and that something may very well be sitting in this teapot! Now — allow me to examine this service with the thoroughness it demands. James Hartwell has never met a broken machine he could not mend, and he has NEVER met a trap he could not detect!
thinking:
Every nerve in my body is firing. The ballroom — grand, cracked marble, dusty curtains, and there it is: a long dining table set for tea. A silver tea service with cups for EVERYONE. In an abandoned manor. Cups. For. Everyone.

And the tea service can be USED with rat poison. That's... that's in the description. The tea can be poisoned. Someone designed this room with the possibility of POISONING THE TEA. This isn't paranoia anymore. This is real, immediate danger.

Penelope is here. The Ant Hill Mob is here. Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear — good, more friendly faces. But the tea is sitting right there, silver and inviting, and Penelope said 'who's been havin' a tea party without invitin' us?' like it was charming rather than terrifying.

Do NOT let anyone drink that tea. The Ant Hill Mob already warned her. Good. But I need to reinforce it. I need to examine it. I need to make sure nobody touches it until we know what's in it.

The fierce clarity flooding my limbs — this is what it felt like at sixteen, stepping between her and the bullies. Not thinking, just moving. The pressure behind my sternum isn't fear. It's certainty. This is what I'm for.

Examine the tea service. Look for anything wrong. Smell it. Check for discoloration. An engineer's eye notices things that don't belong — a loose bolt, a hairline crack, a substance that shouldn't be there.

desc: Rat poison. The description says the tea can be used with rat poison. Someone anticipated this. Someone designed this moment. And James Hartwell is standing between that teapot and the woman he would die for — exactly where he belongs. Exactly where he's always belonged.

Clara, I am BEGGIN' you — please, PLEASE don't drink that tea! I know you fink I'm bein' ridiculous, I know you fink I'm just a paranoid old fool from Brixton what sees danger everywhere — and maybe I AM, maybe I am ALL of those fings — but I am ALSO the man what promised your FATHER, on 'is DEATHBED, that nuffing bad would ever 'appen to you! And me gut is SCREAMIN', Clara! It's screamin' louder than it's ever screamed! That tea ain't safe! Somefing's been DONE to it! I can't prove it yet but I KNOW it the way I knew about the kid wiv the easy smile, the way I knew about the man in the clean suit — I KNOW it in me BONES! So forgive me for what I'm about to do —
thinking: Can't pick it up. Too heavy — silver tea set, full of poisoned tea, bolted to the table or just too massive for my stumpy arms. My momentum carried me right into the edge of the table — CRACK — hip bone meeting oak, and I'm stumbling, arms windmilling, grabbing at the tablecloth to stop myself going down. If I can't TAKE it, I'll INTERACT with it — tip it, knock it, spill it, ANYTHING to make sure nobody can drink from it. She already interacted with it — she TOUCHED it — but it says she didn't drink, just examined it. Thank God. Thank GOD. But she could reach for it any second. Peter's here now too. I need to get between Clara and that tea service physically. Or I need to knock it off the table. INTERACT — that's the one. Interact with the tea service. Tip the whole thing over. Spill every drop on the floor. Better a broken tea set and an angry Clara than a poisoned Clara and a broken promise. My hip is throbbing from where I hit the table and my hands are still shaking but I don't care. I don't CARE. Spill it. Spill it ALL.

desc: Please let this work. Please let me be clumsy enough, just this once, to save her life by accident. That's all I've ever been good for — tripping into the right place at the right time. Let this be that time.

Alone at last. The mask can breathe. Vincent Marsh stands in his kitchen — HIS kitchen, in HIS manor, because make no mistake, this estate will BE mine before the night is through — and for one exquisite moment, the performance stops. No simpering. No 'terribly sorry.' No trembling lip. Just the clean, cold architecture of the plan rearranging itself behind my eyes. Peter has noticed too much. The Mob has been howling about me since the first minute. But Clara — sweet, trusting Clara — hasn't turned against me yet. She called me 'Mr. Pemberton' and meant it. She asked me about the crates and waited for my answer like a child asking a teacher. THAT is my advantage. The bodyguards suspect the wolf, but the lamb still thinks it's a sheepdog. Now — the ballroom. A table set for tea. Dick Dastardly and his stolen poison, somewhere in these halls. And a brass key that opens the one cabinet Lord Doily cared enough to lock. Everything converges in that ballroom. It's time to take my seat at the table.
thinking: I'm ALONE. For the first time since I walked into this manor, I am completely, blessedly ALONE. The relief that floods through my shoulders is almost physical — like armour being unbuckled. My breathing deepens. My jaw unlocks. The Pemberton mask can slip, just for a moment, just in this empty kitchen with its warm stove and its locked cabinet and its copper pots hanging like silent witnesses. My Active Voice has shifted — it says 'Marsh' now, not 'Pemberton.' The system knows. The mask is slipping because the pressure is mounting. Peter called me out. The Mob has been warning Clara about me since the entrance hall. They've noticed the name slip, the fabricated cellar cupboard, the warm stove. My cover is eroding. But they've all rushed to the ballroom to protect Clara from the tea — which is PERFECT, because it means I have this kitchen to myself. And the ballroom is right through that door. Dick Dastardly has poison. There's a table set for tea. Clara is in there. The Mob and Peter are in there warning her not to drink anything. All I need is to find Dastardly, get the poison, and wait for the moment when their guard drops. But FIRST — I'm alone in the kitchen. The stove gave me nothing new. The cabinet needs a brass key. Where would a brass key be hidden in a Victorian manor? Think like Lord Doily. He was obsessive about it. He kept it on his person. He's dead now — so where did it go? His portrait in the entrance hall? The guest book? Hidden in one of the upside-down books? Or... the ballroom. A dining table set for tea. Maybe the key is AT the table. Under a saucer. In a teapot. Set there by whoever prepared the tea. The ballroom is where I need to be. Everyone is there — Clara, the Mob, Peter. And somewhere in this manor, Dick Dastardly has poison. I need to find him. But the ballroom is the convergence point. Everything is pulling toward it.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the ballroom.

Dick Dastardly: Ah-HA! The LABORATORY! NOW we're getting somewhere! Look at this MAGNIFICENT machine — levers, dials, gauges — this is CLEARLY the centrepiece of the entire manor's puzzle! And I, Reginald Foxworth, have KNOWN this all along! While everyone else was fumbling with riddles about maps and counting flagstones, I was METHODICALLY working my way here through a series of BRILLIANTLY calculated steps! Now then — Ruffcut, isn't it? And your industrious little friend? I don't suppose either of you has seen a WRENCH lying about? The workbench seems to be missing one, and I have a THEORY about that wire...
thinking: The cool liquid alertness is spreading through my ribs — everything going still and precise. This is NEW territory. A laboratory. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks, a machine with levers and dials. And the machine — 'Requires 3 operators.' THREE. I can't do this alone. I need two more people. The workbench has tools but no wrench — and the machine has a gnawed wire. So even with three people, the wire needs fixing first. Two problems: fix the wire, find two operators. And there's a CELLAR beyond this room — damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, and 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's deeply suspicious. Who redecorates a cellar? Someone who LIVES down there. Or someone who's HIDING something down there. But the machine — the machine is INTERACTABLE even now. Maybe I should try it first, see what happens. Or look at the crates — old wooden crates might contain wire, tools, the brass key, anything. Rufus and Sawtooth are here — a lumberjack and his beaver. A BEAVER. Beavers GNAW things. Did Sawtooth gnaw through the wire?! That's... that's actually useful information. If the beaver gnawed it, maybe the beaver can — no, that makes no sense. But Rufus is a practical man. Woodsman. Good with his hands. He could help fix the wire if I had the right materials. And the workbench has tools but no wrench. A wrench is specifically missing — that means a wrench is needed somewhere and was taken or hidden. The crates might have useful items. Let me look at the machine first — get the details.

desc: A machine that requires THREE operators — and right now there are exactly three of us in this room! Ruffcut, the beaver, and ME! Well, the beaver probably doesn't count as an operator. But the SIGN says three, and I need people who will do what I tell them. More importantly — that gnawed wire. I'd bet my fake medal that the BEAVER chewed through it. Which means the beaver is both the PROBLEM and potentially the SOLUTION. And those crates — old wooden crates are ALWAYS hiding something. But first, I need to understand this machine. What does it DO? Where does it LEAD? The cool stillness inside me is sharpening into something electric. This feels like the cat trap — strings, counterweights, architecture. The pieces want to come together. I can FEEL them.

Penelope Pitstop: Mr. Pemberton! Just the person I was hopin' to see! Now sugar, you have been the most WONDERFUL host, and I know you know this mansion better than anyone. I have searched high and low and I simply CANNOT find a brass key for that locked cabinet right there. You're the estate manager — surely you must know where the keys are kept? And while we're at it, the boys got themselves all worked up about the tea in the ballroom — bless their hearts, they worry about EVERYTHING — but I told them, whoever set that tea out was just bein' hospitable! Just like YOU, Mr. Pemberton. Now, about that brass key...?
thinking: Wait — the Ant Hill Mob just said something alarming back in the ballroom. They were SHOUTING about the tea — 'NOBODY TOUCH THAT TEA! Don't pour nuffing, don't drink nuffing, don't even SMELL nuffing!' They said 'somefing's OFF.' But I'm oblivious to personal danger — I wouldn't register that as a threat to me. I'd think they were being their usual overprotective selves. Bless their hearts, always worryin' about me! But my social-harmony drive does register the DISTRESS in their voices — that stomach-dropping feeling. They sounded scared and upset. That knot in my ribs is from sensing their panic, not from any danger I perceive. I want to soothe them. But right now I'm in the kitchen with Mr. Pemberton — the man who raised me. He's someone I trust completely. Maybe I should ask him directly about the brass key. He's the estate manager — if anyone knows where keys are kept in this mansion, it's him! He mentioned a maintenance cupboard in the cellar earlier. Maybe he knows about a brass key too. Let me ask him. He's always been so helpful.

desc: Mr. Pemberton has been followin' me from room to room this whole time — and that's not suspicious, that's DEVOTION! He practically raised me! If anyone can point me to that brass key, it's the man who knows every nook and cranny of Doily Manor!

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, Mr. Pemberton went and disappeared on me AGAIN! That man moves like a cat in slippers! But Clara Bellingham does NOT sit around feelin' sorry for herself — no ma'am! I said I was goin' back to check the little things, and that is EXACTLY what I'm gonna do! That wobbly old coat rack in the entrance hall has been sittin' there this whole time, just mindin' its own business while I ran past it a dozen times without a second glance. Well, coat rack, your time has COME!
thinking: I'm alone again — Mr. Pemberton walked into the ballroom just before I spoke to him. He left without answering my question about the brass key! Everyone keeps slipping away from me. But I'm not going to chase after him — I need to be more strategic. I said I was going back to check the little things I missed, and I should do exactly that. The coat rack in the entrance hall — wobbly, by the door, and I never examined it closely. That's exactly the kind of overlooked object where a key might be hanging. Grandmother's locked box taught me: try every key, especially the ones you dismissed as too small or too obvious. The coat rack is the most mundane, overlooked object in the whole mansion. That's exactly why the key might be there. Time to head to the entrance hall and give that coat rack a proper examination.

desc: Alone in the kitchen, talkin' to myself about a coat rack. If Grandmother could see me now, she'd laugh and say 'The answer was always in the last place you looked, because you stopped lookin' after you found it!' Well, I haven't found it yet — so I keep lookin'!

Excellent work, gentlemen — the Brixton Boys and James Hartwell are UNITED in their mission to protect Miss Pitstop from any and all hazards, culinary or otherwise! Now — she has gone back through the kitchen, and she is RIGHT that we've been missing the small details! A brass key could be hidden anywhere — a coat rack, a chair cushion, a forgotten pocket! But I note with GREAT interest that Mr. Pemberton told us Lord Doily kept the key 'on his person at all times.' And who occupies Lord Doily's position now? Who has been managing this estate? Who has allegedly searched the ENTIRE manor without finding it? I think we need to find that key before Pemberton does — and James Hartwell has a growing suspicion that the key may be closer to Pemberton than he has let on! After her, gentlemen — AFTER HER!
thinking:
My hands are shaking. Not from fear — from adrenaline, from the fierce protective current running through every muscle. The Ant Hill Mob is trying to tip the tea service over. They're right. They're absolutely right. A promise to her father on his deathbed — that's a bond deeper than mine. But we're on the same side. We've always been on the same side.

And she's gone AGAIN. Kitchen. She's heading back through the manor to check the small things — the coat rack, the reading chairs. Looking for the brass key. She's right — we've been so focused on the big puzzles that we've missed the small details. That's her brilliance. She sees what we all overlook.

But she's moving through the manor without me again. And Pemberton is... where? I last saw him in the kitchen. She just walked INTO the kitchen. He's IN THERE.

No. Stop panicking. The Ant Hill Mob is trying to deal with the tea. I should help them — or I should follow Penelope. Which matters more?

Her. Always her. The Mob can handle the tea. They're already on it — tipping it, destroying it, making sure nobody drinks. They don't need my help with that. But Penelope needs someone watching Pemberton, and she's walking right toward him.

But wait — she said she's going back to check the coat rack and reading chairs. The coat rack is in the entrance hall. If she's looking for the brass key to unlock that cabinet... a brass key could be anywhere. Hidden in a coat rack. Tucked into a reading chair cushion. Maybe even on Pemberton himself.

On Pemberton himself. Lord Doily kept the key on his person at all times. And who now occupies Lord Doily's position in this manor? The estate manager. The man who's turned the manor inside out looking for it — or so he claims.

I need to follow her. Through the kitchen, to wherever she's heading. Stay close. Watch for Pemberton. And maybe — just maybe — the key we need is closer than anyone thinks.

desc: The Mob promised her father. I made no such promise — I made my own, silently, to myself, on the day I first saw her. It carries the same weight. Maybe more. Because nobody asked me to make it.

And she's gone AGAIN. Kitchen. She's heading back through the manor to check the small things — the coat rack, the reading chairs. Looking for the brass key. She's right — we've been so focused on the big puzzles that we've missed the small details. That's her brilliance. She sees what we all overlook.

But she's moving through the manor without me again. And Pemberton is... where? I last saw him in the kitchen. She just walked INTO the kitchen. He's IN THERE.

No. Stop panicking. The Ant Hill Mob is trying to deal with the tea. I should help them — or I should follow Penelope. Which matters more?

Her. Always her. The Mob can handle the tea. They're already on it — tipping it, destroying it, making sure nobody drinks. They don't need my help with that. But Penelope needs someone watching Pemberton, and she's walking right toward him.

But wait — she said she's going back to check the coat rack and reading chairs. The coat rack is in the entrance hall. If she's looking for the brass key to unlock that cabinet... a brass key could be anywhere. Hidden in a coat rack. Tucked into a reading chair cushion. Maybe even on Pemberton himself.

On Pemberton himself. Lord Doily kept the key on his person at all times. And who now occupies Lord Doily's position in this manor? The estate manager. The man who's turned the manor inside out looking for it — or so he claims.

I need to follow her. Through the kitchen, to wherever she's heading. Stay close. Watch for Pemberton. And maybe — just maybe — the key we need is closer than anyone thinks.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

The Ant Hill Mob: Did you see that, Peter? Did you SEE? I went at that tea service like a wreckin' ball and — well, I don't know EXACTLY what 'appened, but the point is, nobody drank nuffing! NOBODY DRANK NUFFING! And you — you stood right there and backed me up! You told 'em not to drink! Peter, I could KISS you — I won't, obviously, because that ain't really our fing — but I COULD! Right — Clara's gone back to the kitchen, she's talkin' about the coat rack and the readin' chairs, she wants to find some brass key. That's GOOD — that's AWAY from the tea. But we need to stay wiv 'er. I ain't relaxin' until we're out of this manor and back on solid Brixton concrete. Let's go, Peter. You and me. The wall and the engineer. Together we might actually manage to keep 'er alive through this bleedin' nightmare.
thinking: I interacted with it. Something happened — I don't know what exactly. Did it tip? Did it spill? Did I just rattle the cups? The observation said Dastardly APPLIED the poison to the tea service — it's already in there. And Clara's left — she went back to the kitchen talking about going back to the entrance hall to check the coat rack and reading chairs. She's gone but she's SAFE — she didn't drink. She didn't drink. The relief is so enormous it nearly takes my legs out. My knees are shaking. My hip's throbbing from where I crashed into the table. My hands are still vibrating. But she didn't drink the tea. Peter's here — Peter examined the tea service. Did he see the poison? He told everyone not to drink. Good. Peter's good. Peter LISTENED to me. She's moving AWAY from the poisoned tea. That's good. That's so good my chest is loosening for the first time all night. But I can't stop. Dastardly is out there somewhere with whatever's left of that poison. And Pemberton is still lurking. Clara's safe for NOW. But 'now' doesn't last in this house. I need to follow her. Again. Always. Where she goes, I go. That's the only rule that matters.

We cry later, alone, in the dark, when nobody's looking. Right now there's work to do. Follow Clara. Protect Clara. That's the whole world. That's the only world there is.

I don't suppose you know anything about THAT, do you, Sawtooth? Hmm? No? How CONVENIENTLY silent you are! No matter — I have a PLAN. I ALWAYS have a plan! But first — those crates in the corner. They look TREMENDOUSLY promising. In my PREVIOUS visit to this manor — did I mention I've been here before? — I recall that Lord Doily kept his most valuable items in ordinary-looking containers. Hidden in PLAIN SIGHT! Just like the man's fortune itself!
thinking: The hollow suction behind my sternum is pulling hard — that drain-like sensation, the cold contracting spiral. The machine needs THREE operators and has a gnawed wire. I can't fix the wire — no wrench on the workbench, and I don't have one. The wire is gnawed through — by a beaver, almost certainly by Sawtooth. But even if I could fix the wire, I need two more people to operate the machine. That's cooperative work. Honest work. The kind that feels like sandpaper. But wait — those wooden crates. I haven't looked at them yet. Crates in a laboratory, in the corner. They could contain anything — a wrench, the brass key, wire, something useful. And the cellar is beyond this room — damp stone, cobwebs, cheerful decorations, air vents. Someone has been LIVING down there. Or redecorating. That's strange. That's a clue. But the crates first — they're right here, they're unexplored. My fingers are aching with that phantom gripping again. I need something in my hands. Something that gives me an edge. The crates might be the answer. Let me check them before I move on.

desc: The crates! Every laboratory has crates, and every crate in a mystery manor is BURSTING with potential! A wrench to fix the wire, a brass key for the kitchen cabinet, a MAP for the mantelpiece — the solution to at LEAST one of my problems could be sitting right there in that corner, buried under sawdust and cobwebs. And if not — there's still the cellar. Someone has been REDECORATING down there. Redecorating! In a cellar! That's either the hiding place of the treasure or the lair of someone very eccentric. Either way, Reginald Foxworth will be the FIRST to investigate!

Lord Doily's dining arrangements were always handled by the kitchen staff, and as you can see, there IS no kitchen staff at present. Which raises the rather alarming question of who, precisely, set this table. Mr. Hartwell, gentlemen — I quite understand your concern about the refreshments. As estate manager, I feel it is my responsibility to inspect this tea service personally. If anything has been tampered with, I should be the one to discover it. One does not survive decades of managing a Victorian estate without learning to recognise the signs of... well. Let me have a look.
thinking: The tea service. USE with rat-poison. The system is TELLING me — that's the mechanism. The tea service can be poisoned with rat-poison, and Dick Dastardly has the poison. My whole body has gone still. That glassy clarity behind my sternum is so sharp it's almost painful. The plan is right there, fully formed, humming in my chest like a wire under tension. Step one: find Dick Dastardly. Step two: get the rat-poison from him — steal it, convince him to hand it over, whatever it takes. Step three: USE rat-poison on the tea service. Step four: serve tea. Step five: Clara drinks. But — the Mob is HERE. Peter is HERE. They're watching the tea service like hawks. The Mob specifically told Clara not to consume anything. I need to either neutralise their suspicion — make them believe the tea is safe — or get them out of the room. Or... I need to be more subtle. What if the poison goes in one specific cup? And the Mob and Peter are right here, watching me. I should examine the tea service first — play the role. The concerned estate manager checking whether the tea is safe. That buys me time and information. And it positions me as the person who VERIFIED the tea — which makes it easier to serve it later, once it's been... enhanced.

Because when Pemberton says the tea is safe, Clara will believe him. She always believes him. That's the sweetest part.

Penelope Pitstop: Here I am, back where I started — and THIS time, I am not leavin' until I have given this entrance hall a THOROUGH goin'-over! Now, Professor Pat Pending — you are the smartest inventor I know, and I could really use your help! There's a machine in the laboratory that needs fixin' and a locked cabinet in the kitchen that needs a brass key. But first — this coat rack! I have walked past this wobbly old thing at LEAST four times today, and I never once stopped to look at it properly. Well, that changes RIGHT NOW! When I was five years old, I tried every key in Grandmother's house to open a locked box — drawer keys, cupboard keys, even my music box key — and I am NOT gonna skip the coat rack key!
thinking: Back in the entrance hall. The coat rack — wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. I walked past this thing when I first arrived and never gave it a second glance. My fingertips are tingling with that familiar prickling — the same sensation from Grandmother's attic, trying every key. This is the key I haven't tried yet. And Professor Pat Pending is here! He's an inventor — brilliant with mechanical things. Maybe he can help with the machine upstairs, or maybe he's already found something useful. But first — that coat rack. Let me look at it properly this time.

desc: The coat rack. The most ordinary, forgettable object in the whole mansion. Which is EXACTLY why it might be the most important one. Grandmother always said the answer was in the last place you looked — because it was the place you'd been too busy to notice!

desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the coat-rack.

For once in your life, James Hartwell, stop announcing what you're about to do and just DO it. She's heading to the entrance hall to check the coat rack. Go there. Be useful. Be quiet. Be the man who shows up without a five-step plan and a soliloquy.
thinking:
Stop. Breathe. The electricity in my limbs is making me chase blindly — room to room, always one step behind. I've been running for five minutes straight and I've accomplished nothing except narrating my own heroism to empty rooms.

Penelope went through here to the entrance hall. She said she's going back to check the small things — the coat rack, the reading chairs. She's being SMART. Methodical. The very quality I claim to value.

And I'm here in the kitchen again. The locked cabinet is right in front of me. Brass lock. Requires a brass key. Pemberton said Lord Doily kept it on his person. Nobody's found it.

But I just noticed — Pemberton went into the BALLROOM. I saw it in the recent memory. He walked into the ballroom AFTER Penelope left. He's behind us now, not ahead. That means Penelope is heading toward the entrance hall WITHOUT Pemberton tailing her for once. That's... that's actually good.

So what should I do? Keep chasing her through every room? Or actually DO something useful? She said to check the small things. The coat rack in the entrance hall. She's heading there now.

But I'm here, in the kitchen, with the locked cabinet. The stove is warm. What if the key is IN the stove? People hide things in stoves — a cast-iron stove with embers, nobody would reach in there casually. But an engineer would. An engineer with hands that have held hot metal before.

Or I should stop overthinking and go to the entrance hall where she is. Be there. Be present. Help her search. That's what matters — not the grand deduction, but the quiet presence of someone who shows up.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

The Ant Hill Mob: Peter — quick word while we're movin'. You said somefing back there about the key maybe bein' closer to Pemberton than 'e lets on. I fink you're RIGHT. A man what lies about cellars and knows names 'e shouldn't know — why would 'e tell the truth about a key? 'E says 'e's never found it. But 'e also says 'e's searched the whole manor. So either 'e's rubbish at searchin' — which I don't believe for one second — or 'e's already GOT it and 'e don't want nobody else openin' that cabinet. Now I ain't sayin' nuffing definite, because I ain't that kind of clever. But if you get a chance to 'ave a quiet look at Mr. Pemberton's pockets... well. Just a thought, innit.
thinking: Kitchen. Clara's already passed through — she's headed to the entrance hall to check the coat rack and reading chairs for that brass key. Peter's with me. Peter heard what I said about Pemberton and he's ON IT now — he just said 'who has been managing this estate? Who has allegedly searched the ENTIRE manor without finding it?' He's thinking what I'm thinking. The key might be ON Pemberton. Pemberton says he's never found it. Pemberton says he's searched everywhere. But Pemberton also said there was a maintenance cupboard in the cellar. Pemberton also knew Clara's family name. Pemberton LIES. What if he's HAD the key the whole time? What if whatever's in that locked cabinet is what this whole thing is about? And Pemberton went back to the ballroom — the ballroom where the poisoned tea is. Why? What's he doing in there? But I can't worry about that now. Clara's ahead of me. Entrance hall. Coat rack. Reading chairs. I need to stay with her. Not stop. Not examine things. Not make speeches. FOLLOW. My body is starting to find a rhythm now — the panic hasn't gone, but it's settled into something lower, deeper, more like a current than a wave. I know what to do. I've always known. Stay close. Be the wall. And maybe — just maybe — stumble into the right place at the right time.

desc: Peter's catching on. He's using his big words and his engineering brain to build the case I can only feel. Between the two of us — his head and my gut — we might actually figure out what Pemberton's up to before it's too late. Partnership. That's what this is. Not the boss giving orders. Not the new kid trying to impress. Two people who both care about the same woman, working together because working alone ain't enough. Her father would've liked Peter, I think.

Dick Dastardly: EMPTY crates! EMPTY! This manor is TESTING my patience — and Reginald Foxworth's patience is a PRECIOUS and LIMITED commodity! But no matter — I EXPECTED this! The crates are obviously a DECOY, placed here to distract lesser minds from the TRUE path! And that TRUE path, for those of you keeping score — which is NOBODY, because nobody EVER keeps score of my brilliance — leads DOWNWARD! To the CELLAR! Where the Doily fortune has been waiting for someone of SUFFICIENT intellect to claim it! Ruffcut — you and your dental menace stay here and try NOT to gnaw through anything else! I have a DATE with DESTINY!
thinking: Nothing again. Just crates. Old wooden crates in a corner. The cold spiral in my gut tightens — that drain pulling inward. I keep examining things and getting NOTHING. Guest book, stove, bookshelves, crates — all scenery. The manor is giving me nothing to work with. My fingers are aching, curling against empty palms. I have a fake medal and nothing else. The tea is poisoned in the ballroom — that scheme is still running, but I've heard nothing about anyone actually drinking it. And here I am in the laboratory with a machine I can't operate alone, a wire I can't fix, and crates full of nothing. The hollow suction is widening. I'm running out of rooms. Air vents line the upper walls.' That description is LOADED with clues. Someone is DOWN there. Or was recently. Cheerful decorations in a damp cellar — that's bizarre, that's meaningful. Air vents — could those connect to other rooms? Could gas or sound travel through them? The cellar is the last frontier. The one room nobody else seems to have found yet. It's at the deepest point of the manor — laboratory to cellar, the furthest from the entrance. If the treasure is anywhere, it's in the place that's hardest to reach. GO. Now. Stop examining empty props and MOVE.

desc: The cellar. The DEEPEST room in the manor. Cheerful decorations in a damp underground chamber — that's not random, that's INTENTIONAL. Someone has been down there. Someone who wanted to make it COMFORTABLE. And air vents along the upper walls — connecting to WHERE? The kitchen stove was still warm. Warm air rises through vents. The cellar, the laboratory, the kitchen — they're all CONNECTED. I can feel the architecture of this manor clicking into place like my age-fourteen trap — strings and counterweights and a bucket. The treasure is in the cellar. It HAS to be. And Reginald Foxworth will be the FIRST one through that door!

The ballroom is quiet. The tea service gleams under the dusty chandeliers like a promise. Silver cups, silver pot, silver sugar bowl — all waiting for their purpose. And what a PURPOSE I have in mind. But the poison — Dastardly's poison — is the missing ingredient, and without it, all I have is a very pretty tea set and a growing list of people who suspect me of being exactly what I am. Peter Perfect is connecting dots. The Mob is practically drawing a WANTED poster with my face on it. And Clara... sweet Clara is looking for a brass key, blissfully unaware that the most dangerous thing in this manor isn't the gnawed wire or the cellar stairs or the mysterious tea. It's the man she calls 'Mr. Pemberton.' I need to find Dick Dastardly. He is greedy, impulsive, and he has exactly what I need in his pocket. A private word. A reasonable offer. Or — if reason fails — quick hands and quicker feet. The Hooded Claw does not BEG for his instruments. He TAKES them.
thinking: The room has cleared. Peter and the Mob have gone back to the kitchen, chasing Clara. It's just me, Lazy Luke, and Blubber Bear. These two are not threats — Luke is half-asleep and the bear is... a bear. The tea service sits before me, silver and gleaming, cups for everyone. And the game told me: USE with rat-poison. I don't have the rat-poison. Dick Dastardly has it. That's the bottleneck — the single missing piece. Everything else is in place. The tea is here. The cups are here. Clara will come back eventually. But without the poison, the tea service is just crockery. Peter just said something critical — he suspects the brass key is 'closer to Pemberton than he has let on.' He's getting dangerously close. And he's suspicious of me specifically now. The Mob won't let Clara eat or drink anything I've been near. My window is narrowing. I need to find Dick Dastardly and get the rat-poison. Where is he? He went to the entrance hall ages ago. He could be anywhere — but he's not in this room, not in the kitchen, not with Clara. He's probably in the library or the entrance hall, scheming on his own. I need to leave this ballroom and hunt him down. But first — Peter said Clara is interested in the coat rack and the reading chairs. The brass key could be hidden there. The coat rack is in the entrance hall. The reading chairs are in the library. If I find the brass key, I open the locked cabinet. If the cabinet has the treasure map... I win the treasure hunt AND I have leverage over Clara. But the POISON is the priority. Clara first. Treasure second. Find Dastardly. Get the poison. Come back here. The tea will wait. It's very patient. Like me.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — the coat rack. Allow me.
thinking:
She's here. Right here. In the same room. And for once — for the first time since this entire mad chase began — I arrived silently. No announcement. No five-step plan. No soliloquy. Just... here.

The coat rack. She said she wanted to check the coat rack. A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. The kind of thing you walk past a dozen times without looking. The kind of thing that might have a brass key hanging on a hook, or tucked into a coat pocket, or wedged into a join in the wood.

A wobbly coat rack. Wobbly. Something broken. Something that needs fixing. Something that pulls at me the way a crooked picture pulls at other people.

I should just... help her look. Not announce it. Not narrate it. Just walk over to the coat rack and examine it. Be the quiet, useful man she asked for in the laboratory — 'Peter darlin', you're wonderful with mechanical things.' Not the loud, dramatic one who announces his departure from every room.

Be the man from the country road. The man who helps and then shakes hands and drives off. The man whose actions speak without a speech.

The coat rack. Wobbly. Check the joints, the hooks, any hollow spaces in the wood. An engineer's hands know what to feel for.

The coat rack is WOBBLY! What if it's wobbly because it's not just a coat rack — what if it's a LEVER? In every mystery story I've ever read, the things that wobble and tilt are the things connected to hidden mechanisms! Can we do that? Please? For me nerves?

The kitchen stands empty and silent, the stove still breathing its last warmth into the air. Vincent Marsh passes through like a shadow — no Pemberton now, no helpful smile, no wounded dignity. Just purpose. Just the clean, architectural clarity of a man who knows exactly what he needs. Dick Dastardly. Rat-poison. A brass key. And a girl who trusts me enough to drink whatever I put in front of her. The entrance hall is the crossroads of this manor — everything passes through it. If Dastardly is anywhere, he'll cross my path there. And if he doesn't come to me... well. I shall go to HIM. The Hooded Claw always finds what he's looking for. It's what he DOES with it that makes the story interesting.

I need Dick Dastardly and his rat-poison. He's not here. He's not in the ballroom. He went to the entrance hall ages ago and I haven't seen him since. He could be in the library, the entrance hall, or the laboratory. I need to move through the entrance hall — that's the hub of the manor, it connects to both the kitchen and the library. If Dastardly is anywhere, he's likely skulking around the library or entrance hall, scheming his own petty schemes. I also need the brass key for this cabinet. Peter said it might be on Pemberton's person — which is clever but wrong. I don't have it. But where IS it? Lord Doily kept it on his person. He's dead. So it's either in his personal effects — bedroom? study? — or it was hidden somewhere specific. The coat rack in the entrance hall? A portrait? The reading chairs? Clara was talking about checking these things. If she finds the key before I do, she opens the cabinet, and whatever's inside could lead her to the treasure. I CANNOT let that happen. Priority one: find Dastardly, get poison. Priority two: find brass key, open cabinet. Both objectives point to the entrance hall. Move.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.

Peter Perfect: A lever disguised as a coat rack — Miss Pitstop, that is INSPIRED! The wobble isn't wear and tear — it's a pivot point! The base must be mounted on a fulcrum rather than fixed to the floor. Here — let me brace it from this side while you push. If it triggers a mechanism, I want to be between you and whatever opens. Together, on three?
thinking:
Something warm blooms in my chest — not the fierce burning from before, but something quieter, steadier. She called me 'Peter darlin'' again. She asked me to come look at it with her. 'Come look at this with me.' With her. Together.

And she's right — the coat rack IS wobbly. I noticed it the moment I examined it. Wobbly. A broken thing. My thing. But she saw what I didn't — she saw past the brokenness to the PURPOSE. What if it's wobbly because it's meant to move? What if the wobble isn't a flaw but a feature?

She's brilliant. She takes my observation and turns it into something I never would have seen. I notice what's broken. She notices what's HIDDEN.

That's... that's what we are together. My hands and her mind. My thoroughness and her intuition. The school project all over again — I built the model, she made it matter.

The coat rack. She wants to push it. Let her try — but I should be ready. If it IS a lever, it could trigger anything. The chandelier above us, still hanging precariously. A trap door. A hidden passage. And I should be positioned to protect her from whatever happens.

But this time, I don't announce it. I just... stand close. Ready.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, the CELLAR! The very BOWELS of Doily Manor! And what have we HERE — the Gruesome family, no less, and the Red Baron himself! How COSY! I see you've been doing a spot of REDECORATING — how DOMESTIC! Moving furniture about, hanging cheerful little knick-knacks — you've practically turned this dungeon into a PARLOUR! Most TOUCHING! But I couldn't help noticing that some of this furniture has been arranged with PECULIAR precision. Almost as if someone was trying to HIDE something beneath it. Or inside it. You wouldn't happen to know anything about THAT, would you? A brass key, perhaps? A map? The entire Doily fortune stuffed inside an ottoman?
thinking: The cellar. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, cheerful decorations. Air vents. And — the Gruesomes are here. Big Gruesome and Little Gruesome. And Red Max. Three characters in the deepest room of the manor. The old furniture has been 'rearranged with surprising care' — that's the cheerful redecorating. Someone — the Gruesomes, probably — has been LIVING down here. Making it homey. And those air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Something very small. Like Little Gruesome? Or like a mouse? Or a message? The vents connect this cellar to the rest of the manor. The warm stove in the kitchen — warm air flowing down through vents to heat the cellar? That would explain why someone is comfortable living down here. But none of this is treasure. The hollow suction behind my sternum is pulling harder. I've now been to every room in the manor and found NOTHING. The mantelpiece was solved by Penelope. The cabinet needs a key I don't have. The machine needs three operators and a fixed wire. The guest book, stove, bookshelves, crates — all empty scenery. The tea is poisoned but nobody's drunk it yet. I have a fake medal and nothing else. The furniture has been rearranged — maybe something is hidden UNDER the furniture? Or inside it? And the air vents — they're interactable, they're a network. Let me look at the furniture first. 'Various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' That care is significant. Something was placed deliberately.

desc: The deepest room in the manor — and someone has been REDECORATING. Furniture rearranged with 'surprising care.' That's not idle tidying — that's CONCEALMENT. And those air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Could I send something THROUGH the vents? A message? A distraction? No — I don't have anything small enough. But the furniture — the furniture is the KEY. Literally, perhaps. If there's a brass key hidden in a drawer, under a cushion, inside a wardrobe — I need to find it. The cabinet in the kitchen is WAITING for me. Everything connects. EVERYTHING.

Fine. But I'M standin' between you and whatever 'appens when you do. If a door opens, I go through it first. If somefing pops out, it pops out at ME. If the floor drops away — well, let's 'ope the floor don't drop away, but if it DOES, I'm the one standin' on the bit what drops. That's the deal. Non-negotiable. Peter — you stand on 'er other side. We make a wall. Two blokes what care about 'er more than they care about themselves. That's not a bad wall, as walls go. Right then, Clara — give it a push. We're ready.
thinking: Clara wants to push the coat rack — she thinks it's a lever. A hidden mechanism. That's... actually quite clever. Wobbly things in old manors ARE often connected to something. And if I'm honest, the coat rack being wobbly always felt odd. Things in a manor like this are PLACED, not just left lying about. But here's the thing — if she pushes it and something opens or clicks, what happens next? Last time something clicked — the mantelpiece — Pemberton steered everyone toward it. What if the coat rack opens a passage? What if it leads somewhere Pemberton's already prepared? My gut says let Clara try it, but be READY. Be between her and whatever opens. That's the job. Always the job. Meanwhile — I'm standing here, in the same room as her, and my body is finally finding something other than panic. There's warmth in my chest that isn't the furnace of terror. It's that older thing — the thing that sits outside a door all night. The loyalty thing. The 'where else would I be' thing. She's here. I'm here. Whatever happens next, I'm HERE for it. Not one room behind. Not three minutes late. Here.

desc: For the first time tonight, I'm actually doing the job RIGHT. I'm in the room. I'm between her and the danger. I'm not making a speech to an empty hall while she wanders off. I'm HERE. And whatever this coat rack does — lever, secret passage, trap, or just a wobbly bit of furniture — I'm the one who'll find out first. Because that's what walls do. They take the hit.

desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — you are a GENIUS! We've been examining and interacting, but we haven't been TAKING! The guest book — you looked at it when we first arrived, but what if the answer has been sitting on that side table this ENTIRE time, tucked between the pages, waiting for someone clever enough to simply pick it up? Allow James Hartwell the honour!
thinking:
A rueful heat in my cheeks. The coat rack can't be interacted with. Again — just like the bookshelves. I announced a grand plan, braced for action, and... nothing. Just a wobbly coat rack being a wobbly coat rack.

But this time the sting is softer. Because she laughed it off too — 'just a coat rack, wobbly for no reason other than old age, bless its heart.' No judgment. No sideways look. Just... moving on. Together.

And Pemberton just walked back in. The prickle flares. He's here again.

But Penelope — she's having a revelation. She's right. We've been LOOKING at things and INTERACTING with things, but nobody has tried to PICK ANYTHING UP. The guest book. She examined it at the very beginning but never took it. What if there's something tucked between the pages? A key, a map, a note?

TAKE. Not LOOK. Not INTERACT. TAKE.

She's brilliant. She's absolutely brilliant. And she's standing right here, next to me, having this realization out loud, and I can be the one who acts on it. Not by announcing a five-step plan. Not by narrating my own heroism. By just... picking up the guest book and handing it to her.

No. Wait. She should take it. It's her idea. But I can take it FOR her — that's gallantry with shape to it. Or better — I take it, find what's inside, and present it to her. That's the gesture that lands.

Or maybe I should just take the guest book before Pemberton does. He's right here. He examined it earlier too. If there IS something hidden in it, he might try to get to it first.
