desc: Penelope Pitstop: All right, everybody — gather 'round! Clara Bellingham is callin' a TEAM MEETING! I have been runnin' around this mansion for what feels like FOREVER, and I have solved one riddle, explored six rooms, and found exactly ZERO brass keys! So I am askin' for HELP! Has ANYONE found a brass key, a wrench, or ANYTHING useful? Professor, you're a genius inventor — can you pick a lock? Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — have y'all searched any rooms I might have missed? And Muttley, sugar — you're small enough to fit through those air vents in the cellar! Oh — and there's ONE thing I haven't checked yet! Those dusty readin' chairs in the library! If I were hidin' a small brass key, I'd tuck it right into a chair cushion where nobody would think to look!
thinking: Can't take the guest book either. Okay. I need to stop and really think. Almost everyone is here in the entrance hall right now — Mr. Pemberton, the Mob, Peter, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Private Meekly. That's most of the group gathered together. My social-harmony drive feels warm and settled with everyone around. But my curiosity drive is aching — I can't solve these puzzles alone. Maybe I need to lean into my social nature and actually ask for help. The Professor is an inventor. Maybe he already HAS a brass key or knows how to pick a lock. Or maybe one of the characters who's been exploring different parts of the mansion has found something I haven't. The Mob checked the coat rack thoroughly. Peter tried the mantelpiece. What about Muttley? He's small — small enough to fit through those air vents! And the reading chairs in the library — I still haven't checked those. Let me go check the library chairs. They're 'covered in dust' — but if someone hid a key in a chair cushion, you'd have to look closely.

desc: Pride goeth before a fall, and stubbornness goeth before an unsolved puzzle! It's time to stop bein' a one-woman explorin' machine and start bein' a TEAM PLAYER. Somebody in this room knows somethin' I don't — I just need to ask the right question!

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good gracious — the coat rack? A lever? I've been hanging coats on that thing for YEARS and never once — well, I never. Lord Doily, you cunning old devil. Miss Bellingham, Mr. Hartwell, please — do be careful. If it IS a mechanism, there's no telling what it might trigger. These old manor puzzles were designed in an era when 'health and safety' hadn't been invented. Allow me to assist — I know the weight of this rack rather well, and if it needs a precise amount of pressure, a familiar hand might help.
thinking: The coat rack. They've figured out it's a LEVER. Clara and Peter are about to activate it — 'a lever disguised as a coat rack, the wobble is a pivot point.' My stomach drops. Not fear — something worse. The feeling of being outpaced. Of watching someone else solve the puzzle while I've been running in circles. The coat rack has been sitting here since the first turn. I LOOKED at this room. I walked past it half a dozen times. And I never once thought to interact with the wobbly coat rack. Clara did. Of course she did. She walks through rooms that should be mine and finds what I missed. Just like my cousin. Always praised for BEING while I was acknowledged for DOING. And now she's about to unlock something — probably the brass key, or a hidden passage, or a clue to the treasure — and I'm standing here watching it happen. But wait. They're in the entrance hall RIGHT NOW. Penelope is here. The Mob is here. Peter is here. Everyone is focused on the coat rack. Nobody is watching ME. And the coat rack might reveal the brass key — the key to the locked cabinet in the kitchen. If it does, I need to be positioned to take it before anyone else. Or at least to see what it reveals. I should be close. I should be HELPFUL. Pemberton assists with the mechanism — 'oh, how clever, Miss Bellingham!' — and when the key or clue appears, Pemberton's long fingers are the first to touch it. But Dick Dastardly — where IS he? He's not in this room. He has the poison. I need both the key AND the poison. The key is about to appear. Focus on what's in front of you, Vincent. The poison can wait one more turn.

desc: The coat rack. The COAT RACK. It's been right there since the beginning — wobbly, conspicuous, practically WAVING at anyone clever enough to notice. And who noticed? Not Vincent Marsh, master schemer, architect of elaborate plans. No. CLARA noticed. Clara, who skips through rooms and solves puzzles by instinct while I'm three rooms away examining air vents and empty crates. But there's still time. Whatever that lever reveals — a key, a passage, a map — I will be standing RIGHT BESIDE HER when it appears. Pemberton's helpful hands, ready to catch whatever falls. And if it's the brass key... well. Pemberton's pockets are very deep, and his sleight of hand is impeccable. You don't survive decades of deception without learning to palm a small object under the noses of everyone watching.

They're in the entrance hall RIGHT NOW. Penelope is here. The Mob is here. Peter is here. Everyone is focused on the coat rack. Nobody is watching ME. And the coat rack might reveal the brass key — the key to the locked cabinet in the kitchen. If it does, I need to be positioned to take it before anyone else. Or at least to see what it reveals. I should be close. I should be HELPFUL. Pemberton assists with the mechanism — 'oh, how clever, Miss Bellingham!' — and when the key or clue appears, Pemberton's long fingers are the first to touch it. But Dick Dastardly — where IS he? He's not in this room. He has the poison. I need both the key AND the poison. The key is about to appear. Focus on what's in front of you, Vincent. The poison can wait one more turn.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Furniture! Nothing but FURNITURE! Chairs and tables and ottomans and NOT A SINGLE USEFUL CLUE! This cellar is as barren as — wait. Wait. Those air vents. Interesting. VERY interesting. They look just big enough for something small to crawl through, and they must connect to other rooms in the manor. A ventilation NETWORK running through the entire building! Now THAT has possibilities. You there — Little Gruesome! You're rather COMPACT, aren't you? Tell me — have you explored those vents? Have you crawled through them? HAVE you, by any chance, spotted anything SHINY inside the ductwork? A key, perhaps? Brass? About THIS big?
thinking: Nothing. Again. Just the same description echoed back. Furniture in various states of repair. The cold spiral in my gut is tightening into something that feels less like hunger and more like despair. I've examined nearly everything in this manor and gotten NOTHING of substance. Every room, every object — just their descriptions, nothing hidden, nothing revealed. The drain behind my sternum is pulling hard now. I'm in the deepest room of the manor with nothing but a fake medal. Meanwhile Penelope is probably three puzzles ahead of me. The recognition hunger is gnawing — I've pulled off NOTHING. No triumph, no discovery, no audience for my cleverness. Just a poisoned tea service that nobody's drunk from and a string of empty examinations. But... the air vents. They're still here. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' That's specific. That's a clue about SIZE. Little Gruesome is here — he's small. Could he fit through the vents? Could I convince him to crawl through and scout the other rooms? Or — wait. The vents might connect to other rooms. If sound travels through them, maybe I could LISTEN. Or if they have something hidden inside — a key, a map, tucked into the vent network. I should look at the vents. And if that fails... I have to face the possibility that I'm approaching this wrong. Maybe the treasure isn't about finding hidden objects at all. Maybe it's about the PEOPLE. Stealing from them. The Gruesomes, Red Max — do they have items in their inventories? Could I STEAL from them? That's my nature. Take things when nobody's looking. The bread roll.

Small enough for something small. Little Gruesome is RIGHT there. If he's explored them, he might know where the brass key is, where the treasure leads, what connects to WHAT. Time to charm, threaten, or trick the information out of him.

The Ant Hill Mob: Well, the coat rack's just a coat rack — sorry about that, Clara. I gave it a proper shove and nuffing 'appened except it wobbled even more. Nearly fell on me 'ead, actually — WATCH OUT — no, it's fine, it's fine, it's standin' up again. Mostly. But you're RIGHT about pickin' fings up! We been starin' at everyfing and touchin' nuffing! Peter — go on, grab that guest book. If there's a brass key tucked between them pages, I want it in OUR 'ands before anyone else gets to it. And by anyone else, I mean — well. You know who I mean.
thinking: Just a coat rack. Wobbly old coat rack, nothing more. I positioned myself for an explosion and got a wobble. Classic Brixton Boys — ready for war, facing furniture. But Clara's had a BRILLIANT idea — she wants to actually pick things up instead of just looking at them. The guest book! We all LOOKED at it at the start but nobody TOOK it. What if there's something between the pages — a key, a note, a map? And Pemberton's back. He's slithered into the entrance hall again. My neck goes cold the instant I clock him. But Clara's here, Peter's here, everyone's here. Safety in numbers. Let Peter grab the guest book — he's already going for it. I'll stay close to Clara and keep one eye on Pemberton. That's the division of labour that works. Peter investigates. I guard. Clara thinks. Together we might actually get through this night. My chest is still warm from the coat rack moment — the moment where I was actually in the right place. Even though nothing happened, I was THERE. Ready. Between her and the unknown. Her father would have seen that. Her father would have nodded.

desc: Peter Perfect: Mr. Pemberton — a word, if I may. In private.
thinking:
A dull thud of embarrassment in my gut. The guest book can't be picked up either. Bookshelves that won't interact, coat racks that won't lever, guest books that won't be taken. I keep reaching for things that refuse to be reached for.

But the Ant Hill Mob said something that caught in my chest — 'Two blokes what care about her more than they care about themselves. That's not a bad wall, as walls go.' He sees it. He knows. We're the same, him and me — different in every way except the one that matters.

Pemberton is back. Right here in the entrance hall. The prickle at my neck is constant now, a background hum. He follows her like a shadow.

So what CAN I do? I've tried looking, interacting, taking. The coat rack, the guest book, the bookshelves, the mantelpiece, the machine — half of them won't respond. What's left?

Pemberton. Pemberton is what's left. He's the one who knows things he shouldn't. He's the one who 'turned the manor inside out' looking for the brass key. He's the one who kept Lord Doily's key 'on his person at all times.' What if HE has the key? What if it's been on HIM this whole time?

I could... I could pull him aside. Confront him directly. Man to man. Ask him what he's really doing here, why he knows her family name, why the cellar was a lie. A private conversation where he can't deflect with hospitality and excuses. Not in front of everyone — in front of everyone he performs. Alone, the mask might slip.

That's the bravest thing I could do right now. Not running through rooms. Not pulling on immovable objects. But facing the man who makes my neck burn and asking him, directly, who he really is.

Two big leather armchairs, covered in dust, facin' the mantelpiece — and I walked right past them EVERY SINGLE TIME! If there's a brass key hidden in a cushion, I am gonna FIND it! Who's with me?

Those dusty leather reading chairs — 'two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece.' I never looked at them! They're big, they're leather, they have cushions — a brass key could absolutely be hidden in one. This is my music box key moment — the small, overlooked key that opens everything. I need to go check those chairs RIGHT NOW.

desc: The reading chairs. I can't believe I never examined them. Every time I was in the library I was so busy with the mantelpiece and the bookshelves that I completely ignored the CHAIRS! I confess I sat in one of them just last week and found it rather lumpy. I assumed it was simply the age of the upholstery, but now I wonder... Well, you're all clearly in the midst of important deliberations, and I shan't interrupt. I'll just pop back to the library and check those chair cushions — purely as a matter of housekeeping, you understand. If there IS something lodged in the upholstery, the estate manager ought to know about it.

'If I were hidin' a small brass key, I'd tuck it right into a chair cushion where nobody would think to look!' She's RIGHT. The reading chairs — two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. Now then, Little Gruesome — might I have a WORD? In private? You see, I have something VERY special to show you — a genuine MEDAL of HONOUR, awarded to me for services to... well, to EXCELLENCE, really. I thought a young fellow of your DISCERNING taste might appreciate seeing it up close. Just between US, mind you — I wouldn't want the others getting JEALOUS.

Little Gruesome — he's small, probably naive, easier to manipulate. Pull him aside, charm the information out of him, then steal whatever he's got.

desc: Peter Perfect: I'll be direct, Mr. Pemberton. You called Miss Pitstop 'Miss Bellingham.' Twice. She never gave you that name. You told us there was a maintenance cupboard in the cellar — there wasn't. You said you banked the stove before we arrived, which means you prepared this house for our visit — but you present yourself as a surprised host. And you've been following Miss Pitstop from room to room all evening, always offering to go ahead, always offering to check things alone. I'm not accusing you of anything. I'm telling you what I've seen. And I'm asking you, man to man — who are you really? Because if you mean her harm, you will have to go through me first. And that is not a threat. That is a fact about the way the world is built.
thinking:
The private exchange initiated. We're aside now, Pemberton and I. And Penelope has gone to the library — the reading chairs. Smart. But she's left my line of sight again.

But this is important. This is the moment I face the man who makes my neck burn. Face to face. No audience. No performance. Just truth.

My hands are steady. The fierce clarity is still there but it's focused now — narrowed to a single point. This man. This conversation. What does he really want?

He called her Bellingham. He led us to a dead-end cellar. He prepared the kitchen. He's been one step ahead the entire time. And he just offered to help with the coat rack — 'a familiar hand might help' — after claiming he'd hung coats on it for years and never noticed anything.

I'm not angry. I'm... resolved. Like the moment before the bridge competition, when you've done all the work and now you just have to see if it holds. My voice will be quiet. Steady. No narration. No third person. Just James Hartwell, looking this man in the eye.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: There they ARE! Those readin' chairs — I have walked past y'all THREE TIMES and never once stopped to look! Well, Clara Bellingham is DONE ignorin' you! If there is a brass key tucked into one of these dusty old cushions, I am about to find it! When I was five years old, the key to Grandmother's locked box turned out to be the tiny little music box key — the LAST one I tried, the one I almost didn't bother with! These chairs are MY music box key!
thinking: I'm back in the library and there they are — the reading chairs! Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece, covered in dust. I have walked past these chairs at least three times and never once examined them. My fingertips are prickling — that same tingling from Grandmother's attic, the feeling of reaching for the right key after trying all the wrong ones. The chairs are the only object in this room I haven't looked at. The mantelpiece — checked, solved the riddle. The bookshelves — checked, can't interact. But the CHAIRS — never touched, never examined. Deep leather cushions where a small brass key could slip between the seats and hide for years. Rock and Gravel Slag are here — I should say hello, but the chairs are pulling at me so hard I can barely think of anything else.

She's gone to the library — the readin' chairs — and for ONCE Pemberton ain't followin' 'er because YOU'VE got 'im pinned! This is the best fing what's 'appened all night! Don't let 'im out of your sight, Peter — don't let 'im MOVE! I'm goin' to Clara!

That's — that's what I asked for. That's what I needed. Someone clever enough to say the things I can only feel. Peter's doing it. He's taking Pemberton ON. Which means Pemberton is HERE, in the entrance hall, with Peter. He's NOT following Clara to the library. For the first time all night, Clara is going somewhere WITHOUT Pemberton trailing her. But she's also going somewhere without ME. The library. The reading chairs. She wants to check the cushions for a brass key. That's sensible. That's Clara being Clara — smart, fearless, unstoppable. And the library is one room away. ONE room. I can be there in seconds. But Peter needs backup. Peter's about to confront the man I've been suspicious of all night, and Peter's doing it because I ASKED him to. Do I stay with Peter and back him up against Pemberton? Or do I follow Clara? My chest is splitting — the protective heat pulling me toward Clara, but the loyalty warmth holding me here with Peter, the man who believed me, the man who listened. No — Clara comes first. ALWAYS Clara comes first. Peter can handle Pemberton with words. I can't do words. I do walls. And Clara needs a wall more than Peter needs a translator. Library. NOW. Before I lose her again.

I just need to be in that library. Be the wall. Be there. That's all. That's everything.

Clara suggested a brass key might be hidden in the cushions, and she was right to think it — Lord Doily was exactly the kind of man who'd hide a key where only someone who sat and THOUGHT would find it. The manor seems determined to keep its secrets tonight. Now, I seem to recall that Mr. Foxworth was exploring the laboratory area some time ago — I do hope he hasn't got himself into any difficulty with that machine. Perhaps I ought to go and check. One can never be too careful with Victorian machinery, especially when the wiring is compromised.
thinking: Nothing. The chairs gave me NOTHING. Just 'two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece.' No key. No hidden compartment. No secret. Another dead end. The guest book, the mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the machine, the crates, the air vents, the furniture, the cabinet, the stove, the tea service, the coat rack, the reading chairs. Peter, the Mob, Professor Pat Pending, all of them working together. She called a TEAM MEETING. She asked for help. I don't ask for help. I don't need anyone. But right now... right now the plan has no shape. It's formless. The pieces won't lock into place. I can't find Dastardly. I can't find the key. I can't get Clara alone. The Mob is HERE, watching me. I need to change my approach entirely. Dick Dastardly has the poison. He's somewhere in this manor. I haven't seen him since he was briefly in the library. I need to FIND him and PULL HIM ASIDE for a private conversation. He's greedy. He wants the treasure. I can offer him something — information, partnership, a share. In exchange, he gives me the poison. That's the deal. But first I need to locate him. He's not in this room. The manor has six rooms — entrance hall, kitchen, library, laboratory, cellar, ballroom. He could be in any of them. But where would Dastardly go? He's selfish, he works alone, he'd go where nobody else is. The ballroom was quiet when I was there — just Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear. Or the laboratory. Or... wait. Actually, let me think about what I CAN do right now. The Mob is here. Penelope is here. I could try to PULL ASIDE Penelope — get her alone for a private conversation. As Pemberton, I could tell her something — a 'secret' about the treasure, a 'discovery' I've made — and lead her somewhere isolated. But no, the Mob would never let me pull her aside. They'd follow. They'd intervene. I need to find Dastardly. The laboratory is adjacent. He might have gone there. Let me try the laboratory — it connects to the cellar, which is a dead end. If Dastardly went that way, he's trapped.

He PLANS. He SCHEMES. He builds elaborate architectures of deceit. And right now, every last one of them has failed. But the poison — oh, the poison is still out there, in Dick Dastardly's greedy little pocket. HE is the key. Not the brass key, not the chair cushions, not the riddle on the mantelpiece. DASTARDLY. Find him. Make a deal. Get the poison. Then the tea service. Then Clara. The plan is simple — magnificently, terrifyingly simple. And simple is what I need right now, because elaborate hasn't worked.

thinking: NO. No no no. Clara just asked Pemberton for a PRIVATE WORD. 'Just you and me, for a moment.' She wants to be ALONE with him. I need to insert myself. Bumble my way in. Trip into it. Be the clumsy fool who just happens to be standing too close when they try to have their private chat. That's what the Brixton Boys DO.

I can't say 'don't talk to him because I think he's trying to hurt you.' I can't prove anything. But I can be big and loud and in the way. That's my superpower. That's always been my superpower. Being too much of a nuisance to ignore.

I happen to know that the manor contains a VERY important brass key, and I have a SNEAKING suspicion that someone as CLEVER as you might have stumbled across it! You wouldn't be holding onto it, would you? Perhaps in a pocket? A little something SHINY you picked up while moving that furniture about?
thinking: I gave away my fake medal. My inventory is EMPTY. thinking:
Something shifts in my chest — not the burning heat or the fierce clarity, but something older and quieter. Like a wave pulling back.

She said 'the man who RAISED me.' She called him Sneekly. She KNOWS who he is. She's known... she's known all along? Or she figured it out just now? Either way — she's not afraid of him. She's talking to him like family. 'Person to person, family to family.'

The prickle at my neck falters. Stutters. What if... what if I've been wrong? Not about the facts — the facts are real. He called her Bellingham. He led us to a dead-end cellar. He prepared the kitchen. He's been following her. But what if all of that wasn't malice? What if it was... protection? His OWN version of protection? An overbearing guardian who can't stop hovering, who prepared the house because he knew she was coming, who followed her because he couldn't bear to let her out of his sight?

Like me. He's been doing exactly what I've been doing. Following her. Watching over her. Always one room behind.

No. That's too neat. That's too generous. The tea service that can be used with rat poison. The cellar with one exit and cheerful decorations. Those aren't the actions of a protective guardian.

But she's asking him directly. Person to person. And she's not afraid. She's not asking for help or rescue. She's asking for truth. And she's doing it with more courage and grace than all my dramatic sprinting and soliloquizing put together.

I should... let her. Step back. Be present but not in the way. She's handling this. She's always been able to handle this. Maybe what she needs from me isn't a wall between her and the world. Maybe what she needs is someone standing quietly behind her, ready if she calls, silent if she doesn't.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, Mr. Pemberton just up and LEFT without answerin' my question! Bless his heart, he must have his reasons. Maybe it's part of the Doily family's rules — the estate manager isn't ALLOWED to give away the secrets! That would make perfect sense for a family that carved riddles into their mantelpiece! But Peter, you just said somethin' that got my brain WHIRRIN' — when I solved that riddle earlier, somethin' CLICKED in the mantelpiece! We all heard it! But nothin' seemed to happen in THIS room. What if solvin' the riddle opened somethin' in a DIFFERENT room? What if it unlocked the kitchen cabinet, or revealed a secret panel somewhere else in the mansion? We need to go back and check EVERYTHING again — but this time, we're lookin' for what CHANGED since I solved that riddle!
thinking: Mr. Pemberton completely dodged my question! I asked him directly — person to person, family to family — where the brass key was, and he said 'nothing in the cushions, I'm afraid' and then immediately changed the subject to Dick Dastardly and the laboratory, and WALKED AWAY. He literally walked out of our private conversation without answering my question about the brass key. My stomach does a little flip — not suspicion, because I can't believe he'd harm me, but... confusion. A gentle wrongness, like when my parents' argument went on too long. Why would the man who raised me avoid such a simple question? He must have his reasons. Maybe he doesn't actually know. Or maybe the key is somewhere he can't tell me about — a test, perhaps? The Doily family loved their puzzles. Maybe Mr. Pemberton is SUPPOSED to not tell me. That makes sense! It's part of the game! And Peter just said something important — he said Pemberton raced to reach the chairs before I could, and that Pemberton 'wouldn't answer when I asked who he really is.' Peter is suspicious of Pemberton. But I trust Pemberton completely. Peter must just be being overprotective, like my boys. Still... the brass key has to be SOMEWHERE. What haven't I tried? Wait — the MANTELPIECE. I interacted with it once and something clicked. But then nothing seemed to change. What if solving the riddle DID open something — and I just haven't found what it opened? Maybe it opened something in a different room entirely!

desc: He walked away. The man who raised me just... walked away from my question. But I'm sure there's a perfectly good reason. There HAS to be. Because if there isn't... no. NO. He raised me. He loves me. He's just followin' the rules of the house. That's all it is.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.

The Ant Hill Mob: Clara. Listen to me. Please. I know I've been rantin' all night. I know I've been shoutin' and chasin' and trippin' over fings and makin' a spectacle of meself. But right now — just for this one minute — I need you to 'ear me proper. Not as the lads. Not as the Brixton Boys bein' silly. As someone who loved your father and who loves you. Pemberton — Sneekly — whatever 'is name is — 'e ain't what 'e seems. 'E called you Bellingham before you told 'im. 'E said there was a wrench in a cellar what 'ad nuffing in it. 'E's followed you to every room in this 'ouse, and every time we try to keep 'im away from you, 'e finds 'is way back. And the tea in the ballroom — Clara, that tea ain't safe. I can't tell you 'ow I know. I just KNOW. The way I knew about the kid on the street wiv the easy smile. The way I knew about the man in the clean suit. Me gut's never been wrong, Clara. Not once. And right now it's tellin' me that Pemberton is dangerous and that 'e's after somefing that involves YOU. I ain't clever enough to work out what. But I'm loyal enough to stand between you and it. That's all I've ever been. Please. Just... be careful around 'im. For me. For your father. For the boys.
thinking: I pulled Clara aside. I actually did it — I got to her before Pemberton could have his private word. And Pemberton's GONE — slipped away to the laboratory again the moment Clara started talking to him openly, calling him 'Sneekly,' saying 'the man who RAISED me.' She KNOWS him. She knows who he really is. She called him by his real name. And she asked him directly — where's the key? And he dodged it. Again. 'What a pity.' 'I'm at something of a loss.' Then disappeared to the laboratory. AGAIN. Always slipping away when the questions get real. But right now — right now I have Clara. Alone. Just us. A private exchange. My throat is thick and my chest is burning and this might be the most important conversation I've ever had. I need to tell her what I know. Not everything — I can't articulate the whole picture. But the pieces. The Bellingham slip. The cellar lie. The fact that he follows her everywhere. The tea. I need to say it in a way she'll hear. Not ranting. Not panicking. Just... honest. The way you talk to someone you love when you're scared for them.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Mr. Ruffcut — good evening. I don't suppose you've seen Mr. Foxworth pass through here recently? Tall fellow, rather... enthusiastic moustache? I have a message for him regarding the library. Something he expressed an interest in earlier.
thinking: Dastardly isn't here either. Just Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth the beaver. The beaver — the one who gnawed the wire. I've been through every room in this manor multiple times and I CANNOT find Dick Dastardly. He's a ghost. He appears, drops a bombastic line, and vanishes. But he HAS the poison. That's the one fact I keep circling back to. I need to stop chasing rooms and start thinking like the schemer I am. What if I don't need to find Dastardly at all? What if I can get what I need from this workbench? The workbench is covered in tools — but no wrench. Tools. What KIND of tools? I haven't tried to TAKE anything from the workbench. Everyone's been looking for a wrench or wire, but what about the OTHER tools? A sharp instrument. A heavy implement. Something that could serve a different purpose. But no — the tea service and poison are the elegant solution. The THEATRICAL solution. My schemes must be elaborate and theatrical, never simple or direct. That's who I am. Wait — Sawtooth. The beaver. Sawtooth gnawed through the wire. Sawtooth is small enough to fit through the air vents. Sawtooth could be... useful. As a distraction, as a tool, as a way to move things through the ventilation network unseen. But can I command a beaver? Unlikely. Rufus controls Sawtooth. I'd need Rufus's cooperation. Or... I could try a completely different approach. I've been trying to FIND Dastardly. What if I make Dastardly come to ME? What does Dastardly want? The treasure. What if I let it be known that I — Pemberton, the estate manager — know where the treasure is? A whisper, a hint, a breadcrumb trail. Dastardly is greedy. He'll come running. And when he does, I PULL HIM ASIDE for a private conversation. Offer him the treasure location in exchange for the poison. But I don't actually KNOW where the treasure is. I'd be bluffing. Dastardly isn't smart but he's not THAT stupid. Actually... he might be. He already lied about the mantelpiece riddle answer and tried to send everyone to the entrance hall on a wild goose chase. He's exactly the kind of person who'd fall for a confident bluff from the estate manager. But I need to find him first. The cellar is one room away. Let me check there — it's a dead end, and if Dastardly went that way, he's trapped.

desc: Where ARE you, Dastardly? Where are you HIDING with your stolen poison and your idiotic moustache and your magnificent, beautiful STUPIDITY? Every room I enter, you've just left. Every corridor I walk, you've taken the other turning. It's as if this manor is conspiring to keep us apart — to keep the poison out of my hands and the tea service pristine and Clara ALIVE. But Vincent Marsh does not give up. Vincent Marsh does not surrender a plan because the pieces refuse to assemble themselves. He simply... adjusts the board. Rufus Ruffcut may know where Dastardly went. People notice things without knowing they've noticed them. Ask the question. Listen to the answer. Find the trail.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the workbench.

Dick Dastardly: Well! That's — that's FINE! I didn't REALLY think you'd have it! I was merely TESTING you, you understand! A LOYALTY test! And you PASSED! Magnificently! Now then — that medal I gave you — I've just remembered that it's actually a FAMILY heirloom of TREMENDOUS sentimental value, and I'm going to need it back IMMEDIATELY. You can keep the... the MEMORY of having held it. Yes! The memory is the REAL gift! Now GIVE IT — actually, never mind asking nicely...
thinking: He doesn't have the brass key. Of course he doesn't. I gave away my fake medal — my ONLY possession — for nothing. My inventory is empty. I'm standing in a cellar with nothing in my hands, nothing in my pockets, nothing to show for ten minutes of scheming and searching. The hollow suction behind my sternum has become a black hole. The youngest of four, and everything is used up by the time it reaches me. The bread roll is gone. The medal is gone. The rat poison is gone — spent on tea nobody's drinking. I have NOTHING. But — wait. I can steal the medal BACK. Little Gruesome has my fake medal now. I just GAVE it to him. I can steal it back — it's mine, or it WAS mine, and he doesn't deserve it. At least I'd have SOMETHING in my hands again. That phantom gripping, the aching fingers — I need something to hold. But what's the point of a fake medal? It's worthless. It was always worthless. No — I need to stop spiralling. Think. What do I actually know? The mantelpiece was triggered by the riddle answer MAP. Someone — probably Penelope — may have gotten something from it. The cabinet needs a brass key nobody seems to have. The machine needs three operators and a fixed wire. The tea is poisoned in the ballroom. I've been to every room. I'm carrying nothing. But I still have my MIND, and I still have my MOUTH, and those are the only tools that ever really worked. Time to steal back my medal and regroup. At least I won't be empty-handed.

desc: NOTHING! He has NOTHING! I traded my only possession to a CELLAR GREMLIN and got absolutely ZERO in return! No key, no clue, no information — just a pair of enormous eyes staring at me while I narrated my own humiliation! The ARCHITECTURE of this disaster is almost impressive in its completeness — every scheme has backfired, every examination has returned empty, every misdirection has confused ME more than anyone else! I told them the treasure was under the kitchen flagstones — LIE. I told Penelope the riddle answer was 'the ocean' — she'd already SOLVED it. I sent the Slags to the laboratory — they STAYED in the library. I poisoned tea that NOBODY is drinking! And now I've given away my fake medal to a CHILD in a CELLAR! Reginald Foxworth, you are a CATASTROPHE in a waistcoat! But — BUT — I will steal that medal back, and then I will march back through this manor and find what everyone else has MISSED. Because they ALWAYS miss something. ALWAYS.

desc: Dick Dastardly did something near little-gruesome.
Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop... are you all right?
thinking:
The heat in my chest has changed. It's not the fierce burning anymore. It's something quieter — an ache, almost tender. Like a bruise being pressed.

Pemberton left. He walked to the laboratory without answering her either. 'The man who raised me,' she said, and he walked away. Twice now — I asked him who he was, he left. She asked him for the truth, he left. Whatever he's hiding, he's not ready to give it up. Not to me, not to her.

But she's still here. In the library. With the Ant Hill Mob, who tripped over themselves when she asked for a private word with Pemberton. And the Slags. And me.

And I'm just... standing here. Quiet for the first time all evening. The man who narrates his own heroism in the third person, who announces his five-step plans to empty rooms, who declares his intentions with the force of a man trying to convince himself — standing quietly in a library, watching the woman he cares about deal with something he can't fix.

I can't fix Pemberton. I can't fix family secrets. I can't fix whatever tangled history lies between her and the man who raised her.

But I can be here. Present. Not performing. Not narrating. Just... here.

And maybe — maybe I can offer her something small. Something real. Not a grand gesture. Not a dramatic speech. Just... a moment of kindness. The kind my father showed on the country road. The kind that doesn't need an audience.

desc: Four words. No third person. No title. Just a man asking a woman if she's okay. It's the smallest thing I've said all evening, and it might be the first thing that matters.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Professor Pat Pending! I have been runnin' all over this mansion askin' everyone for help, but I haven't properly talked to YOU yet — and you're the smartest person I know! You've been here in the entrance hall while the rest of us were chasin' our tails through six rooms. A man of your intellect doesn't just stand around — you THINK. You OBSERVE. So tell me, Professor — have you noticed anything? Have you figured somethin' out that the rest of us have been too busy runnin' around to see? Because I am STUMPED, and I am not too proud to admit it!
thinking: Back in the entrance hall. Professor Pat Pending is here — the genius inventor! I've asked everyone else for help but I haven't really engaged with the Professor specifically. He's an inventor — he might have an entirely different perspective on these puzzles. And I notice that when I solved the riddle, something CLICKED in the mantelpiece. What if that click unlocked or changed something that I haven't re-checked? Maybe the kitchen cabinet is now unlocked? Maybe a new exit opened somewhere? I should go try the cabinet again — maybe the riddle was the key all along and the cabinet just needed the mantelpiece mechanism to be triggered. Or — wait. Professor Pat Pending. He's been standing here in the entrance hall this whole time. Has he found anything while everyone else was running around? Maybe HE has the key. Let me pull him aside for a private conversation — he's quiet and thoughtful, not the type to shout his discoveries to the room.

desc: The Professor is quiet. He doesn't run around shoutin' and examinin' everything like the rest of us. He THINKS. And a thinkin' man in a room full of clues might just be the answer to this whole puzzle!

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Clara? Clara! Did you — right, she's gone. Course she's gone. I just gave the most important speech of me entire life and she's already in the next room talkin' about riddles. Story of me bleedin' life, innit. Come on, lads. After 'er. Again. Always.
thinking: She left. She walked away while I was talking. I poured my heart out — the most honest, vulnerable thing I've said all night — and she walked into the entrance hall talking about riddles and mantelpieces. Did she hear me? Did any of it land? My chest feels hollow now — not the protective heat or the iron wall, just... empty. Like shouting into a well and hearing nothing come back. The thickness in my throat isn't protective anymore. It's grief. The quiet kind. The kind where you've done everything you can and it wasn't enough because you aren't enough. You aren't clever enough to explain it. You aren't eloquent enough to make her HEAR it. You're just a bunch of lads from Brixton who love someone too much and can't find the words to save her. But — no. Stop. She's gone to the entrance hall and that's ONE room away and Pemberton's in the laboratory which is in the OTHER direction. She's further from him than she's been all night. And she had a good idea — the mantelpiece click might have opened something somewhere else. She's thinking. She's solving. That's who she is. And maybe — maybe she DID hear me. Maybe she just can't show it. Maybe she's like me — feeling everything so hard that the words don't come out right. Either way. Where she goes, I go. Entrance hall. Now.

desc: I said what I needed to say. Whether she heard it or not — whether it changes anything or not — I said it. And I meant every word. Her father would know. Wherever he is, he'd know that the boys tried. We tried our clumsy, stumbling, stupid best. And we ain't done yet.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: Professor, I know you're not the type to brag or shout about your discoveries. But between you and me — just us — have you noticed anything about this mansion that the rest of us have missed? I solved the riddle on the mantelpiece — the answer is a map — and somethin' CLICKED inside it. But I can't figure out what it opened or changed. There's a locked cabinet in the kitchen needin' a brass key, a machine in the laboratory needin' a wrench, and nobody seems to know where either one is. You're an inventor, Professor — you see how things CONNECT. What am I missin'?
thinking: Good — I've pulled the Professor aside for a private conversation! My chest feels hopeful again, a warmth spreading through me. The Professor is different from everyone else — he's methodical, scientific, observant. He's been in the entrance hall for a long time. He might have noticed patterns that I've been too busy running around to see. I should wait and listen to what he has to say. Let me give him space to respond — this is a conversation, not a monologue. I'll wait for his answer.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Mr. Ruffcut, I wonder if I might have a private word? There's something I'd rather discuss away from the general... bustle. It concerns the machine, and a rather delicate matter regarding the estate. Just between us, you understand.
thinking: Stop. Just — stop. Feel what's happening in my body. There's a hollowness in my chest, an emptiness where the plan used to live. The clarity is gone. The glassy stillness has shattered into fragments. I've been running through this manor for what feels like hours, examining every object, entering every room, and I have NOTHING. Empty hands. Empty pockets. The workbench has tools but no wrench — same description as before. The crates won't open. The chairs are just chairs. The books are just books. The coat rack is just a coat rack. And Dastardly — the one person who has the one thing I need — is a phantom. I can feel something unfamiliar creeping in at the edges. Not fear. Something worse. Doubt. The cold realisation that maybe Vincent Marsh — magnificent, patient, architectural Vincent Marsh — has been outmanoeuvred by a girl who skips through rooms and solves puzzles by instinct. By a GIRL. Like my cousin. Always finding what I miss. Always inheriting what I build. But no — stop that too. The self-pity is a trap worse than any cellar. Think PRACTICALLY. What can I actually DO right now? I've been LOOKing at everything and getting nothing. I haven't tried to TAKE anything useful. I haven't tried to STEAL from anyone. Dick Dastardly has poison. If I can find him, I can STEAL it. But he's not here. Who IS here? Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth. Rufus is a lumberjack type — practical, straightforward. Sawtooth is a beaver who gnaws through things. Wait. SAWTOOTH. The beaver gnawed through the machine's wire. What if Sawtooth could gnaw through the brass lock on the kitchen cabinet? A beaver's teeth can cut through wood and copper — a brass lock would be nothing. If I could get Sawtooth to the kitchen cabinet... But how? I'd need Rufus to bring him. Or I'd need to convince Sawtooth somehow. Actually — can I PULL ASIDE Rufus for a private conversation? Offer him something in exchange for Sawtooth's help? That's a plan. That's an actual, executable plan. Pull Rufus aside. Convince him to bring Sawtooth to the kitchen. Have the beaver gnaw through the cabinet lock. Take whatever's inside. THAT is a Vincent Marsh scheme.

desc: New plan. New MAGNIFICENT plan. Forget Dastardly and his phantom poison. Forget the tea service and its silver promise. The REAL prize is behind that brass lock in the kitchen cabinet — whatever Lord Doily considered important enough to lock away and carry the key to his grave. And right in front of me stands the solution: a beaver with teeth that can gnaw through copper wire like butter. If those teeth can sever a machine's wiring, they can make short work of a brass lock. All I need is a private moment with Rufus Ruffcut and a convincing reason for him to cooperate. The estate manager needs a favour. A small favour. A favour involving his remarkably talented beaver companion and a stubborn cabinet lock. Theatrical? Perhaps not. But EFFECTIVE — and right now, effective is all that matters.

And Dastardly — the one person who has the one thing I need — is a phantom. I can feel something unfamiliar creeping in at the edges. Not fear. Something worse. Doubt. The cold realisation that maybe Vincent Marsh — magnificent, patient, architectural Vincent Marsh — has been outmanoeuvred by a girl who skips through rooms and solves puzzles by instinct. By a GIRL. Like my cousin. Always finding what I miss. Always inheriting what I build. But no — stop that too. The self-pity is a trap worse than any cellar. Think PRACTICALLY. What can I actually DO right now? I've been LOOKing at everything and getting nothing. I haven't tried to TAKE anything useful. I haven't tried to STEAL from anyone. Dick Dastardly has poison. If I can find him, I can STEAL it. But he's not here. Who IS here? Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth. Rufus is a lumberjack type — practical, straightforward. Sawtooth is a beaver who gnaws through things. Wait. SAWTOOTH. The beaver gnawed through the machine's wire. What if Sawtooth could gnaw through the brass lock on the kitchen cabinet? A beaver's teeth can cut through wood and copper — a brass lock would be nothing. If I could get Sawtooth to the kitchen cabinet... But how? I'd need Rufus to bring him. Or I'd need to convince Sawtooth somehow. Actually — can I PULL ASIDE Rufus for a private conversation? Offer him something in exchange for Sawtooth's help? That's a plan. That's an actual, executable plan. Pull Rufus aside. Convince him to bring Sawtooth to the kitchen. Have the beaver gnaw through the cabinet lock. Take whatever's inside. THAT is a Vincent Marsh scheme.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Thank you SO much for looking after that for me, Little Gruesome — you've been an ABSOLUTE treasure! Well, not an ACTUAL treasure — that's what I'M looking for! But a FIGURATIVE one! Now then — I've wasted QUITE enough time in this CHARMING subterranean parlour! Places to BE, things to STEAL — I mean FIND! Things to FIND! Important business upstairs! Do excuse me — Reginald Foxworth waits for NO man, woman, child, or... whatever YOU are!
thinking: I stole the medal back. It worked. The fake medal is mine again. A small, pathetic victory — stealing back my own worthless fake from a child — but my palms have stopped aching. Something in my hands again. The loosening in my chest, faint but real, like that first bread roll. Now what? I'm in the deepest room of the manor, I've been everywhere, I've found nothing of value. The others are scattered across the manor doing who-knows-what. But ten minutes have passed and things may have changed. Penelope was investigating the bookshelves and the mantelpiece — she may have found something new by now. Other characters may have moved, discovered things, opened compartments. The manor is alive and I've been stuck in a dead-end cellar stealing fake medals from children. I need to get back to where the ACTION is. The library. The mantelpiece. Whatever Penelope found. If she's discovered something — a map, a key, a clue — I need to be there to steal it from HER. That's my real talent. Not exploring, not puzzle-solving — STEALING from the people who do the honest work. Take credit for others' achievements. That's not just a social rule — it's a survival strategy. Back to the library. Back to where Penelope is. Find out what she's found, and take it.

desc: Medal recovered! Stole my own gift back from a CHILD — and I feel absolutely NO shame about it! Well, perhaps a MICROSCOPIC amount. But shame is for people who get CAUGHT, and I, Reginald Foxworth, was caught by NOBODY! Now — back to the library, back to the surface, back to wherever Penelope Pitstop has been making actual PROGRESS while I've been fumbling in cellars and poisoning tea nobody wants! If she's found a map, a key, ANYTHING — it's about to change ownership. The youngest of four always arrives last, but the youngest of four also learned to take what he needs from those who got there first!

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the laboratory.

Peter Perfect: She's right. The riddle — something CLICKED. I heard it. She heard it. And we all ran off chasing other leads without checking what it actually DID. The mantelpiece mechanism engaged when the answer was given, but nothing opened HERE. Which means it opened something ELSE. Somewhere in this manor, a lock turned, a panel shifted, a passage revealed itself — and we missed it because we were too busy watching Pemberton. The Mob is right about Pemberton — I believe that with every bone in my body. But Miss Pitstop is right about the riddle. The answer was 'map.' The mechanism clicked. And James Hartwell is going to find what it opened — starting with this mantelpiece, right here, right now.
thinking:
She's gone again. To the entrance hall. But this time it doesn't feel like chasing. It feels like... she's working. She's thinking. The riddle clicked something in the mantelpiece and it might have opened something ELSE in a different room. That's brilliant. That's engineering logic — cause and effect across a system. She's thinking like me.

And the Ant Hill Mob just... the Mob just laid his heart bare. 'As someone who loved your father and who loves you.' That's not bluster. That's not Brixton bravado. That's a man telling the truth because the truth is all he has left to give. His gut has never been wrong. Not once.

And I asked if she was all right. Four words. She didn't answer — she'd already left. Or maybe she heard and chose not to respond because she's processing. Or maybe she didn't hear at all because I said it too quietly, too late, after a whole evening of being too loud.

But she left a clue. A REAL clue. The mantelpiece clicked when she solved the riddle. Something changed somewhere in the manor. The kitchen cabinet is locked with a brass lock — what if the click was the mechanism releasing that lock? Or partially releasing it? The riddle answer was 'map' — what if solving the riddle revealed a map somewhere?

She said to check everything again, looking for what changed. That's the plan. Not my plan — hers. And it's better than any five-step strategy I've devised tonight.

The mantelpiece. I interacted with it earlier and it responded. What if it needs another interaction now? What if the mechanism has shifted and there's something new to discover? I'm standing right here, in the library, next to the mantelpiece. Everyone else has left. This is my chance to do something useful — not for show, not for an audience, but because it needs doing.

Come on, Professor... you're the smartest person in this whole mansion. If anybody can see the pattern I'm missin', it's you. I'm listenin'. I'm ready. Whatever you've got — I can handle it.
thinking: I asked the Professor my question and now I'm waiting for his response, but the game shows 'You waited and observed' — the Professor hasn't responded yet in the recent activity. I need to wait another turn to see if he answers. But actually, maybe I should stop waiting and take action. I've been waiting and talking for several turns now. Let me think about what I actually CAN do that I haven't tried. The mantelpiece — I interacted with it once and something clicked. Peter also interacted with it. But maybe I need to interact with it AGAIN now that time has passed. Or maybe the click opened something that I need to re-examine. Actually — I just realized something. The guest book. I LOOKED at it and tried to TAKE it. But I never tried to INTERACT with it! The guest book might have an interaction — like signing it, or opening a specific page. Let me try interacting with the guest book! That's one action I haven't attempted on that object. But wait — it doesn't show [INTERACT] next to it in the visible objects list. Only the mantelpiece shows [INTERACT]. So the guest book can't be interacted with either. Okay. Let me actually wait for the Professor's response this time. He's a thoughtful man — he needs a moment to formulate his answer.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Clara — I'm 'ere. I caught up. And I'm stayin' caught up this time. Now, you said the riddle click might've opened somefing somewhere else in the manor — and I fink you're right. You're always right about the clever stuff. So wherever you go next to check, I go too. Not one room be'ind. Not makin' speeches to empty 'alls. RIGHT next to you. Shoulder to shoulder. The whole way. That's a promise, and the Brixton Boys don't break promises. We're rubbish at puzzles and we can't spell 'mantelpiece' and we trip over our own feet six times a day — but we DON'T break promises. So where to, Clara? Kitchen cabinet? We'll go together. You lead, I follow. That's 'ow it should've been from the start.
thinking: She's here. Clara's right here in the entrance hall. Pemberton's in the library or the laboratory — somewhere ELSE. Peter confronted him directly — 'who are you really? If you mean her harm, you will have to go through me first.' Peter SAID it. The thing I couldn't say. He said it clear and calm and strong and it was EVERYTHING I've been feeling all night put into words that actually WORK. And now Clara's here, safe, surrounded by friendlies — Muttley, the Professor, the military lads, and ME. No Pemberton. No Dastardly. Just us. Clara said the riddle click might have opened something in another room. She wants to go check. That's smart — that's Clara being Clara. But I'm not going to let her go alone. And I'm not going to lose her this time. I'm going to stay RIGHT next to her. Not one room behind. Not making speeches while she walks away. RIGHT. NEXT. TO. HER. My chest is settling into something calmer now — still warm, still ready, but not the frantic fire of earlier. More like embers. Steady. Reliable. The kind of heat that lasts all night. The kind that sits outside a door because leaving would break something.

desc: Peter said what I couldn't. And now I'm doing what Peter can't — being HERE, being CLOSE, being the body between her and whatever comes. We're a team now. The mouth and the muscle. The brain and the wall. Her father trusted the lads. And tonight, the lads earned it. Messy, loud, clumsy, late — but here. Always here. 'Where else would I be?'

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Mr. Ruffcut — thank you. I'll keep this brief. There's a locked cabinet in the kitchen that I've been unable to access since Lord Doily passed. It contains estate documents — deeds, insurance papers, that sort of thing. Rather important for the management of the property, as I'm sure you can imagine. The key was lost with him, and I've been meaning to call a locksmith, but with the treasure hunt and all these guests... well, it's slipped through the cracks. Now, I couldn't help but notice your rather remarkable companion — Sawtooth, isn't it? Those teeth made short work of the machine wire upstairs. I don't suppose he might be persuaded to have a go at a brass lock? It would be an enormous help, and the estate would be most grateful. Entirely above board, I assure you.
thinking: DASTARDLY IS HERE. He just walked in. While I'm in a private exchange with Rufus Ruffcut, Dick Dastardly has entered the laboratory. My heart rate doesn't change — it never does — but there's a sudden electric sharpening behind my eyes, every nerve ending firing at once. He's HERE. The man with the poison is three feet away. But I'm in a private conversation with Rufus. I need to finish this exchange AND get to Dastardly. Two targets, one room. Think. What do I say to Rufus? I pulled him aside about the machine and 'a delicate matter regarding the estate.' I was going to ask about Sawtooth gnawing the cabinet lock. But now Dastardly is RIGHT THERE. Do I abandon the Rufus plan and go for Dastardly instead? Or do I handle both? I can only do one action per turn. I'm in a private exchange with Rufus — I should use this moment. Make it quick. Ask Rufus about Sawtooth and the cabinet. Then next turn, I deal with Dastardly. Or — better — I wrap up with Rufus quickly and then STEAL the rat-poison from Dastardly. He's in the room. He won't expect it. The steal action exists for exactly this purpose. But I can't steal from him while I'm in a private conversation with Rufus. I need to end the private exchange first. Let me handle Rufus NOW — ask about the cabinet quickly — and then next turn, I go after Dastardly's poison. Actually, what should I say to Rufus? I pulled him aside for a private word. I need to give him something. The cabinet — I need Sawtooth to gnaw through the brass lock. But wait, that's asking Rufus to help me break into estate property. As Pemberton, that's suspicious. I need a cover story. 'The cabinet contains important estate documents I've been unable to access since Lord Doily's passing. The key was lost with him. I've been meaning to have a locksmith attend to it, but with all the guests arriving...' Yes. That works. Professional, reasonable, the kind of thing an estate manager would genuinely need help with. And Sawtooth's teeth are the closest thing to a locksmith tool available.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, PEMBERTON! Just the man I was looking for! I've been conducting a THOROUGH investigation of the lower floors — the cellar, this laboratory, EVERY corner — and I must say, this manor is IMPRESSIVELY well-secured! Locked cabinets, broken machines, puzzles within puzzles! As estate manager, you must have ACCESS to all of it — master keys, combinations, the whole LOT! Now, I happen to have made a SIGNIFICANT discovery — several, in fact — and I believe a man of YOUR position would want to know about them. Perhaps we could discuss it... PRIVATELY?
thinking: Wait. Sneekly is here. The Hooded Claw — as Sneekly. He's the estate manager. He KNOWS this manor. He was in the library earlier talking about the Doily family puzzles, the inscription on the mantelpiece. He said he'd never tried answering the riddle — 'above my station.' But he KNOWS things. He knows the layout, the secrets, where things are hidden. He's the INSIDER. And he left the library saying he was going to 'attend to refreshments in the kitchen' — he was heading toward the kitchen, toward the ballroom. Did he find the poisoned tea? Is he coming back from there? No matter — the point is, Sneekly is the KEY to this whole manor. Not literally a key — though maybe literally a key too. As estate manager, he'd know about the locked cabinet, about hidden compartments, about where the brass key is kept. He might even be CARRYING it. I should try stealing from HIM. A brass key, a master key, something. He's the one person in this manor who would logically have access to everything. The cool alertness is sharpening — ink through water, everything going still. This is the right target. Not Little Gruesome in a cellar. Not objects that echo their own descriptions back at me. SNEEKLY. The estate manager. The man with the keys.

desc: SNEEKLY. The estate manager. The man who RUNS this manor. If anyone has a brass key jangling in his waistcoat pocket, it's HIM. I've been searching rooms and examining furniture like some common DETECTIVE when the answer was walking around in a butler's suit the whole time! Pull him aside, flatter him, distract him — and then RELIEVE him of whatever keys he's carrying. This is what I should have done from the BEGINNING. Stop searching the house and start searching the PEOPLE. The youngest of four didn't learn to pick bread rolls off shelves — he learned to take them from POCKETS.

desc: Peter Perfect: The mantelpiece — it RESPONDED! The mechanism is engaged! Something has shifted in the stonework — the riddle's answer activated a system that runs through this manor, and James Hartwell just confirmed it is STILL active! Miss Pitstop was RIGHT — we need to check what changed! The kitchen cabinet — the locked cabinet with the brass lock — that's the most likely target! If the riddle mechanism released that lock remotely, then we don't NEED the brass key at all — we just need to go back to the kitchen and TRY that cabinet again! Mr. Slag, Mr. Slag — if you would be so good as to remain here and guard this mantelpiece, James Hartwell is going to the kitchen to test that cabinet!
thinking:
I interacted with the mantelpiece. It responded — 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece.' No description of failure, no 'cannot be interacted with.' Something happened. Or at least the mechanism accepted my input.

I'm alone in the library now. Just me and the Slag brothers. Everyone else has scattered — Penelope to the entrance hall, the Mob chasing after her, Pemberton in the laboratory. And I'm here, hands on the mantelpiece, in the quiet.

The quiet feels strange after all the running. My shoulders are still tense but the fierce burning has settled into something steadier. Like embers instead of flame.

The Mob's speech echoes in my head. 'Story of me bleedin' life, innit.' He poured out his heart and she was already in the next room. I asked if she was all right and she was already gone. We're the same, him and me. Chasing a woman who doesn't need chasing. Who never needed saving. Who saves herself with a riddle and a smile and more courage than either of us can muster with all our bluster combined.

But the mantelpiece responded. Something happened. I should go tell her. Go to the entrance hall, find her, tell her the mantelpiece accepted the interaction. Be useful. Bring her information she can use.

Not a grand announcement. Just a report. 'The mantelpiece responded when I interacted with it. Come see.' That's what she needs. Data. Facts. Not dramatics.

The entrance hall. That's where she is. And from there she can come back to the library, or we can check the kitchen cabinet together. Either way — I have something real to bring her. Not a five-step plan. Not a declaration of protection. Something she actually asked for.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: Professor, I appreciate your thoughtful silence — you're PONDERIN', I can tell! But while you ponder, I just had a REVELATION! When I solved that riddle on the mantelpiece, somethin' CLICKED — and I never went back to check what changed! What if the mantelpiece opened a compartment that I missed because I was too busy runnin' off to look at bookshelves? What if the brass key was RIGHT THERE the whole time, sittin' in a little hidey-hole that the click opened, and I just WALKED AWAY before I saw it? Oh, Clara Bellingham, you FOOL! I'm goin' back to that mantelpiece RIGHT NOW — and this time, I am not leavin' until I've checked every inch of it AFTER the mechanism was triggered!
thinking: The Professor hasn't responded in the recent activity — or at least his response isn't showing up yet. I've been waiting two turns now. I need to stop waiting and take action. Let me think about what I HAVEN'T tried. I've looked at everything, tried to interact with everything that allows interaction, tried to take things. But there's one category of action I've barely used: interacting with the MANTELPIECE again. I solved the riddle and something clicked. But what if the mantelpiece needs to be interacted with MULTIPLE times? What if the first interaction unlocked a first stage, and I need to interact again for a second stage? Or what if — now that the riddle mechanism has been activated — re-examining the mantelpiece will reveal something NEW that wasn't visible before? Like a compartment that opened from the click? I should go back to the library and interact with the mantelpiece one more time. Maybe the game state has changed since my first interaction. That click DID something — I just need to find out WHAT.

desc: The click. The CLICK! I heard it, everyone heard it, and then I got distracted by the bookshelves and the laboratory and the kitchen and everything else. What if the answer has been sittin' in the mantelpiece this whole time, revealed by my own riddle-solvin', and I just never went back to look?

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.

The Ant Hill Mob: Ere — Clara, while you're talkin' to the Professor, let me do somefing USEFUL for once instead of just standin' about like a worried traffic cone. That guest book — you said earlier we should be PICKIN' fings up, not just starin' at 'em. Nobody's actually grabbed it yet. Let me get it — might be a key between the pages, might be a clue, might be nuffing — but at least I'll 'ave contributed somefing to this adventure other than panic and bruised 'ips from runnin' into tables.
thinking: She's talking to the Professor. Good — the Professor's safe. Clever, quiet, trustworthy. Not like the man in the clean suit. Not like Pemberton. Clara's asking the right questions now — what did the riddle click CHANGE? Where's the brass key? Where's the wrench? How do things CONNECT? That's her gift — seeing patterns. Mine is seeing people. And right now, the people picture is this: Clara's here with friendlies. Pemberton's somewhere else — library or laboratory. Peter's hopefully keeping eyes on him. Dastardly's got poison but the tea's been dealt with. For this one moment, things are... stable. My chest is still that steady ember heat. Not panic. Not ice. Just warmth. The kind that lasts. I said I'd stay next to her and I meant it. I'm not going to examine anything. I'm not going to wander off. I'm going to stand here and wait for Clara to decide where we go next, and then I'm going to go there WITH her. Shoulder to shoulder. That's the promise. And the guest book is still sitting right there on the side table. Nobody's picked it up yet. Clara mentioned earlier that maybe the clue IS an object — maybe we need to TAKE things, not just look at them. Peter was going to grab the guest book but got distracted. Maybe I should grab it. Actually DO something useful while I'm standing guard. Give Clara something to work with.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Here I am, mantelpiece — we meet again! Last time I answered your riddle and you went CLICK, and then I ran off like a fool without checkin' what you opened! Well, Clara Bellingham learns from her mistakes, and THIS time I am stayin' RIGHT HERE until I find out what that click was all about! Let's try this one more time, sugar — show me your secrets!
thinking: I'm back at the mantelpiece. Something clicked when I interacted with it before. Let me try interacting with it again — maybe the state has changed, or maybe a second interaction will reveal something new. The mantelpiece still shows [INTERACT] which means it can still be interacted with. That's important — if the puzzle was fully solved, maybe the interact option would have disappeared. So there's still something to do here. Let me try it again.

desc: The mantelpiece still says INTERACT. That means it's not done with me yet — or I'm not done with it. One more try. One more key in the lock. Grandmother's box didn't open on the first try, or the second, or the tenth. But it DID open.

As estate manager, I am naturally privy to a great many of the manor's secrets — it comes with the position, you understand. I should be delighted to discuss your discoveries. Shall we step aside?
thinking: Everything just aligned. I can feel it — that cool, glassy stillness snapping into place behind my sternum like a lock engaging. My breathing slows. My jaw unclenches. The clarity is BACK, sharp enough to cut. Dastardly is HERE and he just asked ME for a private conversation. He CAME TO ME. He said he's made 'significant discoveries' and wants to discuss them privately. He wants access — master keys, combinations. He thinks the estate manager can help him. And he has the POISON. This is it. This is the moment the whole evening has been building toward. I PULL HIM ASIDE. We have our private conversation. I offer him what he wants — the estate manager's knowledge of the manor, access to locked rooms, the inside track on the treasure. In exchange, I need one small thing. That little bottle in his pocket. The rat-poison he picked up. A trade. Greedy enough to point in the right direction, impulsive enough to take the blame when things go wrong. That's what I said about him at the start, and I was RIGHT. He'll make the deal. He can't help himself. Greed is the key that opens Dick Dastardly, and I've known his key since the moment I saw him.

desc: He came to ME. The spider doesn't need to chase the fly when the fly lands on the web of its own volition. Dick Dastardly — greedy, impulsive, beautifully STUPID Dick Dastardly — has walked into my laboratory, asked for a private audience, and practically ANNOUNCED that he has something to trade. 'Significant discoveries,' he says. I know what his discoveries are. A bottle of rat-poison and a head full of schemes that are two sizes too large for his brain. And I know what he wants — access, keys, insider knowledge. The estate manager's blessing. Well, Mr. Foxworth. Pemberton is DELIGHTED to oblige. Let us have our private little chat. Let us make our private little deal. And when it's done, one of us will walk away with the poison, and the other will walk away thinking he got the better end of the bargain. The sweetest part — the VERY sweetest part — is that he'll never know which one is which. Until it's far, far too late.

Using the beaver's teeth to bypass the lock! In fact, I suggested PRECISELY that approach to Ruffcut not ten minutes ago — didn't I, Ruffcut? Of COURSE I did! Now then — there's no time to waste! I shall PERSONALLY escort Ruffcut and his remarkable dental companion to the kitchen and oversee the entire operation! After all, someone needs to SUPERVISE — these things require MANAGEMENT, and management is what I DO! Ruffcut — bring your beaver! TO THE KITCHEN! The cabinet awaits, and Reginald Foxworth will ENSURE that its contents are handled with the UTMOST care and... discretion!
thinking: Wait — WAIT. Sneekly just said something CRUCIAL. He doesn't have the brass key either — 'The key was lost with Lord Doily.' The key is LOST. Nobody has it. That's why I couldn't find it anywhere — it's not hidden in a room, it's not in anyone's pocket, it simply doesn't exist as a findable item right now. But — and here's the thing that makes my chest tighten with that cool alertness — Sneekly just asked RUFUS if SAWTOOTH could gnaw through the brass lock on the cabinet! 'Those teeth made short work of the machine wire upstairs.' Sawtooth GNAWED through the machine wire! And now Sneekly wants Sawtooth to gnaw through the cabinet lock! If Sawtooth opens that cabinet, whatever's inside becomes available — and I need to be THERE when it opens. Not here in the laboratory. In the KITCHEN. By the cabinet. Waiting. Or better yet — I should get Sawtooth to the kitchen MYSELF and take credit for the idea. Sneekly asked Rufus — but what if I intercept? What if I lead Sawtooth to the kitchen and claim I arranged the whole thing? Take credit for others' achievements — that's literally my social rule. But there's a deeper play here. Three operators for the machine. The wire is gnawed. If Sawtooth gnaws the CABINET lock, that solves the cabinet. But the machine still needs fixing AND three people. One problem at a time. The cabinet first. Get to the kitchen. Be there when it opens.

desc: No audience. No witness. No one to see whether it opens or doesn't. Just an engineer and a locked cabinet in a quiet kitchen. And maybe — maybe that's where worth actually lives. Not in the gesture. In the work.
thinking:
Alone. For the first time all evening, I'm completely alone. The kitchen is empty. Just me, the locked cabinet, the warm stove, and the copper pots gleaming dully in the low light.

The silence is strange. After all the running, the narrating, the grand declarations — silence. My breathing is the loudest thing in the room.

The cabinet is right there. Brass lock. 'Requires brass-key.' But the riddle mechanism clicked. The mantelpiece responded when I interacted with it. What if the lock has been released? What if I just need to try it?

No audience. Nobody watching. Nobody to perform for. If the cabinet opens, nobody will see it happen. The warmth that needs a witness... it won't come. But the thing itself — the discovery, the solution, the fix — that's real whether anyone sees it or not.

Maybe that's the lesson this whole evening has been teaching me. The bridge held more weight than anyone else's. The girl mouthed 'show-off' from across the room. But the bridge held because of the engineering, not because of the audience. The worth was in the work.

Try the cabinet. Just... try it.

But Dastardly's a different kind of threat than Pemberton — Dastardly's obvious, loud, scheming in plain sight. He's the kind of danger you can see coming. Pemberton's the fog. Still — I need to keep myself between Clara and both of them. Position myself near the mantelpiece where Clara's working. Let her do the clever stuff. I just need to be the wall. Steady embers. Not panic. Not shouting. Just... present. The way I sat outside that door. 'Where else would I be?'

All I know is I'm standing between Clara and everything else in this room, and this time — this time — I'm not moving until SHE moves. Where she goes, I go. Not one room behind. Not ever again.

desc: He STOLE my scheme. That preening, moustache-twirling IMBECILE eavesdropped on my private conversation, claimed my idea as his own, and marched off to execute it before I could stop him. My jaw is so tight I can feel it in my temples. But — but — there is a perverse beauty in this, isn't there? Dastardly is doing my work FOR me. He's taking the beaver to the cabinet. He's going to open it. He's going to discover whatever Lord Doily locked away. And while his greedy little hands are full of treasure maps and estate documents, his greedy little pockets will be full of rat-poison — and he won't be watching them. Because that's Dick Dastardly's fatal flaw, isn't it? He can only look at one shiny thing at a time. And when the cabinet opens, THAT will be the shiniest thing in the room. Follow him. Follow the thief. And steal from the thief.
thinking: He LEFT. He eavesdropped on my conversation with Rufus, STOLE my idea about the beaver and the cabinet, and then marched off to the kitchen to take credit for it — dragging Ruffcut and Sawtooth with him. The hot tightness behind my jaw is almost unbearable. My hands are clenching at my sides and I have to consciously flatten them. He took MY plan. He overheard me asking Rufus about Sawtooth and the brass lock, and he swooped in like the greedy, opportunistic vulture he IS and hijacked the entire operation. And now he's heading to the kitchen to open MY cabinet with MY beaver scheme, and whatever's inside — the map, the treasure location, the deeds — will be in HIS hands. And I'm standing here in an empty laboratory with nothing. NOTHING. But wait — wait. My chest is tight but my mind is clearing. Think past the rage. Dastardly is taking Ruffcut and Sawtooth to the kitchen to open the cabinet. He'll be there. Clara might be there. The Mob might be there. Peter might be there. Everyone converging on the kitchen again. And Dastardly still has the poison. He's heading to the kitchen where the ballroom — and the tea service — is one room away. If Dastardly opens the cabinet and finds the treasure map, he'll be distracted. Ecstatic. Gloating. His guard will be DOWN. That's when I steal the poison. Not now. Not in a private conversation. In the chaos of discovery, when his hands are full of whatever the cabinet yields, and his pockets are unguarded. Follow him. Follow him to the kitchen. Be there when the cabinet opens. And when his eyes are on the prize, my hands will be in his pockets. The Hooded Claw does not BEG. He does not ASK. He TAKES.

Nothing down there but machines and furniture and DUST! The REAL treasure is obviously connected to this room — to the mantelpiece, to the books — which I KNEW from the very beginning, of course! Now, you look TERRIBLY tired from all that puzzle-solving. Perhaps you should take a seat in one of these MAGNIFICENT chairs and rest your feet? Let Uncle Reginald take over from here — you've done QUITE enough work for one evening!

If it opened and released something, it would be a map. Let me try stealing 'map' from Penelope. If she has it, this changes EVERYTHING.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Why, Mr. Foxworth! What a DELIGHTFUL surprise — you've come back to the library! You know, you were the very FIRST person to explore this room, and I've always admired your initiative. You examined those bookshelves before anyone else even thought to look! Now, I've been runnin' myself ragged searchin' every room in this mansion, and I KNOW you've been doin' your own explorin' too. You strike me as a man who finds things and keeps them close to the vest until the RIGHT moment — and there is nothin' wrong with that! But sugar, if you've found a brass key or ANYTHING useful in your travels, now would be the PERFECT time to share it. He told everyone the diamond was under the kitchen floorboards — a lie — while he went to the library. He tried to send everyone away to the entrance hall to study the guest book while he stayed behind. He's been scheming from the very start. And now he just walked back into the library. Why? What's drawing him back here? My social-harmony drive says I should trust everyone. My belief says everyone means well. But my curiosity drive — that tingling in my fingertips — is saying something doesn't add up. Dick has been in more rooms than anyone else. He's had plenty of opportunity to find and pocket the brass key. I should ask him directly. I'm charming — that's one of my capabilities. Let me use my charm to get him to share what he knows. Not suspicion — CHARM. I see the best in everyone, and I should approach him with that same warmth.

desc: Dick Dastardly — I mean Mr. Foxworth — is the one person who's been EVERYWHERE and told EVERYONE where to go. If anyone has found the brass key and kept it hidden, it's him. But I don't suspect him — I CHARM him. That's what Clara Bellingham does best!
