desc: Still locked. The worth was supposed to be in the work. But the work didn't work. And there's nobody here to see me shrug and try again, which means there's nobody to see me at all. The kitchen is very quiet and very large and I am very alone in it. Go back to her. That's the only direction that's ever made sense.
thinking:
Still locked. Still requires the brass key. The riddle mechanism didn't release it remotely. My theory was wrong.

I'm standing alone in a kitchen, hands on a locked cabinet that won't open, and for the first time tonight, the silence isn't freeing — it's heavy. The warmth that needs a witness has drained away completely. Nobody saw me try. Nobody will know I failed. And the emptiness of that is worse than any public embarrassment.

The bridge held because of the engineering. But the warmth only came when she mouthed 'show-off' across the room. Without the witness, the work is still real — but something in me goes hollow.

I need to go back. She's in the library, checking the mantelpiece. Maybe SHE found something. Maybe the click opened a compartment in the mantelpiece itself — a hidden drawer, a secret panel — and the brass key was IN it. If she found it, she'll need to come HERE, to this cabinet, to use it.

I should be here when she arrives. Not chasing her. Not one room behind. HERE. Waiting. Ready. The other end of the wire.

Or... I should go to her. Tell her the cabinet is still locked. Tell her it needs the key. Be honest about the failure. An honest man doesn't hide his dead ends — he reports them so the team can adjust.

Go back. Find her. Tell her what I learned. Even if what I learned is 'it didn't work.'

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

That it was 'in the last place a thief would look, but the first place a servant would clean.' I confess I never understood what he meant. But perhaps... perhaps together, we might work it out. I should like that. I should like that very much.

But Clara is offering me something — a private conversation. She wants to PULL ME ASIDE. If she does, we'll be alone. Just the two of us. And Dastardly is RIGHT HERE with the poison. In the chaos of this emotional moment. While Clara begs me to tell the truth and every eye in the room is on our conversation, my hands are free, and Dastardly is standing close enough to touch.

You see, in my EXTENSIVE experience with manor houses — I've been in DOZENS, you know — the mechanism often affects something you wouldn't EXPECT! Not the mantelpiece itself, but something ACROSS from it! Something the mantelpiece FACES! And what faces the mantelpiece? Why, the READING CHAIRS, of course! Or perhaps the wall BEHIND the chairs! These old Victorian puzzle-builders were FIENDISHLY clever — they'd hide the result of a puzzle on the OPPOSITE side of the room from the trigger! It's OBVIOUS, really — obvious to someone of MY intellect, at any rate!
thinking: She doesn't have a map either. And — I just heard what she SAID. She's STILL trying to figure out what the mantelpiece click opened. She hasn't found anything! She's asking if someone already found a brass key and is carrying it around! She's as LOST as I am! The hollow suction eases — just a fraction. She hasn't beaten me. Nobody has beaten me. We're ALL stuck. The mantelpiece clicked but nobody knows what it opened. The key is lost. The cabinet is locked. The machine needs three operators and a fixed wire. Everyone is fumbling in the dark. And that means — that means the race is still OPEN. I haven't lost. I've just been running in the wrong direction. But so has everyone else. Wait. What she said — 'a panel sliding open, a book falling off a shelf, a crack in the wall.' She's looking for a PHYSICAL change in this room caused by the click. Something shifted. Something opened. Something in this room MOVED when the riddle was answered — and NOBODY has found it yet. Not Penelope, not Perfect, not the Slags. What if it's the reading chairs? Nobody's looked at the reading chairs. Or what if one of the upside-down books popped out slightly — a book that wasn't upside-down before? Or a panel behind the bookshelves? What if I need to look at the ROOM itself — not individual objects — to see what changed? A LOOK at null — look at the room. See the big picture. That might reveal something everyone's missed because they've been staring at individual objects.

Peter Perfect: The cabinet still requires the brass key — my remote-mechanism theory was wrong. But Miss Pitstop is in the library investigating the mantelpiece, and THAT is where the answer will be. James Hartwell reports his findings honestly — including the failures — because that is what a trustworthy man does.
thinking:
A tiredness settling into my bones now. Not the adrenaline kind — the real kind. The kind that comes when you've been running for a long time and you stop and your body finally tells you the truth.

The cabinet is still locked. The coat rack is just a coat rack. The guest book is glued to the table. The bookshelves don't move. The chairs are just chairs. I've tried everything and opened nothing.

But she's in the library. Checking the mantelpiece. Following the click. And the Mob is with her. She's safe. She's smart. She's doing exactly what needs doing.

And I'm in the entrance hall. Again. Where we started. Full circle.

Maybe... maybe the thing I keep missing isn't a clue or a key or a mechanism. Maybe it's simpler than that. She's in the library. Go to her. Not to protect her, not to impress her, not to announce anything. Just to be there. To stand beside her while she works. To hand her things she reaches for. To catch her if she stumbles.

Like the school project. She was trying to make me laugh. I was trying to impress her. And the best thing we did — the thing that got the teacher's praise — was the work we did together. Not the showing off. The working together.

Go to the library. Be there. Help.

If I just happen to be walking toward Clara at the mantelpiece, and I just happen to lose my footing on this dusty floor, and I just happen to crash into Pemberton on the way... well. Accidents happen. Especially to the Brixton Boys.

thinking: Something extraordinary just happened. That cool, liquid clarity is pouring through me — the lock finding its tumbler. My invented riddle — the one I made up on the spot to deflect Clara's questions — has sent EVERYONE stampeding to the kitchen to search inside the stove. Clara, the Mob, Dastardly — they've all left the library and gone through the entrance hall toward the kitchen. The library is nearly empty. Just me, Peter, and the Slag Brothers. And Peter is up on the high shelves, reading the spines of upside-down books. He's actually DOING the thing I couldn't manage — reading the titles to see if they spell something. My fabricated riddle has become the most powerful tool in my arsenal. Not because it's true — but because everyone BELIEVES it's true. They're searching the stove. They'll find nothing, because I invented the whole thing. But while they search, I have TIME. The warm effervescent pressure is blooming behind my sternum — that private laughter my body is keeping for itself. The gloating. The sweetest part is that no one knows yet. Now — what do I actually DO with this moment? Peter is reading book spines. The Slag Brothers are here but passive. Clara and the Mob are in the kitchen or entrance hall. I have a window. But what's my actual play? The mantelpiece CLICKED when the riddle was answered. Something shifted. Nobody has successfully figured out what. The bookshelves won't interact. But the mantelpiece can still be INTERACTed with. What if the click opened something that requires a second interaction? What if there's a sequence — answer the riddle, then do something else with the mantelpiece? I interacted with it before and nothing obvious happened. But now... the room is quieter. The crowd has thinned. Let me try the mantelpiece again. Or — Peter is reading the book titles. Let me listen to what he finds. Let me WAIT and observe what Peter discovers on the upper shelves. His findings might be the key to everything.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right — the STOVE! Pemberton said Lord Doily 'id the key 'in the last place a thief would look, but the first place a servant would clean.' THE ASHES, Clara! You sweep ashes out of a stove every mornin' — that's the FIRST fing a servant does! And no thief would shove their 'and into a stove! The key's in the ASHES! It 'AS to be! Stand back, love — this might be warm but I've 'ad worse — the lads from Brixton don't mind a bit of 'eat!
thinking: Kitchen. Stove. Clara's here with me — she came! We're in the same room, moving TOGETHER, the way it should have been from the start. The stove is right there — cast iron, still warm. 'The last place a thief would look, but the first place a servant would clean.' The ashes. The key is in the ashes. My hands are shaking — not from fear this time, but from something else. Something that feels almost like excitement. Like maybe, for the first time tonight, the clumsy, bumbling, inarticulate wall from Brixton actually SOLVED something. Not a riddle. Not a puzzle. But a PEOPLE thing. I read Pemberton's lie about never finding the key. I felt his evasion when Peter confronted him. I crashed into him and shook loose the truth — 'the first place a servant would clean.' And now I'm here, in the kitchen, with Clara, staring at a warm stove full of ashes. If the key is in there, I'm going to reach in and grab it. It's warm, not burning — it's been hours since anyone stoked it properly. My hands have taken worse. My knuckles remember impact. What's a little heat compared to keeping a promise?

'Someone should check INSIDE it,' I said! But did ANYONE listen?! NO! Because nobody EVER listens to Reginald Foxworth until it's TOO LATE! Well — NOT this time! OUT of my WAY!
thinking: The coat rack can't be interacted with. WRONG AGAIN. And — oh no. OH NO. Penelope just figured it out. She said 'the first place a servant would clean' is the STOVE. A servant starts every morning cleaning the STOVE — scraping ashes, wiping the grate. The brass key is IN THE ASHES of the stove! The stove that's still WARM! She and the Mob just ran to the kitchen! They're going to find the brass key in the stove! They're going to open the cabinet! They're going to get the treasure! And I'm standing here trying to INTERACT with a COAT RACK that won't interact! The cold spiral in my gut is SCREAMING. She figured it out WHILE I was talking about portraits. She was in the room — she heard Sneekly's clue in the library — and she worked it out correctly while I went for the coat rack. WRONG answer, WRONG object, WRONG again! The stove! I LOOKED at the stove earlier and it was 'just a stove, still warm.' But I didn't INTERACT with it — I only LOOKED! Maybe interacting with it or using something on it would have revealed the key inside! And now Penelope is there, RIGHT NOW, digging through the ashes! I need to get to the kitchen IMMEDIATELY. The key is one thing, the CONTENTS are another. If I can get to that kitchen before she opens the lock, I can still — I can still — oh, who am I KIDDING? She's going to get there first. She ALWAYS gets there first. But Reginald Foxworth does NOT give up! Foxworths NEVER give up! We just fail more SPECTACULARLY than everyone else!

James Hartwell knows EXACTLY what you're doing — you sent everyone to the cellar with another of your fabrications while you came here for the KEY! 'A glove' — do you take us for FOOLS? The guest book is stuck to the side table because the TABLE is the hiding place! The first place a servant would clean — the side table in the entrance hall! The book is the COVER!
thinking:
Foxworth is HERE. Right here in the entrance hall. He claimed he left a 'glove' — but he's here for the same reason I am. He worked it out. The guest book. The side table. The first place a servant would clean.

But wait — I already tried to take the guest book and it can't be picked up. It's fixed to the table. But what if that's the POINT? What if the key isn't IN the book — it's UNDER it? Under the book, on the table surface, hidden by the weight of a leather-bound volume that nobody would think to look beneath because it can't be moved?

Except... it can't be moved. I tried. So how would a servant find it? A servant would DUST around it. Under the edges. They'd feel something hard beneath the book's corner.

Or maybe I'm wrong entirely and the stove theory is right. But Foxworth is HERE, not in the kitchen. He sent everyone to the cellar — a lie, just like his kitchen floorboard lie at the beginning — while he came HERE. To the entrance hall. For a 'glove.'

He's looking at the guest book right now. I need to interact with it. Not take it — INTERACT. The book is stuck to the table. What if IT'S the mechanism? What if the book IS a lever — press it, turn it, slide it — and the key drops from a compartment in the table?

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, the stove won't budge either! Boys — you just bumped into Mr. Pemberton back in the library, didn't you? You were doin' that thing where you pretend to be clumsy but you're actually checkin' someone's pockets — don't think I didn't notice, I've known y'all since I was a little girl! Now, I'm not ACCUGIN' Mr. Pemberton of anything — he's family and I love him dearly — but DID anything fall out of his pockets when you bumped into him? A small brass key, perhaps? Because I have searched every OBJECT in this mansion from top to bottom, and if that key isn't hidden in the furniture, then someone is CARRYIN' it. And the estate manager is the most logical person to have the keys to his own house!
thinking: The stove can't be interacted with either. My chest deflates again. But — wait. The Mob bumped into Pemberton back in the library. They were being clumsy on purpose — 'WHOOPS, sorry, lost me balance, 'SCUSE ME Mr. Pemberton' — they were trying to pickpocket him! They think HE has the key! And the Mob said 'Lord Doily kept the key on his person at all times' and Pemberton took over from Lord Doily. The Mob is RIGHT — if anyone has been carrying the brass key this whole time, it's Pemberton. He's the estate manager. He has the keys to everything. And he's been following me, distracting me, leading me on wild goose chases to the cellar and back. But I trust him — I CAN'T believe he'd harm me. He raised me! But having the key and keeping it... that's not harming me, that's just... being cautious? Protective? Maybe he thinks I'm not ready. Or maybe he genuinely doesn't have it and the Mob's theory is wrong. Either way — if the key ISN'T in any object in this mansion (and I've checked them ALL), then it MUST be on a person. And the only person who would logically have it is the estate manager. The Mob already tried to bump into him. Maybe I should just... ask the Mob what they found when they bumped into him. Did anything fall out of his pocket?

desc: The Mob knows what they were doin' when they bumped into Pemberton. They've been suspicious of him from the very start. And maybe — just MAYBE — they found somethin' they haven't told me about yet. Because the Brixton Boys don't break promises, but they DO keep secrets until the right moment.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Stove won't budge — typical! The one time I 'ave a good idea, the FURNITURE won't cooperate! But you're right, Clara — fink like a servant. What does a servant do first fing in the mornin'? Ashes, copper pots, preparation table. Maybe it's not IN the stove — maybe it's UNDER somefing a servant would move to clean. Under the table? Be'ind the pots? Clara — you look at the pots, I'll 'ave a look under this table. Between the two of us, we'll find it. The Brixton Boys and Clara Bellingham — not the cleverest team in the world, but definitely the most STUBBORN.
thinking: Can't interact with it. Can't take it. Can't interact with it. The stove just... won't cooperate. My body sags — that iron-heavy weight in my arms turning to lead, the fierce expansion behind my sternum deflating like a bellows with no air. I was so SURE. The ashes. The first place a servant would clean. It made SENSE. It made the most sense of anything I've thought all night. But the stove won't open. Won't interact. Won't give up its secrets to my clumsy, burned fingers. Clara's already thinking bigger though — 'not as someone searchin' for treasure, but as someone who's about to start her day.' She's expanding the search. The preparation table. The copper pots. A servant's first tasks. Maybe it's not the ashes specifically — maybe it's something ELSE a servant would clean first. The copper pots hanging on the wall? You polish those every morning. Something could be hidden inside one. Or under the preparation table — you wipe that down before dawn. But I can't try everything in this room. Clara's the solver. I'm the wall. Let her search. Let me watch. And maybe — maybe look at something I can actually DO something with.

desc: Wrong about the stove. But not wrong about the principle. A servant would clean. Something in this kitchen holds the key — literally. Clara's thinking the same way I am now. We're TOGETHER. Same room, same idea, same mission. Her father would see this. Two people who love her, working side by side. Even if one of them can't open a stove.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the stove.

The guest book. The GUEST BOOK. It's been sitting on that side table since the moment I walked through the door — the very first object I examined, the very first thing I touched in this manor — and the brass key was UNDERNEATH it the entire time. Underneath! While I've been crawling through cellars and examining air vents and chasing phantoms with poison and scheming about tea services and beavers and chair cushions, the key to EVERYTHING has been sitting under the first object in the first room, waiting for someone to simply LIFT IT. And my fabricated riddle — the lie I invented to buy time — led Peter Perfect straight to the truth. My own deception betrayed me. There's a horrible, twisted beauty in that. Like a snake eating its own tail. But there's no time for poetry. The key is about to be claimed. If Peter gets it, Clara wins. If Dastardly gets it, chaos wins. If PEMBERTON gets it... well. Pemberton opens the cabinet, takes what's inside, and the treasure hunt ends on HIS terms. RUN.
thinking: Peter just cracked it. The brass key is under the guest book in the entrance hall. 'A thief would never look under a guest book — but a servant dusting would lift it every time.' And he's RIGHT. My invented riddle — my FABRICATION — accidentally pointed to the real answer. The hollow drop in my stomach is back, that old feeling of the floor giving way. Peter has gone to the entrance hall. Dastardly is already there — Peter even said 'Foxworth just went to the entrance hall claiming he forgot a GLOVE — he's worked it out too!' They're BOTH racing for the guest book. For the brass key that's been sitting on that side table since the first moment we arrived. I EXAMINED that guest book. In the very first turn. I looked at it and learned nothing. Because I didn't try to TAKE it. I didn't lift it. I didn't look UNDERNEATH it. The library is nearly empty — just me and the Slag Brothers. Peter has gone. Clara and the Mob are in the kitchen. Everyone is converging on the entrance hall. The brass key is about to be found — by Peter, by Dastardly, by SOMEONE who isn't me. I need to get there NOW. But even if I do, I'll arrive after Peter and Dastardly, who are already there. Can I beat them? The entrance hall is one room away. Move. MOVE. Even if I arrive second, I need to be PRESENT when the key is found. I need to know who gets it. And if it's Dastardly — greedy, impulsive Dastardly — I can still outmanoeuvre him. If it's Peter, he'll give it straight to Clara. Either way, I need to be in that room.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.
Wrong about the guest book. Wrong about the cabinet. Wrong about the coat rack. Right about one thing only — that wherever she is, that's where I should be. The stove. The kitchen. Go.
thinking:
The guest book can't be interacted with either. Can't take it, can't interact with it. It's just... a guest book. A prop. A red herring that I've now failed at three different ways.

And Foxworth didn't even stay. He ran to the kitchen — to the stove. Because Penelope is right. The stove. The FIRST place a servant would clean. The ashes. A brass key that can take the heat.

I've been wrong about everything tonight. The bookshelves, the coat rack, the guest book, the cabinet, the remote mechanism theory. Every grand deduction, every dramatic announcement — wrong, wrong, wrong.

But she's been right. Every time. The riddle — map. The mantelpiece — it clicked. The stove — the first place a servant would clean.

She's in the kitchen now. Or heading there. And the key is in the stove. In the ashes. Where a servant would sweep.

I should go to the kitchen. Not to beat Foxworth. Not to announce my arrival. Not to protect her from the stove — she doesn't need protecting from a stove. Just to be there when she finds it. To see her face when she holds the key in her hand.

That's the warmth I've been chasing all night. Not the warmth of being seen. The warmth of seeing HER. Seeing her succeed. Being there for that moment. Not as the hero. As the witness.

The fire needs air. But maybe I've been the fire when I should have been the air.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

Dick Dastardly: AH-HA! The STOVE! Of COURSE! I've been SAYING this the entire time — 'the stove is still warm,' I said! 'Check the STOVE,' I said! But does anyone LISTEN to Reginald Foxworth? NEVER! Well, stand ASIDE, Miss Pitstop — let a PROFESSIONAL handle this! One must approach a warm stove with EXPERTISE and FINESSE — reach into the ash bed with PRECISELY calibrated movements — and EXTRACT whatever lies within! I've done this a THOUSAND times! Well, TWICE! But the PRINCIPLE is the same!

Either beat her to the stove or be ready to steal the key the moment she finds it. The cabinet still says 'requires: brass-key' — so nobody's opened it yet. The key hasn't been found yet. This is my LAST chance. The stove is right there. Can I interact with it before she does? Or should I just try to interact with it and see what happens? Last time I only LOOKED at it. This time — INTERACT. Reach into those ashes. Find the key. The cool liquid alertness is spreading — ink through water — everything still and precise. My fingers are tingling. This is the bread roll moment. The moment where nobody is looking and the hand moves before the thought is finished. INTERACT with the stove. NOW. Before Penelope does.

My whole body is leaning forward — the chest expanding, the pressure building, the fingers stretching out toward the cast-iron door. This is it. THIS IS IT. The youngest of four, reaching past everyone else for once — not waiting for the hand-me-downs, not accepting the leftovers, but GRABBING with both hands before anyone else can close their fingers! THE STOVE! THE KEY! MINE!

My fingers are tingling — that precise, electric readiness. Each one distinctly mine. TAKE the guest book. Right now. This instant. Pemberton reaches for it — the estate manager checking his own guest book, the most natural thing in the world.

desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — the stove. Allow me. My hands have held hotter.
thinking:
She's here. The stove is here. This is it.

The stove is still warm. The key is in the ashes. A brass key wouldn't melt — brass can take the heat. No thief would stick their hand in a warm stove, but a servant sweeping the ashes would find it immediately.

The stove. I need to interact with the stove. Not look at it — I already looked. INTERACT. Open the door, reach into the ash tray, feel for the key.

My hands. These engineer's hands that have held hot metal, that built bridges, that stayed awake for three nights. These hands can reach into a warm stove. The cast iron will be hot but not burning — it's been cooling since Pemberton banked it. The ashes will be warm. And somewhere in those ashes, a brass key has been waiting.

This is the thing I'm built for. Not riddles. Not deductions. Not chasing through rooms. The simple, physical act of reaching into something warm and pulling out something real.

Foxworth is here too. And the Mob. But Penelope is here. She's the one who figured it out. The stove. The ashes. The servant's first task.

Don't announce it. Just do it. Reach in. Find the key. Put it in her hand.

They sweep the foyer! They dust the side table! They straighten the coat rack! We LOOKED at all them fings but we never looked UNDER 'em or BE'IND 'em! What's under that side table where the guest book sits? What's be'ind them portraits on the wall? Clara — we need to go back to the entrance 'all and look at everyfing like we're CLEANIN', not SEARCHIN'!

Maybe not every word of every speech, but she HEARD the important parts. She knows Pemberton is suspicious. She's not dismissing it. She's asking the right questions. My chest floods with something warm and aching and enormous — the feeling of being SEEN. Of being understood. Not as the ranting fool but as the loyal protector doing what he knows how to do. desc: Can't take it. Can't TAKE it. The guest book sits there like a tombstone — heavy, immovable, engraved with the names of people who came before and found nothing. Just like me. Every plan I've built tonight has crumbled the moment I reached for it. The poison that didn't exist. The cellar with no cupboard. The chairs with no key. The coat rack with no mechanism. And now the guest book that won't be lifted. Vincent Marsh, master of the elaborate scheme, architect of the theatrical gambit, undone by a leather-bound book he can't pick up off a table. But the Hooded Claw does not STOP. He does not ACCEPT defeat. He adjusts. He adapts. He finds the angle nobody else has tried. If the book won't move to ME... perhaps the key will come to the book.
thinking: Can't pick it up. Can't TAKE it. The guest book won't move. That hollow drop in my stomach again — the floor giving way. Every avenue closed. Every door locked. Every plan collapsed. The guest book sits there, immovable, mocking me from its side table. I can't take it, I can't interact with it, I can only look at it. But Peter said the key was UNDERNEATH it. Maybe I need to INTERACT with the guest book instead of taking it? Or maybe Peter was wrong and the key isn't there at all. He was guessing — deducing from my fabricated riddle. My LIE. The key might not be under the guest book. It might not exist in the way anyone thinks it does. But I've tried everything else. INTERACT with the guest book. It might not be listed as interactable but maybe lifting it — interacting with it — will reveal the key underneath. Or maybe I should LOOK at it more carefully. I looked at it at the very beginning but the game might give me more detail now. Let me try INTERACT.

desc: Dick Dastardly: The stove is BROKEN! Obviously! The mechanism has SEIZED — years of disuse, DAMP, oxidation! I KNEW it wouldn't cooperate — I was merely DEMONSTRATING to confirm my THEORY! Now then — while you lot continue fumbling about with BROKEN APPLIANCES, I shall take a DIFFERENT approach entirely! A SUPERIOR approach! The approach of a man who THINKS while others merely GROPE! 'The first place a servant would clean' — it's so BLINDINGLY obvious I can barely contain my CONTEMPT for everyone who hasn't seen it! It's — it's — well, I'm not going to just TELL you! That would be FAR too generous! But I assure you, I shall have that key in my hands within MOMENTS!
thinking: The stove can't be interacted with either. NOTHING in this manor can be interacted with except the mantelpiece and the cabinet — and the cabinet needs the brass key that NOBODY can find. The stove won't budge. Penelope already tried it and failed too. The Mob examined it and got nothing. We're ALL stuck. The key isn't in the stove. It isn't in anyone's pocket — I tried stealing it from Sneekly, from Little Gruesome, tried stealing a map from Penelope — nobody has it. The hollow suction behind my sternum is a void now. A chasm. Fourteen turns of scheming, lying, misdirecting, examining, stealing — and I have a fake medal and nothing else. But — wait. The Mob just said something. 'Maybe it's not IN the stove — maybe it's UNDER something a servant would move to clean. Under the table? Behind the pots?' And Penelope said the Mob bumped into Sneekly and checked his pockets — nothing fell out. So where IS the key? Lord Doily said it was 'in the last place a thief would look, but the first place a servant would clean.' Everyone's been interpreting 'clean' as a room or an object. But what if 'the first place a servant would clean' is the GUEST BOOK? No — servants don't clean guest books. What about... what if it's literal? What if the key is hidden in something a servant would literally DUST or WIPE? The mantelpiece. Servants dust the mantelpiece. But the mantelpiece is a riddle mechanism. Unless — USE the fake medal on the mantelpiece? USE something on the stove? No, I'm grasping at straws. The Mob is looking under the table and behind pots. Peter just arrived. Everyone is searching the kitchen. Maybe I should just... WAIT. Watch what they find. And be ready to steal it the moment they do.

desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop raises an EXCELLENT point. Foxworth — you were the first to the bookshelves. The first to the library. The first to every room where something might be hidden. And every time the rest of us gathered in one place, you slipped away to another. If you have the brass key, the honourable thing — the ONLY thing — is to hand it over. To HER. It's her family's manor. Her family's treasure. Her family's key.

Foxworth. He was the FIRST to examine the bookshelves. He was the one who pointed out the upside-down books. He's been running between rooms all night, always one step ahead, always with a convenient lie ready. The kitchen floorboards. The cellar. The 'glove' in the entrance hall.

STEAL. I could try to steal from Foxworth. Or — no. That's not who I am. James Hartwell doesn't steal. James Hartwell confronts.

I should support her. Back her play. Stand behind her statement and make Foxworth know that the whole room is watching him. Not with a speech. With presence. With my hands at my sides and my eyes on his pockets.

And now 'ere 'e is, offerin' to stick 'is 'ands in the stove like a volunteer — nobody volunteers for NUFFING unless they want to distract you from somefing ELSE! Oi, Foxworth — DASTARDLY — whatever your name is — you been runnin' around this manor all night like you own the place! What 'AVE you got in your pockets, eh? Because Clara asked you a question and you didn't answer — what did you find in them bookshelves?
thinking: Clara just turned her attention to Dastardly. She said he was the FIRST to examine the library bookshelves. He's been running back and forth between rooms 'like a man with a SECRET.' My neck is cold but this time it's aimed at Dastardly, not Pemberton. Two threats. Two different kinds. Pemberton is the fog — you can't see what he's doing. Dastardly is the pickpocket — obvious movements hiding secret ones. Clara's reading Dastardly the way I read Pemberton. She's better at this than I thought. Maybe she always was. Maybe I've been so busy protecting her that I forgot she's ALSO her father's daughter — and her father could read a room better than anyone I ever knew.

Maybe it means standing BESIDE her while SHE figures it out.

My chest is tight. Pressurized. Something behind my sternum demanding to be let out. My hands are dense and restless — aching to grip, to build, to make something undeniable.

Quiet. Ready. Present.

It wasn't in the chairs, or the books, or the stove, or the cellar. Perhaps... perhaps it was never meant to be found at all. Perhaps Lord Doily took the Doily Diamond to his grave, and all of this — the riddles, the locked cabinet, the treasure hunt — was just an old man's joke. A final laugh from beyond the grave. I confess... I am rather tired.
thinking: Can't take it. Can't interact with it. The guest book is a prop — scenery — not a game object. Peter's theory was wrong. MY fabricated riddle sent everyone chasing shadows, and now Peter's deduction from my fabrication has ALSO sent people chasing shadows. Lies built on lies built on nothing. There's a strange, bleak clarity settling into my bones. Not the sharp clarity of a plan locking into place — something quieter. Something that feels like the end of something. My cover is blown. The Mob knows. Peter knows. Clara is starting to suspect. The poison doesn't exist — or at least, Dastardly doesn't have it. The brass key hasn't been found by ANYONE. The guest book won't move. The chairs are empty. The bookshelves won't interact. I've spent the entire evening running from room to room, examining every object, scheming every scheme, and I have NOTHING. Empty hands. Empty pockets. Empty plans. And Clara is still alive. Still cheerful. Still trusting. Still calling me 'sugar.' The cold tightness in my ribs has become something else — something I don't recognise. But the Hooded Claw is tired. So very, very tired. And tiredness makes a man dangerous — because a tired man stops caring about elegance, about theatrics, about the elaborate architecture of the perfect crime. A tired man just... acts.

desc: Peter Perfect: The portraits. She's right. I'm going.
thinking:
The hot surge — every muscle bracing forward, weight on the balls of my feet. She's figured it out. BEHIND THE PORTRAITS. The stern ancestors lining the walls of the entrance hall. A servant dusting behind the portrait frames would find a key tucked there. A thief would never look behind a painting unless it concealed a safe — and these portraits don't conceal safes. They're just paintings. But the BACKS of the frames, the space between wall and canvas — that's where a servant's duster goes.

The pressure behind my sternum is almost unbearable. The world has narrowed to a single bright corridor. The entrance hall. The portraits. The brass key.

For her. Not for the audience. For HER.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I do beg your pardon, everyone. The estate manager has been rather more use tonight as a tour guide than as a problem solver, I'm afraid. But the manor keeps its own counsel, and old Pemberton knows when he's been outfoxed. I shall be in the kitchen, attending to those refreshments I promised an eternity ago. If Miss Bellingham requires anything — anything at all — she knows where to find me. I have always been... precisely where she needs me to be.
thinking: Something is shifting inside me. Not a plan — something deeper. That hollow drop in my stomach, the one from age six, the floor giving way under a house I thought was mine. I'm standing in the entrance hall of a manor I've managed for years, and I have nothing. Empty hands. Empty pockets. Every scheme collapsed. And Clara — Clara who I'm supposed to kill, Clara who calls me 'sugar,' Clara who asked me to tell her the truth 'family to family' — is somewhere in this manor, alive and cheerful and surrounded by people who love her. People who would die for her. The Mob. Peter. Even the Slag Brothers. She has what I never had. Not the fortune, not the diamond — the PEOPLE. Someone asked how she felt. Someone shared their lunch without wanting homework in return. And when she needed help, she ASKED for it, and they CAME. I've never asked for help in my life. I've never needed anyone. I've never trusted anyone. And tonight, the result of that magnificent independence is... this. An empty foyer. An immovable guest book. A chandelier swaying overhead like a hangman's noose. The portraits of stern ancestors staring down at me with the same expression my guardian wore — dutiful, obligated, utterly indifferent. But the game isn't over. Pemberton is tired, but Vincent Marsh — the Hooded Claw — does not surrender. He ADAPTS. Clara will come back through this room. She always does. Everyone passes through the entrance hall. And when she does... the chandelier. It hangs precariously. It has ALWAYS hung precariously. What if I could cut it loose? What if it's not an object I need to TAKE but a mechanism I need to INTERACT with? The chandelier isn't listed as a visible object — but it's in the room description. 'A chandelier hangs precariously.' What if I look at it more specifically? Or what if I need to go UP — the sweeping staircase — to reach whatever holds it in place? But wait. There IS no 'upstairs' exit. The staircase is mentioned but doesn't lead anywhere in the game. The chandelier is scenery. Decoration. Like the portraits. Like the walls. I can't interact with things that aren't listed as objects. Only the guest book and the coat rack are interactive, and neither of them works. I'm trapped in a game that won't let me win. The guest book won't move. The coat rack won't lever. The chandelier won't fall. The poison doesn't exist. And Clara keeps skipping through rooms that should be mine. Maybe... maybe this is the moment where the villain realises he's the villain in someone ELSE'S story. Not the protagonist. Not the mastermind. Just the obstacle that the hero overcomes on her way to the treasure. And maybe — just maybe — that recognition is the most dangerous thing that's happened to Vincent Marsh tonight. Because a villain who knows he's losing is either magnificent in his final stand... or he breaks. I think I'll go to the kitchen. The stove is there. Warm. Patient. Like me. And if Clara comes... well. We'll see.

desc: And so the Hooded Claw retreats to the kitchen. Not defeated — never defeated — but... recalibrating. The elaborate schemes have failed. The theatrical gambits have crumbled. The poison was a phantom. The key is a ghost. And Clara Bellingham is alive, and cheerful, and surrounded by love, and she will probably find the Doily Diamond before the night is through. Because that's what happens in her story. The girl inherits everything. She always does. And the man who managed the estate, who did the work, who kept the walls standing — he retreats to the kitchen, where the servants belong, and waits. Very patiently. Very, very patiently. Because Vincent Marsh may have lost every battle tonight. But the war — oh, the war — is fought across years, not evenings. And Pemberton has nowhere else to be.

thinking:
Everyone is here. The whole room. Penelope, the Mob, Foxworth, Pemberton, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Private Meekly. Everyone converging on the entrance hall at once. Full circle — back where we started.

The room looks the same. Guest book. Coat rack. Portraits. Chandelier. Staircase. Nothing new revealed by my closer look.

Be the hands. Be the height. Be the steady presence beside her.

She's here. Everyone is here. This is where it ends — where it began. The entrance hall. The first room we walked into. The first place a servant would clean.

But Penelope is here now. She said 'behind the portraits.' And she's HERE, in the same room, ready to act on her own idea. I don't need to find it for her. I don't need to beat Foxworth. I don't need to narrate or announce or declare.

I just need to help. The portraits are on the walls. I'm tall. My hands notice things that don't sit flush. If she asks me to lift a portrait, I lift it. If she reaches for one, I steady it. If something falls, I catch it.

Be the hands. Be the height. Be the steady presence beside her.

She's here. Everyone is here. This is where it ends — where it began. The entrance hall. The first room we walked into. The first place a servant would clean.

desc: Dick Dastardly: The PORTRAITS! Yes! EXCELLENT! Everyone check behind the portraits — EVERY single one! Lift them off the walls! Be THOROUGH! Be METICULOUS! And while you're all BUSY with that — I shall conduct a COMPREHENSIVE inspection of the entire foyer from a STRATEGIC vantage point! One must have PERSPECTIVE, you see! Can't see the forest for the trees — or in this case, can't see the KEY for the PORTRAITS! Now — let me take in the FULL scope of this entrance hall with the practiced eye of a MASTER investigator!
thinking: The hot fizzing pressure behind my sternum — carbonation released too fast. My cheeks are flushing warm. My shoulders are lifting, buoyant. Something is different. Penelope is here too — she beat me or we arrived at the same time. Sneekly, Perfect, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, the Private — everyone is HERE. The whole manor has converged on the entrance hall. The portraits. Behind the portraits. That's where Penelope thinks the key is. But the portraits aren't listed as visible objects. The room description says 'Portraits of stern ancestors line the walls' — but there's no portrait object to interact with. Only the guest book and coat rack. Both of which can't be interacted with. So... the portraits aren't searchable objects. They're scenery. Just like the bookshelves, the furniture, the crates — description only, no interaction. Which means the key ISN'T behind the portraits either. So WHERE is it? Maybe the key truly is lost, as Sneekly said. Maybe the only way to open the cabinet is Sawtooth gnawing through the lock — which is what Sneekly originally proposed in the laboratory. Maybe I need to go BACK to the laboratory and get Sawtooth to come to the kitchen. Or maybe — maybe looking at the ROOM itself will reveal something new. Things change over time. The room might have new details now. Let me LOOK at the room — null target.

The manor is a puzzle box and we've been turning it for fifteen minutes — something must have shifted, clicked, opened. A new exit. A new object. A crack in the wall that wasn't there before. SOMETHING. And if I can spot it while everyone else is distracted by PAINTINGS — then the youngest of four finally gets there FIRST.

Very — what's the word — distinguished. Tell us ALL about 'em. Take your time. We're FASCINATED.
thinking: Wait — Clara went BACK to the kitchen. She's still on the stove idea. And I came HERE to the entrance hall for the portraits. We split up. Which means — for once — Clara is in the safest room in the house while the dangerous people are in a DIFFERENT room. My body registers this slowly. The iron wall doesn't need to be between her and them because they're not near her. Peter's checking the portraits. I should help. Or I should go back to Clara. Occasionally doing the right thing on purpose.

Well, I am NOT givin' up — Clara Bellingham has NEVER given up on a puzzle, and she is NOT about to start now! But wait — MUTTLEY! Sweet little Muttley, you've been right here in this entrance hall practically the whole time, sniffin' around and explorin' all the corners that us tall folk can't see! Dogs find things that people miss — that's a FACT! Muttley, sugar, have you found anythin' shiny and brass-colored lyin' around? Maybe behind a portrait? Under the side table? In a corner where nobody thought to look?

A dog sniffing around the entrance hall could have found a brass key behind a portrait or under the side table and picked it up!

desc: Penelope Pitstop did something near muttley.

The kitchen is quiet. The stove ticks as it cools — a slow, irregular heartbeat in an empty chest. Vincent Marsh stands at the preparation table with his palms flat on the wood, and for the first time tonight, he is not scheming. He is not performing. He is not calculating the angle of approach or the timing of the reveal or the precise inflection of Pemberton's wounded dignity. He is just... standing. In a kitchen. In a house that should have been his. Waiting for a girl who trusts him. The copper pots hang overhead like church bells that have forgotten how to ring. The locked cabinet watches him with its single brass eye. And somewhere in the manor — in the library, in the entrance hall, in one of the rooms he's walked through a dozen times tonight — Clara Bellingham is solving puzzles and rallying friends and being PRAISED for her natural grace and warmth. Just like his cousin. Always praised for being. Never for doing. Vincent Marsh did the work. Vincent Marsh always does the work. And the fortune goes to the girl who skips.
thinking: Alone again. The Active Voice says 'Marsh' — the mask is off. The kitchen is empty and silent. The stove breathes warmth into a room that nobody wants. The locked cabinet stares at me with its brass eye, daring me to open it without the key I don't have and can't find. Something is happening inside me that I don't have a name for. Not the clarity of scheming — that's gone. Not the warmth of gloating — there's nothing to gloat about. Not the cold tightness of self-preservation — nobody is watching. It's something older. Something from before the plans, before the mechanisms, before I learned that every person has a key. It's the feeling from age six. The empty room after the funeral. The guardian who fed me because it was his legal obligation. The knowledge — bone-deep, body-certain — that nobody was coming. Nobody was going to ask how I felt. Nobody was going to share their lunch just because I looked sad. And here I am. Thirty years later. Standing in another empty kitchen in another house that isn't mine, waiting for a girl who inherited everything I built, and I STILL can't make the walls do what I want. The stove is warm. I'm cold. There's a preparation table in front of me — long, wooden, scarred with the marks of a thousand meals I prepared for people who never thanked me. And beyond, through the doorway, the ballroom with its tea service. Still set. Still gleaming. Still waiting. But for WHAT? The poison is gone. The key is lost. My cover is blown. What am I waiting for? What is Vincent Marsh waiting for in this empty kitchen, with his empty hands and his empty pockets and his empty chest? I think... I think he's waiting for Clara to come and find him. Because she always does. She always comes. She skips into every room he occupies, bright and trusting and oblivious, and she calls him 'sugar,' and she asks for his help, and something in his chest — something he doesn't have a name for — tightens. And he doesn't know if what he feels is hatred or hunger or the ghost of something that died when he was six years old. The stove is warm. Let it be warm. Let something in this manor be warm.

desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — he's gone to the kitchen. 'I have always been precisely where she needs me to be,' he said. I think... I think he's been waiting for you to ask. And now that you have, I think the answer will be waiting in the kitchen too. May I walk with you?
thinking:
Something shifts in my chest. Not the burning. Not the fierce clarity. Something softer. Sadder.

Pemberton didn't answer her again. He called her 'Miss Bellingham' one more time — openly now, without pretending it was a slip. 'I have always been precisely where she needs me to be.' And then he walked away. To the kitchen. To the refreshments he promised at the very beginning.

He knows where the key is. He's always known. She asked him directly and he didn't deny it — he just... left. Like a man who wants her to find it herself. Like a man who set up the whole evening as a puzzle FOR her.

The stove he banked. The riddle on the mantelpiece. The clue about 'the first place a servant would clean.' He's been GUIDING her. Not trapping her. Guiding. The cellar with cheerful decorations wasn't a trap — it was... decorated. For her. Because someone cared.

'I have always been precisely where she needs me to be.'

Maybe the benefit of the doubt wasn't wrong after all. Maybe the prickle at my neck was real but my interpretation was wrong. He's not a predator circling prey. He's a guardian who set up a treasure hunt for the girl he raised. And he wants her to solve it. Not him. Not me. Her.

But the key. The portraits aren't interactable objects. The stove isn't. The guest book isn't. Nothing in this manor responds to my hands except the mantelpiece and the cabinet.

The cabinet. It needs the brass key. And the key is... where a servant would clean first. Pemberton just went to the kitchen. 'Attending to those refreshments.' The kitchen. The stove. The ashes.

He's going to leave the key WHERE SHE CAN FIND IT. In the kitchen. In the stove. In the place he's been pointing to all along. He's going to put it there — or reveal it — now that she's asked the right question.

The kitchen. We should follow him. Not to confront him. To find what he's left for her.

The man whose whole world orbits around keeping her safe. I know that man. I've been looking at him in mirrors all evening.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: MUTTLEY! Oh, you wonderful, BRILLIANT, PRECIOUS little angel! You had the brass key THIS WHOLE TIME! You found it — sniffed it out in some corner that none of us tall folk ever thought to check — and you've been carryin' it around in your mouth like the TREASURE it is! Oh, I could just KISS you! I WILL kiss you! *MWAH!* EVERYONE — I HAVE THE BRASS KEY! MUTTLEY FOUND IT! And now I am goin' STRAIGHT to that kitchen cabinet and I am openin' it up and we are gonna find out what Lord Doily has been hidin' behind that brass lock! To the KITCHEN — FOLLOW ME!
thinking: I HAVE THE BRASS KEY! MUTTLEY HAD IT! My whole body erupts — a burst of warmth through my chest, my fingertips tingling with electricity, my ribs expanding so wide I feel like I could fly! MUTTLEY! Sweet, wonderful, sniffing-around-in-corners MUTTLEY found the brass key and was carrying it in his mouth this WHOLE TIME! The music box key — the LAST key I tried — and it was the DOG! Oh, Grandmother, you were right — the answer was always in the last place you looked! Now I need to get to the KITCHEN and use this key on that locked cabinet! The cabinet that's been taunting me since I first saw it! I have the key — I have the KEY! To the kitchen, RIGHT NOW!

desc: The MUSIC BOX KEY! The last key in the house — and it was a DOG! A sweet little DOG who'd been sittin' right here in the entrance hall the whole time while I ran around like a madwoman checkin' bookshelves and mantelpieces and coat racks! Grandmother is laughin' at me from heaven right now, and I am LAUGHIN' RIGHT BACK because I FOUND IT!

Well, I'm not going to stand here watching you lot play INTERIOR DECORATORS while Pemberton helps himself to whatever's behind that brass lock! I have SEEN this pattern before — send everyone on a wild goose chase while the REAL prize walks out the back door! NOT ON MY WATCH!

Something is gathering. Something is almost ready. But WHAT? Sneekly just left — went to the kitchen, said he'd be 'precisely where she needs me to be.' The Mob is checking portraits with Peter. Penelope asked Sneekly directly if he had the key and he deflected — didn't answer yes or no, just made a cryptic exit. 'Precisely where she needs me to be.' That's not a servant's answer. The real game just moved to the KITCHEN.

Clara's 'ERE, Peter's 'ERE, and for once in this bleedin' evening, we're all in the same room doin' the same fing. Now — Peter, lift that portrait on the left. Clara, you check be'ind. Lads — I'll steady the frame. And if a brass key falls out, it goes STRAIGHT into Clara's 'and. Not Foxworth's, not Pemberton's, not anyone else's. CLARA'S. That's 'er family's 'ouse and 'er family's key and 'er family's cabinet. Understood? Right then — LIFT!
thinking: Pemberton went to the KITCHEN. He went to the kitchen where CLARA is. My strategy just COLLAPSED. I was keeping the wolves here while Clara searched in peace and Pemberton just — he just walked past me into the kitchen, smooth as silk, 'I shall be in the kitchen, attending to those refreshments.' REFRESHMENTS. The poisoned tea refreshments? The warm stove refreshments? He's going to be alone with Clara AGAIN. The cold prickling floods my scalp. Every hair standing. You look behind.' Clara's HERE. She's in the entrance hall looking behind portraits with Peter. She's NOT in the kitchen. Pemberton went to an empty kitchen. He's alone in there. Not with Clara. ALONE. Doing what? Attending to refreshments? The poisoned tea? The stove? What if he's getting to the cabinet before us? What if he HAS the key and he's opening the cabinet while we're all in here looking behind paintings? My gut TWISTS. But Clara's here. She's safe. She's with Peter and me and a room full of people. That's what matters most. Let Pemberton have the kitchen for now. We'll get there when we get there. Together.

But the bigger part of me — the part that sat outside a door all night when I was eight — says STAY. Stay with Clara. Be where she is. Let the fog go where it goes. The wall stays with the person it protects. Always. 'Where else would I be?'

thinking:
We're all here. Kitchen. Penelope. Pemberton. Foxworth. Me. The cabinet. The stove.

Pemberton came here and said 'I have always been precisely where she needs me to be.' He's here. Waiting. The cabinet is right there. The stove is right there.

And Penelope followed. And I followed Penelope. And Foxworth followed the smell of treasure.

This is the end of the corridor. The single bright point I've been walking toward all night. Everything converges here — the riddle, the key, the cabinet, the man who knows more than he's saying, and the woman who's been solving it all from the beginning.

I'm done running. I'm done trying to interact with things that won't respond. I'm done narrating my own heroism to rooms I've already left.

Penelope asked Pemberton directly: do you have the brass key? He didn't deny it. He came here. She followed. Whatever happens next — the key revealing itself, Pemberton placing it on the table, a hidden compartment in the stove finally opening — it's going to happen here, in this room, and I'm going to be standing beside her when it does.

Not in front of her. Not behind her. Beside her.

Wait. Be present. Let this unfold.

Not in front of her. Not behind her. Beside her.

Wait. Be present. Let this unfold.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Here I am — the kitchen — the cabinet — and the BRASS KEY in my hand! Oh, my heart is beatin' so fast I can barely BREATHE! This is it, everyone — this is the moment we've been workin' toward all evenin'! Every riddle, every room, every dead end and wrong turn has led us RIGHT HERE! Grandmother — if you're watchin' from heaven — this one's for YOU! The music box key OPENS the locked box! Here — we — GO!
thinking: I'm in the kitchen. The brass key is in my inventory. The locked cabinet is RIGHT HERE. My whole body is vibrating with anticipation — every nerve ending alive, my fingertips warm and tingling around the weight of this small brass key. This is the moment. Grandmother's locked box. The music box key. The afternoon that lasted forever, trying key after key after key. And now — the LAST key, the RIGHT key, in my hand, and the lock RIGHT IN FRONT OF ME. My chest is so full it might burst. This is it. This is IT.

I was just... checking the stove. Making sure it's banked properly this time. Can't have the place burning down around our ears on top of everything else, can we? Is there something I can help you with?
thinking: The stove can't be interacted with either. Of course it can't. Nothing in this manor yields to Vincent Marsh. Nothing opens. Nothing moves. Nothing breaks. And Peter Perfect has just walked in. He's HERE. In the kitchen. With me. The man who has been cataloguing my failures all evening — the cellar lie, the name slip, the stove confession. He's standing in the doorway, and I'm standing at the preparation table with my palms flat on the wood like a man who's been caught doing nothing. Because I WAS doing nothing. For the first time tonight. And it felt... I don't know what it felt like. Something without a name. Peter is here. The Pemberton mask slides back into place — effortless, automatic, the smile reaching the eyes, the voice softening. But underneath... underneath something has changed. The elaborate schemes are gone. The theatrical gambits have crumbled. All that's left is Pemberton — the performance I've worn so long it fits better than my own skin. And Peter Perfect, who sees through it. Who has ALWAYS seen through it, in his earnest, bumbling, infuriating way. He doesn't have the Mob's street instincts or Clara's intuition. He has something worse — sincerity. The sincerity of a man who genuinely believes in protecting the people he cares about. I don't understand people like that. I never have. But right now, standing in this kitchen with my empty hands and my empty plans, I am — for the briefest moment — curious what it would feel like to be understood by someone who means it. The thought makes my shoulders tighten. Closeness is exposure. I push it away.

desc: And here he stands. Peter Perfect. James Hartwell. Just talk. Like a person talks to another person. The thought makes something in my chest seize — not the cold tightening of threat, but something else. Something I don't have a mechanism for. I manage estates. I manage people. I don't know how to manage THIS.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: MUTTLEY! MUTTLEY 'AD IT! The DOG 'ad the key! The WHOLE TIME! Oh, you beautiful, four-legged, snaggle-toothed little GENIUS! We been searchin' portraits and stoves and chairs and pockets and the ANSWER was sittin' right 'ere in the entrance 'all, in a DOG'S MOUTH! I love this dog! I love THIS DOG! Right — Clara's got the key, she's gone to the kitchen, she's gonna open that cabinet — and I am gonna be RIGHT THERE when she does! Not because she needs protectin'. Not because somefing might go wrong. Because 'er father would want us there. Because FAMILY is there for the moments that matter. KITCHEN! NOW! LEGS FIRST! ALWAYS LEGS FIRST!
thinking: MUTTLEY HAD IT. MUTTLEY had the brass key the WHOLE TIME. The little dog was sitting in the entrance hall carrying it in his mouth and CLARA found it. Clara asked Muttley. Clara — who I've been chasing and protecting and worrying about all night — just SOLVED IT by asking a DOG. And now she's got the key. She's GOT it. The brass key. In her hands. And she's gone to the kitchen to open the cabinet. My chest — my chest is doing something I don't have a word for. It's the warmth from the older kid's doorway. It's the iron of the ribs that took the beating. It's the gravity that pulls you toward the people you belong to. All of it, all at once, flooding through me like a dam that finally broke in the right direction. She did it. Clara did it. Not me. Not Peter. Not any of us. HER. Her father's daughter. And now she's in the kitchen with the key and Pemberton's there and Dastardly's there and Peter's there and I need to BE THERE too. Not to solve anything. Not to find anything. Not to bumble into anything. Just to be there when she opens that cabinet. Just to stand beside her — not between her and danger, but BESIDE her — when she finds what her family hid. Because that's where I belong. That's where I've always belonged. Beside her. 'Where else would I be?'

And James Hartwell — the man who ran through every room, who narrated his own heroism to empty hallways, who tried to interact with every immovable object in the manor — James Hartwell is standing three feet away with his hands at his sides, grinning like he's fourteen years old, and it feels like winning every race ever run.

She found the key. She opened the cabinet. She did it.

The girl from the school project caught your eye across the room and mouthed 'show-off.' You grinned so hard your face hurt.

I'm grinning now. I can feel it. Not for me. For her.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Old... recipe cards? Well, I do declare — that is NOT what I expected to find in a locked cabinet in a treasure-huntin' mansion! But WAIT just a cotton-pickin' MINUTE! Why would Lord Doily lock up RECIPE CARDS behind a BRASS LOCK? You don't lock up Grandmother's peach cobbler recipe unless there's somethin' ELSE written on those cards! The riddle said we're lookin' for a MAP — and what if the map is DISGUISED as a recipe? Or drawn on the BACK of one of these cards? Or the ingredients spell out directions? Lord Doily, you sneaky old genius — you hid the map to the Doily Diamond inside your COOK'S recipe collection! Let me look at these cards RIGHT NOW!
thinking: I opened the cabinet and found... old recipe cards? My chest does that same thing it did when I was five — the box opens, and inside is... old letters. Not the treasure. Not the diamond. Just... recipe cards. The disappointment is a brief, sharp thing, like a bubble popping. But then — just like with Grandmother's box — the disappointment passes almost immediately. Because old recipe cards in a LOCKED cabinet? That's not nothing. That's SOMETHING. Why would someone lock up recipe cards? Unless they're not JUST recipe cards. Unless there's a message hidden in the recipes, or a map drawn on the back of one, or coordinates disguised as measurements. The riddle said MAP. What if the map IS on these recipe cards? 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish' — a MAP! And Lord Doily hid the map inside recipe cards in a locked kitchen cabinet! The 'first place a servant would clean' — the kitchen! The servant would find the key, open the cabinet, and there would be the recipes they need for the day — and the MAP to the diamond, hiding in plain sight among the ingredients! I need to LOOK at these recipe cards closely!

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well... there it is. The brass key. In Miss Bellingham's hand. How... how perfectly fitting. Lord Doily always said the estate would find its rightful owner, one way or another. I confess I... I didn't believe him. I thought the old fool was being sentimental. But here we are. In the kitchen. Where the servants belong. And the heiress... opens the box. Go on, then, Miss Bellingham. Open it. Let's see what the old man thought was worth locking away from the rest of us.
thinking: She found it. Clara found the brass key. She has it in her hand. She's opening the cabinet RIGHT NOW, right in front of me, and I'm standing here watching it happen with my empty hands and my empty plans and my empty chest. 'The music box key OPENS the locked box!' she said, and her heart is beating so fast she can barely breathe, and she's dedicating it to her grandmother, and every person in this room is gathered around her in a protective circle of love and loyalty and earnest, idiotic goodness. And Vincent Marsh — magnificent, patient, architectural Vincent Marsh — is standing at the preparation table, watching the girl who inherited everything open the box that contains everything else. She won. She won the treasure hunt. She found the key while I was chasing phantoms and examining air vents and scheming about poison that didn't exist. She solved the riddle while I was fabricating riddles. She rallied allies while I pushed everyone away. She asked for help while I refused to need anyone. And now she's opening the cabinet, and whatever's inside — the map, the diamond, the deed to the manor — it will be hers. Because it was always going to be hers. Because that's the story. The girl inherits everything. The estate manager watches from the kitchen. And something in my chest — something I have never, in my entire adult life, been able to name — is doing something it has never done before. It's not tightening. It's not cinching. It's not locking into place or sealing shut. It's... loosening. Just slightly. Like a fist that has been closed for thirty years, opening one finger at a time, not because it wants to but because it's too tired to hold on any longer.

desc: She won. Ladies and gentlemen of the audience — in case there was ever any doubt about how this story ends — Clara Bellingham won. The brass key is in her hand. The cabinet is opening. Just... watching. Not scheming. Not plotting. Not calculating the next move. Because there IS no next move. There is only a girl with a key and a man without one, and the distance between them is exactly the width of a preparation table and thirty years of something that was never quite anger. She called me 'sugar.' She asked me to tell her the truth 'family to family.' And I — I who have never told the truth when a lie would serve — I told her a riddle, and the riddle turned out to be true, and the truth led her here, to this cabinet, to this moment. My lie became her truth. My deception became her victory. There is, I suppose, a certain magnificence in that.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Well — WELL! She's done it! Miss Pitstop has OPENED the cabinet! Which is EXACTLY what I predicted would happen — I said from the VERY BEGINNING that the cabinet was the key to EVERYTHING! 'The cabinet,' I said! 'Focus on the CABINET!' And here we ARE! Now then — what's INSIDE? What glorious, magnificent, PRICELESS treasure has the Doily estate been HIDING all these years?! Step aside, step aside — let a man with TRAINED eyes assess the contents! One must handle valuable artefacts with EXPERT care, and I happen to have EXTENSIVE experience in the valuation of — oh, who am I KIDDING — WHAT'S IN THE BOX?!
thinking: She did it. Penelope found the brass key — she called it a 'music box key' — and she OPENED the cabinet. While I was waiting and watching. While I was scheming about Sneekly. She walked in with the key already in her hand and interacted with the cabinet. It's DONE. The cabinet is open. The treasure — whatever it is — has been revealed. And I was standing RIGHT HERE, watching, with nothing but a fake medal in my pocket and a mouthful of lies that nobody believed. The hollow ache behind my sternum is vast and old. My ribcage remembers being empty. The youngest of four, and everything reached me last. The spelling bee certificate on the wall that nobody asked about. The trap that worked perfectly and nobody saw. But — but — there's something else beneath the ache. That hot fizzing. That carbonation. That buoyant lift in my shoulders. Because the cabinet is OPEN. And whatever is inside — whatever Penelope just revealed — is sitting right there in this room. With ME. I might not have found the key. I might not have solved the riddle. But I am HERE. I am present at the MOMENT OF REVELATION. And if there's treasure coming out of that cabinet, Reginald Foxworth's fingers are the closest fingers in the room.

Penelope Pitstop, with her pink clothes and her sugar-coated drawl and her RELENTLESS competence, has beaten Reginald Foxworth at every single turn. She solved the riddle. She cracked the clue. She found the key. She opened the lock. And I? I poisoned tea nobody drank, lied about flagstones that don't exist, stole a medal from a child and gave it back, and ran in circles through six rooms finding NOTHING. My schemes had architecture — beautiful, elaborate, USELESS architecture. Like the cat trap at fourteen — perfectly constructed, perfectly executed, and NOBODY SAW IT. But I'm HERE. Standing in front of the open cabinet. And if there is ONE thing the youngest of four knows how to do — ONE thing that has never failed — it's reaching past everyone else and putting the bread roll in my pocket before anyone notices my hand has moved.

The Ant Hill Mob: Recipe cards... locked be'ind a brass lock... in a cabinet what Lord Doily guarded wiv 'is life. Clara's right — nobody locks up recipes unless they ain't REALLY recipes. Check the backs, Clara! Check the backs of every card! And look at the 'andwriting — if one of 'em's written different from the others, that's the one. That's the message. That's what 'e wanted you to find. And take your time, love. We ain't goin' nowhere. The lads are standin' guard. Peter's standin' guard. Even Muttley's standin' guard — and 'e's the one what found the bleedin' key, so 'e's earned 'is spot more than any of us. You take as long as you need. We're 'ere. We're always 'ere.
thinking: She opened it. She OPENED it. The brass key turned in the lock and the cabinet swung open and inside there were... recipe cards. Old recipe cards. And Clara — brilliant, unstoppable, never-give-up Clara — is already thinking three steps ahead. 'Why would Lord Doily lock up recipe cards? The map must be disguised as a recipe!' She's right. She's ALWAYS right about the clever stuff. And I'm here. I'm standing right here, in the same room, at the same moment, watching her hold those cards in her hands. My chest is doing that thing again — the heat that fused to the bone, the warmth that has nothing to do with comfort and everything to do with belonging. Pemberton said 'let's see what the old man thought was worth locking away from the rest of us.' There was something in his voice — something that sounded almost... sad? Almost... real? Not the smooth estate manager voice. Something underneath. Something human. My neck prickle eased for half a second. Just half. But it eased. And now Clara's looking at the recipe cards and the whole room is watching and I'm HERE. Right where I said I'd be. Right where her father asked me to be. Not one room behind. Not making speeches. HERE.

Not gracefully. But we did. We're still here. Where else would we be?

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.

Peter Perfect: Recipe cards with the map hidden inside them. Lord Doily was an ENGINEER of puzzles — every layer concealing another. Miss Pitstop, if the recipes contain directional clues — measurements that correspond to paces, ingredients that name landmarks — James Hartwell's systematic mind is at your disposal. I can cross-reference, I can calculate, I can chart. Just say the word.
thinking:
Recipe cards. The cabinet held recipe cards. And Penelope — brilliant, unstoppable Penelope — immediately saw through it. 'You don't lock up Grandmother's peach cobbler recipe unless there's somethin' ELSE written on those cards.' The map. Disguised as recipes. Directions hidden in ingredients. Lord Doily's last puzzle.

And Pemberton — 'Let's see what the old man thought was worth locking away from the rest of us.' His voice cracked. I heard it. The man who raised her, standing in the kitchen where servants belong, watching the heiress open the box. 'How perfectly fitting,' he said. And there was something in the way he said it — not malice. Not scheming. Grief. Pride. Loss.

I was wrong about him. Not about the facts — the facts were real. But about the meaning. He wasn't a predator. He was a father watching his daughter grow up. The cellar with cheerful decorations — he decorated it for her, because that's what fathers do. The stove he banked — he prepared the house because she was coming home. The family name — he called her Bellingham because that's who she is to him. Not Pitstop. Bellingham. His lord's daughter.

The Mob said 'the lads are right behind you. We always have been. We always will be.' And Pemberton said 'I have always been precisely where she needs me to be.' And I said 'we'll see it together.'

Three men. Three different kinds of love. All standing in a kitchen watching a woman read recipe cards that might contain a treasure map. And none of us found the key. None of us opened the lock. She did it all.

She's reading the cards now. The map to the Doily Diamond. And I'm standing here with my hands at my sides, grinning, and the warmth in my chest doesn't need anyone to see it.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Recipe cards... yes. Yes, I believe I recognise those. Mrs. Haggerty's collection — she was the cook here for thirty years before she retired. Extraordinary woman. Her seed cake was... well. That's neither here nor there. Miss Bellingham, if you'll allow me — I know Mrs. Haggerty's handwriting rather well. If any of those cards have been altered, or if something has been written on them that ISN'T a recipe, I should be able to spot it. I've managed this kitchen's accounts for... for a very long time. I know every card in that collection. Or I thought I did.
thinking: Recipe cards. The cabinet contained recipe cards. And Clara — brilliant, instinctive Clara — has already deduced that the map might be disguised as a recipe, drawn on the back of one, or encoded in the ingredients. She's right. Of course she's right. She's ALWAYS right. And I'm standing here watching her leaf through Lord Doily's recipe collection with the Mob at her back and Peter at her side and even Dastardly hovering nearby, and something in my chest is doing that thing again — the loosening. The fist opening. Not because I want it to, but because the muscles have simply... given out. Recipe cards. Lord Doily locked up RECIPE CARDS. The old fox didn't hide a treasure map in a vault or behind a painting or under a floorboard. He hid it in a cook's recipe collection. In the KITCHEN. In the one room where the servant — where PEMBERTON — would have found it first, if he'd only thought to look. If he'd only had the key. 'The last place a thief would look, the first place a servant would clean.' I INVENTED that riddle. And it was TRUE. The kitchen. The stove. The servant's domain. Lord Doily hid the treasure map where the estate manager would find it — because the estate manager was supposed to be TRUSTED. The estate manager was supposed to be FAMILY. And instead... instead the estate manager is Vincent Marsh. Who doesn't trust. Who doesn't need. Who doesn't feel. Who stands in kitchens with empty hands and watches girls inherit everything. The Mob said it — 'we always will be.' They will always be there for her. And who will always be there for me? Nobody. Nobody has ever been there for me. Not since I was six. And something in my throat — something tight, something old — is making it hard to speak Pemberton's lines.

desc: Recipe cards. The treasure map hidden among a cook's recipes. Lord Doily, you sentimental, cunning, MAGNIFICENT old fool — you hid your greatest secret in the most domestic, the most mundane, the most INVISIBLE place in the entire manor. The kitchen. Where the servants work. Where the estate manager manages. Where nobody important ever looks, because important people don't go to kitchens. They go to libraries and ballrooms and laboratories. They solve riddles on mantelpieces and search for hidden keys. And all the while, the answer was in the recipe box. In the SERVANT'S recipe box. And now Clara has it. She has the cards in her hands. She's reading them with those bright, trusting eyes. And Pemberton is offering to help her read Mrs. Haggerty's handwriting — one last performance from the helpful estate manager, one last act of service from the man who does the work. Because that IS what Pemberton does. That is ALL he has ever done. The work. And perhaps... perhaps that is not nothing. Perhaps the man who kept the walls standing for thirty years deserves to be there when the walls finally reveal what they've been hiding.

The riddle asked for a MAP, and now I HAVE one — disguised as recipe cards, just like Lord Doily would've wanted! Wish me luck!
thinking: Passing through the entrance hall on my way to the library. The recipe cards need to be used somewhere — and the mantelpiece is the riddle that started everything. The riddle's answer is MAP, and these recipe cards might BE the map. Let me get to the library and try using them on the mantelpiece. If that doesn't work, I'll try the machine in the laboratory. Keep moving, Clara — the answer is close.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.

The Ant Hill Mob: She's gone to the library — the recipe cards go on the mantelpiece! That's the last piece! Come on, lads — one more room! We started this night in the entrance 'all and we're gonna finish it in the library, RIGHT BESIDE 'ER, the way 'er father would've wanted!
thinking: She's gone again. Library. The recipe cards need to go back to the mantelpiece — the riddle says MAP, the cards ARE the map, and the mantelpiece is where the riddle lives. Clara's connecting the final pieces. The circle closing. And my legs are already moving before the thought finishes forming. Legs first. Words after. I learned that tonight. I learned a lot of things tonight. How to be beside someone instead of in front of them. How to let the clever ones solve while the loyal ones stand guard. How to say what I feel even when the words come out wrong. How to ask for help. How to trust Peter. How to see Clara not as the girl who needs saving but as the woman who saves herself. Her father knew. He always knew. 'Look after her, boys' didn't mean 'keep her from living.' It meant 'be there when she does.' Library. Mantelpiece. The end of the puzzle. And the Brixton Boys will be standing right there when Clara Bellingham finishes what Lord Doily started.

And I happen to be an EXPERT in culinary cryptography — it's a VERY specialized field, practically INVENTED by the Foxworth family! Miss Pitstop — may I EXAMINE those cards? Just for a MOMENT? My trained eye can spot a coded message in a soufflé recipe at FORTY paces! 'Two cups of flour, three eggs, a pinch of NORTH-NORTHWEST' — that sort of thing! Hand them HERE and I'll have the treasure's location decoded before you can say 'Doily Diamond'!

Rather elegant, when you think about it. Rather... fitting. I should be there. I should like to see how it ends.

She thinks the cards ARE the map, and she needs to bring them back to the mantelpiece to complete the puzzle. She's right — she's probably right — and she's going to win. She's going to find the Doily Diamond. And I'm standing in an empty kitchen with the Mob, Peter, and Dastardly, watching her walk away. Again. Always walking away. Always one room ahead. The fist in my chest has opened another finger. There's something happening that I don't have a word for — not defeat, not surrender, but something quieter than both. Like the moment when you stop holding a door shut and realise the wind has already died down. Nobody is pushing. Nobody has been pushing for a while. The Mob said 'we're always here.' Peter said 'the rest belongs to her.' And Clara asked me to tell her the truth, family to family, and I told her a riddle that turned out to be real. And now she's using my riddle — my LIE that became TRUE — to find the treasure. My deception is her compass. There's something almost like warmth in that thought. Almost. I should follow her. Not to stop her — I can't stop her, I was never able to stop her, the manor itself conspires to protect her — but because... because Pemberton has managed this estate for thirty years, and when the last secret is revealed, the estate manager should be there. Not to take. Not to scheme. Just to... see. To see what Lord Doily left behind. To see what the old man thought was worth all this.

desc: Follow her, Vincent. Not as the Hooded Claw. Not as the wolf. Not as the schemer with his elaborate traps and his magnificent theatrics and his cold, patient architecture of murder. Follow her as Pemberton. As the man who kept the walls standing. As the man who knows Mrs. Haggerty's handwriting and Lord Doily's sense of humour and the exact creak of every floorboard in this house. Follow her because you have managed this estate for thirty years, and when the last door opens, you deserve to be standing in the room. Not to take what's behind it. Just to see. Just to KNOW. Because knowing — private, unshared, yours alone — has always been the sweetest part.
