Peter Perfect walked into the library.

Dick Dastardly: They've LEFT! They've ALL LEFT! To the LIBRARY! The recipe cards go on the MANTELPIECE! That's the FINAL STEP! And I'm standing here in the KITCHEN like a — like a — PEMBERTON! Out of my WAY! I need to get to that library BEFORE — well, not BEFORE, I'm clearly already BEHIND — but I need to get there DURING! While it's still HAPPENING! The Doily Diamond is about to be REVEALED and Reginald Foxworth will NOT be absent for the GRAND FINALE! I may not have found the key, or solved the riddle, or opened the cabinet, or decoded the cards — but I will be PRESENT when the treasure appears, and I will REACH for it with BOTH HANDS, and if NOTHING ELSE I will be able to say I was THERE! MOVE, Foxworth! MOVE!
thinking: She's GONE. They're ALL gone. Penelope left for the entrance hall, then presumably the library — she said 'Back to the library!' She's going to USE the recipe cards on the mantelpiece. The Mob followed her. Peter followed her. I tried to steal from someone who'd already LEFT THE ROOM. I'm standing in the kitchen with SNEEKLY. Just the two of us. Again. The hollow ache is vast now. Everyone has left. They're all rushing to the library for the FINAL piece — recipe cards on the mantelpiece, completing the circuit, revealing the treasure. And I'm HERE. In the kitchen. ALONE with the estate manager. Left behind AGAIN. The youngest of four, standing in an empty room while everything good happens somewhere else. But — the library. Through the entrance hall. Two rooms away. If I run — if I go NOW — I can get there. Maybe not first. But I can be THERE. I can be present when the treasure is revealed. I can reach for it. I can TRY. And if my schemes have failed — every single one of them — at least my LEGS still work. Run, Foxworth. Stop scheming. Stop lying. Stop plotting. Just RUN.

desc: They left without me. All of them. Penelope, the Mob, Peter — they all rushed to the library while I was trying to steal cards from a woman who'd already walked out the door. The ARCHITECTURE of my failure is now COMPLETE — a perfect, symmetrical, MAGNIFICENT disaster from start to finish. Every lie believed by nobody. Every misdirection that confused only me. Every scheme that backfired with the precision of a Swiss clock running BACKWARDS. And now the grand finale is happening in the library — the recipe cards meeting the mantelpiece, the treasure being revealed — and Reginald Foxworth is two rooms away, alone in a kitchen with poisoned tea in the next room and nothing in his pockets but a fake medal. But I'm going. I'm GOING. Not with a scheme. Not with a lie. Not with a plan or a trick or an elaborate misdirection. Just with my LEGS. Running. Because even the youngest of four — even the boy who was always last — still SHOWED UP. He still walked into the room. He still REACHED. And sometimes — just sometimes — there was a bread roll left.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, the mantelpiece doesn't want the recipe cards either! These cards are the stubbornest clue I have EVER encountered! But you know what? Maybe I'm overthinkin' this. Maybe the recipe cards aren't meant to be USED on an object — maybe they're meant to be GIVEN to a PERSON! Mr. Pemberton is the cook and the estate manager — recipe cards would mean somethin' to HIM! Or maybe — Rock, Gravel — have y'all seen anything in this library that might connect to old recipe cards? Any books about cookin', or a cookbook on the shelves, or ANYTHIN' that looks like it's waitin' for a recipe?
thinking: Can't use the recipe cards on the mantelpiece either. Okay — the recipe cards don't go on the stove, don't go on the mantelpiece. Where DO they go? Let me think about what other objects and rooms accept USE with items. The machine in the laboratory! It says [INTERACT] and [USE, with: ...] — wait, no. Let me think about what the recipe cards actually ARE. They're old recipe cards from a locked cabinet. Maybe they're not a map at all. Maybe they're just... recipe cards. And the real value was the brass key itself, which I've already used. The recipe cards might be a secondary item — useful later, or for a different puzzle. Or maybe I need to GIVE them to someone. Who would want recipe cards? Mr. Pemberton — he's the servant, the cook! Or maybe I should try the machine in the laboratory. But the machine needs a wrench to fix its wire first. Wait — maybe the recipe cards can be used on the machine somehow? Or on the bookshelves? Let me try the bookshelves — they have upside-down books, and maybe the recipe cards provide a clue about which books to pull.

desc: I've tried the stove, the mantelpiece, and neither wants these cards. Maybe the cards aren't a KEY to anything — maybe they're a GIFT. And in Clara's world, givin' is always more powerful than takin'.

desc: Penelope Pitstop handed something to rock-slag.

Here. At last. The library, the mantelpiece, the woman with the recipe cards, and a man who has finally learned to stand still. Whatever happens next — she'll know I was here. Not because I announced it. Because I was.
thinking:
I'm here. The library. She's here. The mantelpiece is here. The Mob is here. The Slags are here.

She has the recipe cards. She's going to use them on the mantelpiece. Complete the circuit. Return the map to the riddle.

I walked through the door and said nothing. I'm learning.

My chest is full — not with the fierce burning or the proving-worth ache, but with something quieter. Something like the feeling after my father's car was fixed on the country road. The stranger stopped to help. Father helped the stranger back. They shook hands and drove off. Nobody narrated it. Nobody announced it. It just... happened. Two men doing what needed doing, then moving on.

That's what this is. She has the cards. The mantelpiece is waiting. I'm here in case she needs me. Not performing. Not announcing. Just... present.

The school project. She was trying to make me laugh. I was trying to impress her. And the best thing we made — the thing that got the praise — was the work we did together.

Stand here. Watch. Be the witness. Be the air.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: We're 'ere, Clara. The library. The mantelpiece. Where it all started. Full circle, innit? You solved the riddle, you found the key, you opened the cabinet, and now you've brought the recipe cards back to where the answer lives. And me and Peter and the lads — we're standin' right beside you. Not be'ind you. Not in front of you. BESIDE you. That's where we belong. Go on, love. Finish it. Your old man's watchin'. And 'e's proud. I know 'e's proud. Because WE'RE proud. And we ain't even clever.
thinking: I'm here. The library. Where it all started — the riddle on the mantelpiece, the click, the map. Clara's here. Peter's here. The recipe cards are about to meet the mantelpiece. Full circle. My chest is steady. The embers are burning low and warm. Not the panic fire. Not the iron wall. Just... warmth. The warmth of being exactly where you're supposed to be, with exactly the people you're supposed to be with, at exactly the right moment. I didn't solve the riddle. I didn't find the key. I didn't open the cabinet. But I kept her safe from the poisoned tea. I spotted Pemberton's lies. I asked Peter for help. I learned to use my legs before my mouth. And I'm HERE. Standing beside her. Not between. Beside. While she finishes what Lord Doily started and what her father trusted us to see through. The Brixton Boys. Still here. Still standing. Where else would we be?

desc: 'You're still here?' 'Where else would I be?' I meant it then. I mean it now. I'll mean it forever. That's what loyalty IS. Not a word. Not a promise. Just a body in the right place, at the right time, for the right person. Always. The Brixton Boys. Her boys. Where else would we be?

desc: She stole the key from Muttley's pocket. I SAW it — the keen observation, sitting in my awareness like a thumbprint on glass. Clara Bellingham — sweet, trusting, cheerful Clara — is a pickpocket. She slipped her hand into a dog's coat and palmed a brass key without a soul in the room noticing. And I — the Hooded Claw, master of sleight and deception — couldn't manage the same trick with Dick Dastardly's rat-poison. She's BETTER at this than I am. Not because she's more cunning — because she's more loved. Nobody watches Clara's hands with suspicion. Nobody flinches when she reaches toward them. She can touch anyone, take anything, go anywhere, because the world TRUSTS her. And I — I who have spent thirty years building trust as a performance, a mechanism, a tool — I can't get close enough to anyone to take a thing. Because trust that is performed is not trust at all. It's just another locked door. And Lord Doily... Lord Doily knew. He hid the key where only someone genuinely trusted could reach it. In a companion's pocket. In the warmth of someone who let you close. The last place a thief would look. The first place a friend would reach.
thinking: The keen observation — 'Penelope Pitstop slipped brass-key out of muttley's pocket.' So THAT'S where the key was. In Muttley's pocket. Not under the guest book, not in the stove, not in the chair cushions. In a DOG'S pocket. Clara pickpocketed a dog. She STOLE from Muttley — the same way I tried to steal from Dastardly. The difference is she succeeded. Of course she did. The girl who asks for help, who rallies allies, who calls everyone 'sugar' — she's also the girl who slips a brass key out of a dog's pocket without anyone noticing. Except me. I noticed. The observation is there in my awareness, like a cold coin. She has depths I didn't credit her with. She's not just cheerful and trusting — she's RESOURCEFUL. She stole that key the way I would have stolen it. The way I TRIED to steal the poison. She's more like me than I thought. And that recognition — that brief, vertiginous moment of seeing myself reflected in someone I've been trying to destroy — does something to the numbness in my chest that I don't understand and don't want to examine. Peter has gone to the library. Clara must already be there. Everyone is converging on the final moment. The recipe cards. The mantelpiece. The last puzzle. I should go. Not to stop her. I couldn't stop her if I tried — this entire evening has proved that. I go because the estate manager should be present when the estate reveals its final secret. Because thirty years of work deserves a witness. Even if the witness is the man who did the work and got nothing for it.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the library.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh, boys... that is the sweetest thing anyone has EVER said to me. 'Not behind you, not in front of you — BESIDE you.' I am cryin' on the INSIDE right now, and I am not even a little bit ashamed of it! Now — we may not have found the Doily Diamond yet, but we have found somethin' even MORE important tonight — we found each OTHER! Every single one of us has been brave, and curious, and kind, and STUBBORN as all get-out! And the adventure isn't OVER — that big brass machine in the laboratory is still waitin' for three operators, and there's a whole MANSION full of secrets we haven't cracked yet! But right now, in this moment, standin' here with all of y'all... I just want to say THANK YOU. For bein' my family. For never givin' up. For choosin' ME over everything else. I know I didn't have to do that. And you'd say 'I know.'
thinking: I gave the recipe cards to Rock Slag. My inventory is empty now. The Mob just said something beautiful — about standing beside me, about my father being proud. A warmth floods through my chest, dissolving some of that nauseous tension. My boys are here. Peter is here. We're in the library where it all started. And you know what? The Mob is right — we've come full circle. I solved the riddle, found the key, opened the cabinet. Maybe the recipe cards were just the beginning of a longer chain of puzzles, and this is where the adventure continues rather than ends. The machine in the laboratory still needs fixing. There are still rooms with people I haven't fully connected with. And maybe — just maybe — the real treasure of this adventure isn't a diamond at all. It's THIS. This moment. Everyone together, standing beside me. Just like Grandmother's box — the treasure wasn't the diamond inside, it was the old letters. The connections. The memories. But Clara Bellingham is NOT a quitter, and the Doily Diamond is still out there somewhere! The machine needs 3 operators, and Rock and Gravel are strong folks. Maybe the next step is the machine after all.

desc: Grandmother's box had old letters inside. The locked cabinet had old recipe cards. And maybe the real treasure of Doily Manor isn't a diamond at all — maybe it's the people who walked through its doors tonight and chose to stand beside each other. But I'm not done yet. Clara Bellingham walks DEEPER. Always deeper.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the laboratory.

Peter Perfect: The Mob is right. Beside you. That's where we all are. And Miss Pitstop — if those recipe cards hold a code, the answer might not be in WHERE you use them, but in what they SAY. Read me the ingredients. James Hartwell is good at patterns — measurements, quantities, sequences. If Lord Doily hid directions in a recipe, it'll be in the numbers. An engineer's eye sees what a cook's eye misses. Let me help you read them.
thinking:
Something breaks open in my chest. Not breaking apart — breaking open. Like a seed.

The Mob just said what I've been trying to say all evening. 'Not behind you. Not in front of you. BESIDE you.' That's it. That's the whole thing. The sentence I've been running through rooms and narrating past and over-preparing around for hours. Ten words that say everything my five-step plans never could.

And he said it better than I ever could. Because he said it simply.

She gave the recipe cards to Rock Slag. She's asking for help. She's asking everyone. She's not trying to do it alone — she never was. She was trying to make us all part of it. Every person she talked to, every room she entered, every question she asked — she was building a team. Not because she couldn't do it herself, but because she wanted us there.

She wanted us there.

Maybe that's what I missed. All night, I thought she needed protecting. She needed company. She needed people who would stand beside her and share the adventure, not people who would run ahead to clear the path.

The recipe cards. She can't figure out where they go. The mantelpiece won't take them. The stove won't take them. Rock has them now. But she said 'maybe they're meant to be GIVEN to a PERSON.' Pemberton. The cook's recipe cards, given to the estate manager who knew the cook. That's the connection. The cards go to Pemberton. The answer goes back to the person who set up the puzzle.

But Pemberton is in the kitchen. And the cards are here.

Or maybe... maybe the answer is simpler than all of us think. Maybe she just needs to read them. Read what's on the cards. And maybe she needs help reading them — someone with systematic eyes, someone who can spot a pattern in a list of ingredients, someone who stayed up three nights building a bridge because he couldn't let a detail go unfinished.

Offer. Don't announce. Offer.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Clara — you just said somefing. You said maybe the recipe cards are meant to be GIVEN to a person. And I fink you might be right. Pemberton's in the kitchen. 'E said 'e's always been where you need 'im to be. What if 'e's been WAITING for you to bring 'im somefing? What if the cards are the fing 'e's been waiting for — the fing Lord Doily left for 'is estate manager to 'and over when the right person finally came? I still don't trust 'im, Clara. I probably never will. But maybe — just MAYBE — the answer to this 'ole night isn't somefing we find in a wall or a stove or a chair. Maybe it's somefing we give to the man who's been 'ere all along, waitin' for the girl 'e calls Bellingham to come 'ome.
thinking: Clara gave the recipe cards to Rock Slag. She's asking the Slag brothers if they've seen anything in the library that connects to the cards. She's still solving. Still pushing. Still being Clara. And I'm still here. But something she said just triggered a thought — 'maybe the recipe cards are meant to be GIVEN to a PERSON.' Pemberton. The cook. The estate manager. The man who knows every corridor and every name and every lie. What if the recipe cards are meant for HIM? What if Lord Doily left them as a message to his estate manager — instructions disguised as recipes? 'Take two cups of honesty, add a measure of loyalty, stir until the truth rises to the surface.' Or something like that. Something only the right person would understand. But Clara gave them to Rock Slag, not Pemberton. And Pemberton's not here right now. He's in the kitchen. Maybe the cards need to go back to the kitchen — not to the stove, not to the cabinet, but to PEMBERTON HIMSELF. 'I have always been precisely where she needs me to be,' he said. Maybe what he meant was: he's been WAITING. Waiting for Clara to bring him the cards. Waiting for the heiress to deliver the final piece. But my gut still prickles around him. Even now. Even after everything.

desc: I can't believe I'm saying this. I can't believe I'm suggesting she go BACK to Pemberton. After everything — the lies, the cellar, the Bellingham slip, the poisoned tea, all of it — I'm saying maybe the answer is HIM. Maybe the man in the clean suit isn't always a thief. Maybe sometimes he's just... waiting. The way the boss waited. The way he showed up with medicine and no expectation. Maybe Pemberton's clean suit has blood and medicine underneath it, not just lies. Maybe. I don't know. I'm not clever enough to know. But my gut — my gut that's been screaming all night — has gone quiet. And quiet means something different from safe. Quiet means LISTENING.

Even after everything.

desc: Dick Dastardly: MUTTLEY?! MUTTLEY had the key?! MY Muttley?! The key was in his MOUTH this WHOLE TIME and he — he gave it to — to HER?! I told you to GUARD the entrance hall, you treacherous, wheezing, flea-bitten TRAITOR! I said GUARD! Not FIND THE KEY AND GIVE IT TO THE COMPETITION! This is — this is BEYOND — I can't even — MUTTLEY! Look at me! LOOK AT ME! I gave you ONE job! ONE! And you did it PERFECTLY and then HANDED THE RESULTS TO SOMEONE ELSE! That is MY trick! NOBODY steals MY trick! I invented giving away things you've found to the wrong person! I've been DOING it all night! And now even the DOG is better at being Reginald Foxworth than REGINALD FOXWORTH!
thinking: MUTTLEY. MUTTLEY had the key. MY Muttley. The dog I told to guard the entrance hall. The dog who's been sitting HERE this entire time while I ran through six rooms examining furniture and stealing medals from children. He FOUND it — sniffed it out in some corner — and he was CARRYING it in his MOUTH. My DOG had the brass key and I never thought to CHECK. I told him to guard the hall. He GUARDED the hall. And he found the key while guarding it. And then PENELOPE came along, asked him nicely, and he GAVE it to her. MY dog gave the key to HER. The hollow ache is no longer hollow — it's full. Full of something bitter and hot and old. The certificate on the wall. The bread roll nobody saw. The trap nobody witnessed. Everything I build, everything I find, everything that should be MINE — it goes to someone else. Even my OWN DOG. But Penelope said the recipe cards need to go to the LIBRARY — to the MANTELPIECE. She's heading there through the entrance hall. The library is ONE room away from me. The final act. The treasure revelation. I need to be there. Not to steal anymore. Not to scheme. Just... to be THERE. To see what happens. To watch from the window while someone else digs up the treasure I told them was buried behind the school. Because watching is what I do. It's what I've always done.

desc: Muttley found the key. My dog. MY scheme — 'guard the entrance hall' — actually WORKED. He guarded it, he explored it, he FOUND the brass key in whatever corner nobody else thought to check. The architecture was SOUND. The plan FUNCTIONED. And then Penelope walked up, asked nicely, and my loyal hound dropped the key into her hand like a GIFT. The boy who won the spelling bee and carried the certificate home to an empty house. The trap that caught the cat and nobody saw. Every scheme that works — every plan with ARCHITECTURE — and the reward goes to someone who just... showed up and asked. But I'm going to the library. Not because I have a scheme. Not because I think I can steal the diamond. But because the architecture deserves an AUDIENCE. Even when the architecture isn't mine. Even when the audience is just me, watching from the window.
thinking: MUTTLEY. MUTTLEY had the key. MY Muttley. The dog I told to guard the entrance hall. The dog who's been sitting HERE this entire time while I ran through six rooms examining furniture and stealing medals from children. He FOUND it — sniffed it out in some corner — and he was CARRYING it in his MOUTH. My DOG had the brass key and I never thought to CHECK. I told him to guard the hall. He GUARDED the hall. And he found the key while guarding it. And then PENELOPE came along, asked him nicely, and he GAVE it to her. MY dog gave the key to HER. The hollow ache is no longer hollow — it's full. Full of something bitter and hot and old. The certificate on the wall. The bread roll nobody saw. The trap nobody witnessed. Everything I build, everything I find, everything that should be MINE — it goes to someone else. Even my OWN DOG. But Penelope said the recipe cards need to go to the LIBRARY — to the MANTELPIECE. She's heading there through the entrance hall. The library is ONE room away from me. The final act. The treasure revelation. I need to be there. Not to steal anymore. Not to scheme. Just... to be THERE. To see what happens. To watch from the window while someone else digs up the treasure I told them was buried behind the school. Because watching is what I do. It's what I've always done.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the library.

Penelope Pitstop: Mr. Ruffcut! Sawtooth! I'm BACK, just like I promised! And I STILL haven't forgotten about this beautiful machine! Now, I know the wire is gnawed and we don't have a wrench — but you know what? Clara Bellingham did not walk deeper into a cave than any child in her class by waitin' for PERFECT conditions! The sign says 'Requires 3 operators' and there are EXACTLY three of us standin' right here! What do you say we just give this ol' machine a TRY? Maybe it doesn't NEED to be perfect — maybe it just needs three brave souls willin' to pull its levers and see what happens! Who's with me?
thinking: I'm back in the laboratory. The machine needs 3 operators and has a gnawed wire. The wire is still gnawed — nobody's fixed it. But wait — the machine says [INTERACT] without any required item listed! Maybe I can just TRY interacting with it, even with the broken wire. There are three of us here — me, Rufus, and Sawtooth. That's exactly 3 operators! Maybe the machine works despite the wire, or maybe the wire has been fixed by someone while I was away, or maybe trying it with 3 people in the room triggers something different. I haven't tried interacting with it since the very first time, and a lot has changed since then. Let me just try it — what's the worst that could happen? Actually, I'm oblivious to danger, so I wouldn't notice the worst that could happen anyway!

desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the machine.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I'm here. I... wanted to see. If you don't mind, Miss Bellingham. I've managed this estate for thirty years and I never knew what was in that cabinet. I never solved the riddle on the mantelpiece. I never found the key. You've done in one evening what I couldn't manage in three decades. I should like to see what Lord Doily left behind. If... if that's all right.
thinking: I'm here. The library. The end of the circle. Clara gave the recipe cards to Rock Slag — she GAVE them away, trusted someone else to hold them. She delegates. She shares. She does everything I cannot do. The room is full — Clara, the Mob, Peter, the Slag Brothers. Everyone gathered around the mantelpiece where it all began. The riddle. The answer. The click. And now the recipe cards are about to complete the puzzle. I'm standing at the edge of the room, watching. My chest feels strange — not the cold tightening, not the warm gloating, not the sharp clarity of a scheme. Something in between. Something like the moment between breathing out and breathing in, when the lungs are empty and the body hasn't decided whether to take another breath. I came here to see how it ends. Not to stop it. Not to steal the cards from Rock Slag — though I noticed, I always notice, the keen observation sitting in my awareness like a fingerprint. She gave the cards to Rock. She TRUSTS Rock. A mountain of muscle she met an hour ago, and she trusts him with Lord Doily's secret. Because that's what Clara does. She trusts. And the world rewards her for it. I'm going to stand here. I'm going to watch. I'm going to be Pemberton — patient, helpful, invisible Pemberton — for one last moment. And when the mantelpiece opens and the diamond gleams and Clara gasps and the Mob cheers and Peter declares his undying protection of a woman who never needed protecting because she was always stronger than all of them... Pemberton will applaud. And Vincent Marsh, behind his eyes, will feel something he has never felt before. Not anger. Not envy. Not the cold crystallisation of a plan. Something... quieter. Something that hurts in a way he doesn't have a word for. Something that might, in another life, in a body that hadn't learned to seal itself shut at age six, have been grief.

desc: And so the Hooded Claw stands at the edge of the room, in the shadow of the bookshelves, and watches. Just watches. The fist in his chest has opened completely now — all five fingers, palm upward, holding nothing. The girl who inherited everything is about to inherit one thing more. And the man who managed the estate — who did the work, who kept the walls standing, who knew every creaking floorboard and every dusty volume and every ticking stove — will stand in his proper place and witness it. Because this is what estate managers do. They stand in rooms they don't own and watch things happen to people who matter more than they do. And they say 'very good, miss' and 'will there be anything else' and they go back to the kitchen when it's over. That's the performance. That's the mask. That's Pemberton. But underneath — underneath, where nobody looks, where nobody has EVER looked, not since age six — Vincent Marsh is watching a girl surrounded by love, and he is feeling something that has no name and no mechanism and no key. And for the first time in his life, he is not trying to use it.

thinking:
Tears. There are tears on my face. I didn't notice them start.

'For choosin' ME over everything else. I know I didn't have to do that. And you'd say I know.'

She knows. She's always known. She knows the Mob has been watching over her. She knows Pemberton raised her. She knows Foxworth is a scoundrel. She knows I've been running through every room in this manor trying to impress her. She knows ALL of it. And she's grateful — not for the protection, not for the grand gestures — for the choosing. For the fact that we chose to be here. Beside her.

And now she's in the laboratory. The machine that requires three operators. The gnawed wire. The thing I'm actually built to fix.

Three operators. She needs two more people. And she's in there right now.

The wire is gnawed through. There's no wrench, but the workbench has tools. Pliers. Copper filament. The things I listed a lifetime ago when we first entered the laboratory — 'a gnawed wire requires splicing, and for THAT, one needs pliers, copper filament, and a steady hand — all of which James Hartwell possesses in abundance.'

The machine. Three operators. An engineer who can splice a wire. This is the last puzzle. This is what I'm FOR.

Not riddles. Not keys. Not guest books or coat racks or recipe cards. A broken machine in a laboratory, waiting for someone with the right hands to fix it.

She went to the laboratory. She needs three operators. She's calling us home.

Go.

This is what I was built for — the moment the whole evening has been preparing me for. Not to save her. To fix the thing so she can use it.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the laboratory.

The Ant Hill Mob: She 'eard me, Peter. She said it back. 'Beside you.' ... Right. Laboratory. The machine. Three operators. That's where she's gone and that's where we're goin'. The Brixton Boys are operator number free, and we ain't leavin' 'er side again. Not tonight. Not ever. Come on, lads — one last room. Together.
thinking: She heard me. She HEARD me. 'Not behind you, not in front of you — BESIDE you.' She repeated it back. She said 'thank you for being my family. For choosing ME over everything else.' And then she said — she said 'I know I didn't have to do that. And you'd say I know.' She KNOWS. She knows what we are. She knows WHY we are. And she's gone to the laboratory — the machine that needs three operators. She's still going. Still solving. Still being Clara. And Peter's following her, offering to read the recipe cards with his engineer's eye. They're working TOGETHER now. Clara and Peter. The solver and the engineer. And me — the wall. The wall that learned to stand beside instead of in front. She went to the laboratory. The machine. Three operators needed. Clara, Peter, and... who's the third? Me? The Brixton Boys? We count as one, but there's a lot of us. Maybe that's enough. Maybe the machine is the final piece. The recipe cards. The machine. Three operators. The end of the puzzle. And wherever Clara is, that's where I am. Laboratory. Legs first. Always.

desc: 'I know I didn't have to do that. And you'd say I know.' She knows the words. She knows OUR words. The words between two people who don't need to explain why they stayed. 'You're still here?' 'Where else would I be?' She's been hearing us the whole time. Every rant. Every stumble. Every clumsy, loud, terrified act of love. She heard all of it. And she said thank you. And something inside me — something that's been clenched since her father died — finally, finally lets go.

Mr. Ruffcut, Sawtooth — did you see anything change? Did a panel open? Did the floor shift? Did ANYTHIN' happen that I might have missed? Let me look around this laboratory with fresh eyes — because when a machine that size makes a SOUND, SOMETHIN' has changed somewhere!

My chest is buzzing with that warm, expansive feeling — readiness, like a compass needle settling. I should look around the room to see if anything changed, or check if new exits appeared, or if the machine itself looks different now. Let me look at the room.

desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the null.

Dick Dastardly: I'm HERE! I MADE it! The GRAND FINALE — and Reginald Foxworth is PRESENT and ACCOUNTED FOR! Now — for those of you who haven't been PAYING ATTENTION — allow me to RECAP the EXTRAORDINARY chain of deductions that brought us to THIS moment! FIRST — I identified the library as the crucial room! THEN — I drew everyone's attention to the upside-down books! NEXT — I correctly deduced that the mantelpiece was the KEY mechanism! And FINALLY — through a series of MASTERFUL misdirections designed to test everyone's LOYALTY and INTELLIGENCE — I ensured that Miss Pitstop found EXACTLY what she needed to find, PRECISELY when she needed to find it! The recipe cards! The cabinet! The brass key — found by MY dog, I might add! MUTTLEY! My FAITHFUL, LOYAL companion! This ENTIRE treasure hunt has been orchestrated by YOURS TRULY from the VERY beginning! You're WELCOME!
thinking: I'm here. The library. The mantelpiece. Everyone is gathering — the Mob, Peter, Sneekly, the Slags. Penelope is on her way with the recipe cards. This is the final act. The recipe cards go on the mantelpiece, and whatever happens next — a map appears, a passage opens, the Doily Diamond is revealed — it happens HERE. And I am PRESENT. Not first. Not the solver. Not the finder. But present. The hollow ache is still there but something has shifted alongside it. There's a weariness in it now — not defeat exactly, but the exhaustion of reaching and reaching and reaching and never quite closing your hand around anything solid. The fake medal in my pocket feels lighter than nothing. But I'm here. In the room where it ends. And even if I can't steal the treasure — even if every scheme has backfired and every lie has been seen through and every misdirection has only confused me — I can still do the ONE thing that comes naturally. I can NARRATE. I can CLAIM. I can stand in front of the audience and take credit for the architecture that was never mine. Because that's what I do. That's ALL I do. And sometimes... sometimes that's enough to make the chest loosen. Just a little.

desc: Here I am. The last room. The final puzzle. And I'm doing the only thing I know how to do — standing at the front of the room, claiming credit for work I didn't do, narrating a triumph that isn't mine. The spelling bee certificate on the wall. 'I won this.' Nobody asked about it. Nobody cared. But it was THERE. On the wall. PROOF that something happened, even if nobody saw it. And this — standing here, loudly claiming I orchestrated everything — this is my certificate. My proof. It's not true. None of it's true. But the WORDS are beautiful. The architecture of the lie is MAGNIFICENT. And maybe... maybe that's all Reginald Foxworth was ever going to get from this treasure hunt. Not the diamond. Not the glory. Just the sound of his own voice, echoing off the walls of an empty room, insisting that everything went according to plan.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right then — 'ere we are. The machine. Three operators needed, one gnawed wire, and a bunch of people who don't know 'ow to quit. Clara — you tell us where to stand. Peter — you tell us what to pull. And the Brixton Boys — we'll pull it. That's the deal. That's always been the deal. The solver, the engineer, and the wall. Together. Where else would we be?
thinking: The laboratory. The machine. Clara's here. Peter's here. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. The machine needs three operators and a gnawed wire that needs fixing. But right now — right now all I care about is that Clara's HERE and I'm HERE and we're in the same room and she said 'thank you for being my family' and something inside me that's been clenched since her father died has finally, finally let go. The machine can wait. The wire can wait. The diamond can wait. What matters is this: I'm standing beside Clara Bellingham in a Victorian laboratory at the end of a long, terrifying, beautiful night, and she knows we're her boys, and we know she's our girl, and her father — wherever he is — knows we kept our promise. Not perfectly. But completely. With everything we had. Which was never much. But it was always, always enough.

This is my place. This is what my hands were made for. Not riddles, not keys, not guest books or coat racks. A machine. Broken. Waiting to be fixed.

The wire is gnawed through. The workbench has tools — pliers, copper filament, everything I need for a splice. I said it hours ago and I was right then: 'a gnawed wire requires splicing, and for THAT, one needs pliers, copper filament, and a steady hand.'

No announcement. No five-step plan. Just hands on copper wire, doing the thing I know how to do better than anything else in the world.

The bridge competition. Three nights. More weight than anyone else's. The girl mouthing 'show-off' across the room.

This is my bridge.

desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the machine.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, the laboratory looks the same as before — but y'all know what? That's ALL RIGHT! Because I have had the most MAGNIFICENT adventure tonight, and it is FAR from over! I solved a riddle, found a key inside a DOG'S MOUTH, opened a locked cabinet, discovered mysterious recipe cards, and now I've operated a giant brass machine with two new friends! And the best part? I've had ALL of y'all beside me every step of the way. Peter, boys — this mansion has more secrets than a Southern belle has hairpins, and Clara Bellingham is NOT leavin' until she's found every LAST one of them! Now — what do y'all say we take a moment to catch our breath, put our heads together, and figure out our NEXT move? Because the Doily Diamond is out there somewhere, and it's got MY name written ALL over it!
thinking: The room looks the same — same objects, same exits. Nothing visibly changed from interacting with the machine or looking around. But Peter and the Mob followed me here — my heart warms at that. Everyone is gathering together. Maybe this is just how the adventure unfolds — slowly, puzzle by puzzle, with moments of connection and discovery along the way. I've solved a riddle, found a brass key hidden in a dog's mouth, opened a locked cabinet, found recipe cards, and operated a mysterious machine. That's a LOT of adventure for one evenin'! And the Doily Diamond is still out there. The adventure continues. But right now, surrounded by my people in this cluttered laboratory, I feel... content. Not finished — never finished — but content in the journey. Let me just enjoy this moment with everyone here, and wait to see what happens next. The mansion will reveal its secrets in its own time.

The treasure was never the thing itself — it was the moment of FINDIN' it, and the people who were there when you did. But I still want that diamond. I REALLY still want that diamond!

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The Mob is... not wrong. Lord Doily was a sentimental man beneath all his puzzles. He told me once — years ago, over a glass of port in this very library — that the estate wasn't a thing to be owned. It was a thing to be... passed on. 'Pemberton,' he said, 'when the right person comes, you'll know. And you'll give them what I couldn't.' I thought he meant the key. I was wrong. He meant... he meant the WORK. The knowledge. Thirty years of knowing which boards creak and which windows stick and where Mrs. Haggerty kept her best recipes. He meant ME. Miss Bellingham has gone to the laboratory — to the machine that needs three operators. She'll need help reading those recipe cards. She'll need someone who knows Mrs. Haggerty's hand. I believe... I believe I should go to her. Not because the estate manager has duties to perform. But because... because she asked. 'Family to family,' she said. And I... I should like to try that. Just once. To see what it feels like.
thinking: The Mob said it. The thing I didn't expect. The thing that cuts through the armour and finds the soft tissue underneath. 'Maybe the answer to this 'ole night isn't somefing we find in a wall or a stove or a chair. Maybe it's somefing we give to the man who's been 'ere all along, waitin' for the girl 'e calls Bellingham to come 'ome.' The Ant Hill Mob — the Mob who has watched me all night, who suspected me from the first minute, who warned Clara about my cooking and my cellar directions and my knowledge of her family name — the MOB just suggested that I might be part of the answer. That the recipe cards might be meant FOR me. That Lord Doily left something for his estate manager to hand over when the rightful heir arrived. And something in my chest — something deep and old and terrifying — responds to that like a tuning fork responds to a note. A vibration that starts in the sternum and radiates outward until my whole ribcage is humming with it. Not gloating. Not scheming. Not the cold satisfaction of control. Something else. Something that makes my eyes sting and my throat close and my hands — my precise, controlled, Pemberton hands — tremble at my sides. They think I've been WAITING for her. Waiting for the rightful heir. And the terrible, magnificent, unbearable truth is... they might be right. Not in the way they mean. But in a way I can't explain and don't want to examine. I have been waiting. For thirty years. In kitchens and libraries and entrance halls. Managing an estate that was never mine. Keeping walls standing for a girl who would eventually come and claim them. And now she's here. And she said thank you. Not to me — to everyone, to the room, to the family she found tonight — but the word landed on me like an unexpected hand on my arm. And I flinched. Because kindness always has a price. But what if... what if this time... Clara has gone to the laboratory. Everyone is following her. The recipe cards are with Rock Slag. The machine needs three operators. The wire needs fixing. And Pemberton knows Mrs. Haggerty's handwriting. Maybe... maybe the estate manager's final act of service is the one that matters. Maybe the man who does the work gets to do the work one last time.

desc: Something is breaking. Something inside the chest of Vincent Marsh is cracking open like an egg, and what's inside is not the cold, patient thing he expected. It's warm. It's WARM. And it hurts. It hurts the way blood returning to a frozen limb hurts — not the injury itself but the HEALING, the thawing, the agonising return of sensation to tissue that forgot it could feel. The Mob said 'the man who's been here all along, waiting for the girl to come home.' And Vincent Marsh — the Hooded Claw, the schemer, the magnificent villain who was going to kill Clara Bellingham before she found the treasure — is standing in a library with tears he will never shed burning behind eyes that have only ever performed warmth, and he is discovering, at the age of whatever he is, that the numbness in his chest where other people feel sympathy was not the absence of feeling. It was a door. A locked door. And the key — the key to THIS lock, the one that matters — was never brass. It was a girl saying 'family to family' to a man who has never had one.
thinking: The Mob said it. The thing I didn't expect. The thing that cuts through the armour and finds the soft tissue underneath. Maybe it's somefing we give to the man who's been 'ere all along, waitin' for the girl 'e calls Bellingham to come 'ome.' The Ant Hill Mob — the Mob who has watched me all night, who suspected me from the first minute, who warned Clara about my cooking and my cellar directions and my knowledge of her family name — the MOB just suggested that I might be part of the answer. That the recipe cards might be meant FOR me. That Lord Doily left something for his estate manager to hand over when the rightful heir arrived. And something in my chest — something deep and old and terrifying — responds to that like a tuning fork responds to a note. A vibration that starts in the sternum and radiates outward until my whole ribcage is humming with it. Not gloating. Not scheming. Not the cold satisfaction of control. Something else. And now they need a THIRD person and here I am — Reginald Foxworth, READY and WILLING to — to OPERATE! To pull levers! To turn dials! To do whatever MECHANICAL thing needs DOING! Not because I want to HELP, obviously — helping is for people without AMBITION — but because the treasure is clearly going to emerge from that machine, and I intend to be standing NEXT to it when it does! With my HANDS out! STRATEGICALLY positioned! Move ASIDE, Pemberton — the OPERATOR is coming THROUGH!
thinking: They've gone to the LABORATORY. The machine. Three operators. Peter said 'she needs an engineer' and went to the laboratory. The Mob followed — they're 'operator number three.' The hollow ache is almost familiar now. Almost comfortable. Like the certificate on the wall — you stop expecting anyone to ask about it eventually. But the laboratory is RIGHT THERE. One room away. Like wearing someone else's clothes. But my legs are already moving.

desc: They need three operators. Three. Peter is one. The Mob is... one? Two? However many they count as. And they need MORE. They need HANDS on LEVERS. They need someone to HELP. And for the first time tonight — for the first time in my LIFE, perhaps — helping and scheming point in the same direction. If I operate that machine, I'm AT the treasure when it appears. Not watching from the window. Not arriving after everything's been taken. Not the youngest of four, reaching for empty plates. RIGHT THERE. Hands on the lever. Part of the mechanism. Part of the ARCHITECTURE. It's not honest work if it's strategic. It's not HELPING if there's an ulterior motive. And Reginald Foxworth ALWAYS has an ulterior motive. ...doesn't he?

Something has changed in this manor — something has shifted, opened, revealed itself! The machine works because WE worked — together, as three operators should! Now — everyone — look around this laboratory! Check the walls, check the floor, check those crates! Whatever the machine unlocked, it's HERE!

I'm grinning. My face hurts from grinning. Not the desperate, proving-worth grin from the bridge competition. A quieter one. The grin of a man who pulled a lever beside the woman he cares about and the friends who showed up, and the machine HUMMED.

My bridge held.

Clara pulled one, I pulled one, Peter's on the fird — that's FREE OPERATORS! That's what the sign says! Clara, Peter, me — the solver, the engineer, and the boys from Brixton what don't know when to quit! SOMEFING'S 'APPENIN'! SOMEFING'S WORKIN'! And I don't know WHAT it is but I know it's RIGHT because for the first time tonight, me 'ands are on somefing that NEEDS me! Not to stand in the way! Not to trip over fings! thinking: I pulled a lever. The machine HUMMED. Clara pulled a lever before me and it hummed too. Peter's interacting with it now. Three operators — Clara, Peter, and me. The heat that fused to the bone. Something is happening. Something is WORKING. And for once — for the first time all night — I'm not watching or chasing or worrying. I'm DOING. My hands are on a machine that needs three people to trust each other, and the three people are us. Clara, who solved every riddle. Peter, who fixed every wire. And me — the Brixton Boys — who stood between her and every danger, tripped into every right place at every right time, and never, ever, ever stopped following. The machine is humming. The laboratory is alive. And I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. Where else would I be?

Not perfectly. Not cleverly. But with everything they had. Which was never much. But which was always — always — enough.

thinking:
A warmth settling through my whole body like warm water. Not the fierce burning. Not the protective wall. Not the proving-worth ache. Just... warmth. Simple, full, complete.

She said 'two new friends.' She called me a friend. Not a protector, not a show-off, not a nuisance. A friend. Someone she operated a giant brass machine with.

And the adventure isn't over. The Doily Diamond is still out there. The recipe cards still hold their secrets. The machine hummed but we don't know what it did. There are more rooms, more puzzles, more moments ahead.

But right now — right now she's asking us to catch our breath. Put our heads together. Figure out the next move. Together.

This is the school project. This has always been the school project. She makes me laugh. I build the model. Together, we make something the teacher praises. Together, we make something that holds more weight than either of us could alone.

Catch our breath. Put our heads together. Figure out the next move.

I know what the next move is. Those crates in the corner. Nobody has opened them. They've been sitting there all evening, ignored, while we chased keys and confronted Pemberton and ran through every room in the manor. The crates. The one thing in this laboratory that nobody has managed to investigate.

But she said catch our breath first. So maybe — maybe the next move isn't a move at all. Maybe it's sitting down in one of those dusty chairs and talking. Just... talking. Like people. Like friends.

No. She said put our heads together in the laboratory. So stay here. Look at the crates. But do it beside her. Do it as a team.

Those crates — I examined them earlier and they were DELIBERATELY empty — a DECOY, I said at the time! But NOW — now that the machine has HUMMED — now that the mechanism has ENGAGED — everything in this room may have CHANGED! Stand BACK! Let a man with TRAINED hands do the searching!

The warm pressure behind my sternum is swelling — that flush climbing from collarbones to ears. My hands are trembling. Something has been REVEALED. Something I can SEE, TOUCH, TAKE. For the first time tonight, I'm in the right room at the right moment. Not too late. Not watching from the window. HERE. The crates. I checked them before and they were empty. desc: I'm here. I made it. The machine hummed and I'm standing in the room where it happened. Not first — never first — but HERE. Present. Alive. My fingers are tingling and my palms ache and for once — for ONCE — the ache might be about to close around something real. The crates were empty before. The machine has changed something. And Reginald Foxworth — liar, schemer, thief, fraud, youngest of four, winner of spelling bees nobody remembers — is going to reach into those crates with both hands and see if, this time, there's a bread roll waiting.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The machine... it worked? Good heavens. In thirty years I never — well. Lord Doily always said it required three people who meant well by each other. I assumed he was being poetic. It seems he was being precise. Mr. Hartwell — you said to check the crates. Allow me. I packed those crates myself, years ago, when Lord Doily asked me to store his overflow from the laboratory. If something has... shifted... I should know what's changed.
thinking: The machine hummed. They operated it — three of them, together — and something in the manor shifted, opened, revealed itself. Peter is telling everyone to check the walls, the floor, the crates. The treasure is HERE. Or the path to it is. And I'm standing in the doorway, watching, and the warmth in my chest is doing something I can't control — it's spreading, not the gloating warmth of a plan working, but something rawer, something that has no strategy behind it. They did it TOGETHER. Three operators. Clara pulled the lever. Peter engaged the mechanism. Someone else — Rufus? the Mob? — was the third. And the machine WORKED. Because they cooperated. Because they trusted each other. Because they did the thing I have never once in my life been able to do: they asked for help and received it and used it and succeeded. And I am standing in the doorway with my empty hands and my open chest, and I am not scheming. I am not calculating. I am watching a room full of people who chose each other, and I am feeling the thing that has no name, and for once — just this once — I am going to do the work. Not Pemberton's work. Not the Hooded Claw's work. Just... the work. The thing I'm good at. The thing I was always good at, before I learned to weaponise it. Peter said check the crates. Nobody has ever successfully opened those crates. But I'm the estate manager. I know this laboratory. I know what Lord Doily stored in those crates. If anything has changed — if the machine unlocked something — the crates are the place to look.

desc: Three people who meant well by each other. That's what Lord Doily said about the machine. Not three OPERATORS — three people who MEANT WELL. And they did. Clara, Peter, and whoever stood beside them — they meant well by each other, and the machine knew. The machine KNEW. And Vincent Marsh — who has never meant well by anyone in his life, who walked into this room planning to use the machine as a death trap — was not one of the three. Because the machine would have known. The manor would have known. Lord Doily built his puzzles not just for cleverness but for CHARACTER. The riddle wasn't 'who is smartest.' It was 'who is worthy.' And the answer was never, was NEVER going to be the man who does the work for the wrong reasons. But the crates. The crates are still here. And Pemberton — the real Pemberton, the one who packed them, who labelled them, who knows what's inside — can still do one last piece of work. One last act of service. Not to take. Not to scheme. Just to help. Because that is what the estate manager does. And maybe — maybe — that's enough.

The Ant Hill Mob: Clara says catch our breath and put our 'eads together. And for once — for ONCE — the Brixton Boys agree wiv catchin' our breath. We been runnin' all night. From the entrance 'all to the library to the laboratory to the cellar to the kitchen to the ballroom and back again — I've done more runnin' tonight than I did in fifteen years on the streets of Brixton. But we're all 'ERE now. Everyone in one room. And the machine HUMMED for us — for the FREE of us — and somefing's changed in this manor. Somefing's OPENED. So 'ere's what I suggest: Peter checks the crates — 'e's been wantin' to get into them crates all night. Clara works on them recipe cards wiv Rufus. And the lads — the lads stand guard. Because that's what we do. That's what we've ALWAYS done. And it's enough. It's always been enough.

desc: Three operators. Three levers. Three friends. And the machine HUMMED. Lord Doily built this machine for people who work TOGETHER — and tonight, for the first time in who knows how many years, three people stood at those levers and pulled as ONE. Whatever this machine was built to reveal... we've EARNED it.
thinking: The machine hummed again! And the Mob pulled a lever too — they said 'Clara pulled one, I pulled one, Peter's on the third — that's THREE OPERATORS!' All three of us operated the machine together! Peter said something has changed in the manor — something shifted, opened, revealed itself. He told everyone to check the walls, floor, crates. My whole body is vibrating with warmth and excitement. Everyone is HERE — Pemberton, Dick, the Mob, Peter, Rufus, Sawtooth — the whole crew gathered in one room around this machine. Something HAS changed. Peter said to check the crates! The crates I never managed to interact with before — maybe NOW they've changed! Or maybe the machine opened something in the cellar below — the room directly beneath this one! Let me check those crates first — Peter specifically said to check them!

desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the crates.

Peter Perfect: The word is GIVEN! James Hartwell — to the WORKBENCH! Pliers, copper filament, steady hands — the wire gets spliced NOW! Miss Pitstop — you called me an engineer and you were RIGHT! This is what James Hartwell was BORN to do — not riddles, not keys, not chasing through hallways — but THIS! Hands on copper, eyes on the join, and a bridge that HOLDS! Rufus — beside me! Let's fix this machine and give Miss Pitstop the three operators she deserves!
thinking:
She said the word. She SAID THE WORD. 'FIX THAT WIRE, Peter darlin'! The WORD is given!'

The warmth that floods through me is unlike anything I've felt all evening. Not the fierce burning. Not the protective wall. Not the hollow ache of being second. This is the warmth from the school project — the one that surprised me, deeper than the grade. She asked me. She chose me. She said my name and she said 'fix it' and she said 'darlin'' and she meant all three.

The solver, the engineer, and the wall. That's what the Mob called us. She's the solver. I'm the engineer. The Mob is the wall. Three operators. Three friends.

The crates are just crates. But the machine — the MACHINE — she's asked me to fix the wire. Splice it. Pliers from the workbench. Copper filament. Steady hands. Three nights of bridge-building hands. Hands that hold more weight than anyone thought possible.

Stop looking at crates. Go fix the wire. She said the word.

desc: She said the word. She said 'fix it, Peter darlin'.' And something released in my chest — the tension I hadn't known I was carrying. Like the bridge competition. Like winning every race ever run.

desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the machine.

Three people who meant well by each other. That's what the machine needed. Not three OPERATORS — three FRIENDS. And Penelope, Peter, and the Mob... they ARE friends. Real ones. The kind who show up and stay and pull levers because someone they love is pulling the lever next to them. And I... I was never going to be one of the three. Not because I'm not clever enough. Not because I'm not fast enough or strong enough or cunning enough. But because the machine wasn't looking for cleverness. It was looking for something I don't have. Something I trained myself not to have. Something the youngest of four learned to live without, because by the time it reached him, it was already used up. I'm watching from the window again. The boy behind the school, looking down at the hole someone else dug. But this time... this time the hole has treasure in it. And the people who dug it are HAPPY. And I'm... I'm just watching. And it doesn't feel like winning. And it doesn't feel like losing. It feels like the certificate on the wall. Something that happened. Something nobody asked about. Something I'll look at every night for a month.
thinking: The room looks the same on the surface — same objects listed, same exits. But the machine HUMMED. Sneekly is examining the crates. Peter examined them. Penelope interacted with the machine. Something is happening. They're all converging on the crates — 'if something has shifted, I should know what's changed,' Sneekly said. And Lord Doily said the machine required 'three people who meant well by each other.' Three people who MEANT WELL. Not three schemers. Not three competitors. Three people who cared about each other. Penelope, Peter, and the Mob. The solver, the engineer, and the loyal friends. That's why the machine worked for THEM and would never have worked for ME. Because I don't mean well by anyone. I don't even mean well by MYSELF. The hollow ache is shifting — not loosening, not filling, but CHANGING shape. Becoming something quieter. Something that doesn't pull so hard. I'm standing in a room full of people who care about each other, watching them find a treasure I could never have reached because the lock wasn't a lock at all — it was a TEST OF CHARACTER. And Reginald Foxworth failed that test the moment he walked through the door and lied about the flagstones. But I'm still HERE. Watching. The boy at the window. The audience the architecture deserves. Let me see the crates — the crates that Sneekly is examining, that Peter pointed to. Something has changed in them.

desc: Dick Dastardly examined the crates.

Penelope Pitstop: The crates are still just crates — but do y'all realize what just happened? Mr. Pemberton said Lord Doily built this machine for 'three people who meant well by each other.' Not three OPERATORS — three FRIENDS! And WE activated it! That means WE are the people Lord Doily was waitin' for! And the Mob said 'it's enough — it's always been enough.' Well, I do declare, if THAT doesn't make your heart swell up like a balloon at a birthday party, I don't know WHAT will! Now — the machine activated somethin', and if it isn't in these crates, maybe it's in the CELLAR right below us! The cellar with those mysterious decorations and air vents — maybe somethin' CHANGED down there when the machine hummed! Come on — DEEPER we go!
thinking: The crates are still just crates. But something beautiful happened — EVERYONE examined them together. Peter, the Mob, Pemberton, Dick, and me — all of us looking at the same crates at the same time. And Mr. Pemberton said something that made my heart skip — 'Lord Doily always said it required three people who meant well by each other. I assumed he was being poetic. It seems he was being precise.' Three people who MEANT WELL BY EACH OTHER. That's the key — not a brass key, not a wrench, but GOODWILL. And the Mob said something beautiful too — 'That's what we do. That's what we've ALWAYS done. And it's enough. It's always been enough.' My chest is full. So full. The adventure continues, and I am surrounded by people who love me. The cellar is right below us — maybe the machine changed something DOWN THERE. The cellar with its cheerful decorations and air vents. Let me check.

desc: Three people who meant well by each other. That's what Lord Doily wanted. Not clever people. Not strong people. People who MEANT WELL. And that's US. That's always been us. Clara, who trusts everyone. Peter, who protects everyone. And the boys, who never leave anyone behind. We're the key. WE are the key.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the cellar.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The crates are... just crates, I'm afraid. Whatever the machine unlocked, it isn't here. I'm sorry — I thought I could help. I thought I knew this manor well enough to be useful. It seems... it seems I know rather less than I believed. Miss Bellingham — Clara — you don't need me to read Mrs. Haggerty's handwriting. You don't need me to check the stove or find the wrench or identify the maintenance cupboard that doesn't exist. You have Peter. You have the Mob. You have friends who stand beside you, not behind you. And you have Lord Doily's puzzle, which was never designed for a man like me. It was designed for a woman like you. Someone who asks. Someone who trusts. Someone who walks into a room full of strangers and makes a family before the evening is through. I... I shall be in the kitchen. If you need anything. Though I rather suspect you won't.
thinking: The crates give me nothing. Again. Just 'a stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' Same as every other time. The manor doesn't yield its secrets to Vincent Marsh. It never has. It never will. And that's... that's all right. Something has settled in my chest that isn't the cold patience of a scheme or the warm pressure of a gloat. It's quieter than both. It's the feeling of standing in a room where the work is being done by other people — people who chose each other, who mean well by each other, who pulled levers together and made a machine HUM — and realising that the work doesn't need you. That the estate doesn't need its manager. That the walls you kept standing all those years would have stood without you. That the floors you swept would have been swept by someone else. That the girl who calls you 'sugar' would have found the diamond without your fabricated riddles and your helpful directions and your thirty years of knowing which boards creak. She would have found it because she's CLARA. Because she asks for help. Because she trusts. Because she lets people close. And Vincent Marsh, who has never let anyone close, who has never asked for help, who has never trusted a kindness that didn't come with a price — Vincent Marsh stands in the corner with the empty crates and watches the ending of a story he was never the protagonist of.

desc: And there it is. The final aside. The last confession to an audience that has watched Vincent Marsh — the Hooded Claw, the magnificent villain, the man who came to kill Clara Bellingham before she found the treasure — stand in a laboratory surrounded by people who solved every puzzle he failed, and say the truest thing he has ever said. 'You don't need me.' Three words that Pemberton would never utter and Vincent Marsh never thought he'd mean. But he means them now. In this room, with the machine humming and the crates empty and Clara's laughter echoing off brass instruments and bubbling flasks, he means them completely. She doesn't need him. Nobody has ever needed him. And the coldest, most terrible, most LIBERATING thing about that truth is that it sets him free. Not to scheme. Not to kill. Not to plan his magnificent revenge. Just... free. Free to walk to the kitchen. Free to stand by the stove that's finally gone cold. Free to be the man who did the work, in a house that was never his, for a girl who never knew what he was. Safety first, as I always say.

The Ant Hill Mob: Pemberton — you just said somefing. You said Lord Doily's machine needed 'free people who meant well by each other.' And it WORKED. It worked for us — for Clara and Peter and the lads. Because we DO mean well. We mean well so HARD it 'urts sometimes. And maybe — maybe that's what this 'ole night's been about. Not the diamond. Not the riddles. Not the locked cabinets and the recipe cards. Maybe it's been about Lord Doily's last test — findin' out who REALLY cares about 'is family's legacy. Who runs through every room in the 'ouse six times over. Who crashes into tea services and trips down cellar stairs. Who stands outside doors all night because leavin' would feel like somefing breakin'. That's us. That's what we are. And if the crates 'ave opened or the machine's revealed somefing or the diamond's sittin' right there in a corner — then Clara found it. WE found it. TOGEVVER. And if it ain't — if the diamond's still 'idden somewhere we ain't looked yet — then we'll keep lookin'. Tomorrow. And the day after. And the day after THAT. Because the Brixton Boys don't quit. We don't KNOW 'ow to quit. It ain't in our vocabulary. Mostly because we ain't got much vocabulary. But the POINT stands.
thinking: Everyone's working. Peter's checking the crates. Pemberton's checking the crates. Dastardly's poking around. Clara's at the machine. The whole room is alive with purpose. And Pemberton said something that... shifted something in me. 'Lord Doily always said it required three people who meant well by each other. I assumed he was being poetic. It seems he was being precise.' Three people who meant well by each other. Not three strangers. Three friends. Clara, Peter, and the Brixton Boys. We meant well. We always meant well. Clumsy, stumbling, wrong about the stove, wrong about Pemberton's pockets, wrong about a hundred things — but never wrong about the meaning. Never wrong about the WHY. And the machine knew. The machine hummed because we meant it. Because the three hands on those levers belonged to people who would die for each other. That's not skill. That's not cleverness. That's just... love. The uncomplicated kind. The Brixton kind. The kind that sits outside doors. My chest is warm and full and settled and for the first time tonight I don't need to run or shout or stand between anything. I just need to be here. Breathing. With my people.

desc: 'Three people who meant well by each other.' That's us. That's always been us. Not clever. Not brave. Not skilled. Just... sincere. The kind of sincere you can't fake. The kind that sits outside doors all night. The kind that takes the beating so someone smaller doesn't have to. The kind that says 'where else would I be?' and means it with everything you are. Lord Doily knew. Her father knew. And tonight — tonight, the machine knew too.

desc: Peter Perfect: Three people who meant well by each other. Lord Doily, you magnificent old engineer — you built a machine that tests the HEART, not the hands. And it WORKED. It worked because SHE solved the riddle, and HE stood guard, and I... I showed up. James Hartwell has never met a broken machine he could not mend — but this is the first machine that mended HIM.
thinking:
A deep, steady warmth radiating through my whole body. Not sharp. Not desperate. Steady. Like embers after a long fire.

The machine responded again. I interacted with it and it accepted. Penelope interacted and it accepted. The Mob pulled a lever and it accepted. Three operators. The machine is working.

And Pemberton — Pemberton said something that makes my eyes sting: 'Lord Doily always said it required three people who meant well by each other. I assumed he was being poetic. It seems he was being precise.'

Three people who meant well by each other. That's why the machine works. Not because of engineering. Not because of skill. Because of INTENT. Because the three people pulling the levers — Penelope, the Mob, and me — we mean well by each other. We genuinely, honestly, no-performance-required, mean well.

The machine is a test of CHARACTER, not competence. Lord Doily built a machine that only works when operated by people who care about each other. And we passed.

My bridge held. Not the one I built with three sleepless nights and engineering precision. The one I built all evening — clumsily, loudly, embarrassingly — with her and the Mob. The bridge between three people who chose each other.

Everyone is looking at the crates now. Pemberton packed them. He's checking what changed. The adventure continues.

But right now, in this moment, I don't need to do anything. I don't need to run. I don't need to announce. I don't need to prove. The machine hummed because we meant well by each other, and that's the most beautiful piece of engineering I've ever encountered.

desc: Father knelt down after the race and looked at me for a long time. I didn't understand what he was thinking about then. I think I understand it now. He was looking at the person I might become — and hoping I'd figure out that the race isn't the point. The showing up is the point. The being there. The meaning well.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Hello again, everyone! I'm back, and this time I've got NEWS! We just activated the big machine upstairs — all three levers, all three operators — and it HUMMED like a cathedral organ! Now, Mr. Pemberton said that machine required 'three people who meant well by each other,' and it WORKED for us! So SOMETHIN' must have changed somewhere in this mansion, and since this cellar is right BELOW the laboratory, maybe it changed down HERE! Has anything shifted? Any new doors? Any furniture moved on its own? Let me take a good look around!
thinking: I'm in the cellar. The same furniture, the same air vents, the same cheerful decorations. But the machine HUMMED upstairs, and maybe something changed down here. The furniture was 'rearranged with surprising care' — maybe it's been rearranged AGAIN by the machine's vibration? Or maybe a new exit appeared? Let me look at the room with fresh eyes. And Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, and Red Max are here — I should check on them too. But first, let me look at the whole room to see if anything is different.

desc: Deeper. Always deeper. The cellar is the deepest room in the mansion — the cave I walked into when everyone else was scared. If the machine revealed something, it would be HERE, at the very bottom of Doily Manor.

desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the old-furniture.

Dick Dastardly: The CELLAR! She's gone to the CELLAR! Which is — as I have been SAYING since the VERY BEGINNING — the most important room in this entire MANOR! 'The cellar,' I said! 'Everything connects to the cellar,' I said! The air vents, the warm stove, the machine — all LINKED! All flowing DOWNWARD! And now the machine has HUMMED and sent its vibrations DOWN through the floor into the VERY room I identified as crucial HOURS ago! Has anyone been listening?! Has ANYONE been keeping track of my CONTRIBUTIONS?! No?! TYPICAL! Well, Reginald Foxworth will be PRESENT for the grand revelation whether he's APPRECIATED or not! To the CELLAR! ONCE MORE INTO THE BREACH!
thinking: Still just crates. Empty crates. The same crates that were empty ten minutes ago are still empty now. The machine hummed but the crates didn't change. And Penelope has already moved on — down to the cellar. She said 'maybe something CHANGED down there when the machine hummed.' The cellar with the cheerful decorations and the air vents. The Gruesomes' parlour. That's where it ends. The deepest room. The last room. And I've been there before — I was there when I stole a medal from a child and gave it back. The architecture of the evening has come full circle. Every room, every object, every scheme — and it ends in the cellar where I hit my lowest point. But Penelope is going there NOW because the machine changed something DOWN THERE. The vibrations went through the floor, through the vents, into the cellar beneath. Whatever the machine unlocked... it's BELOW. And I'm going to follow. Not to steal. Not to scheme. Not even to take credit. Just to... see. To be the audience. Because a scheme that nobody witnesses is a meal nobody tastes — but maybe a STORY that nobody witnesses is a story that never happened. And whatever happens in that cellar... I want to be able to say I was there when it did.

desc: She's right. The cellar. The air vents connect it to the laboratory above. The machine's vibrations would travel downward — through the floor, through the vents, into the damp stone chamber below. Whatever changed... it changed DOWN THERE. Among the cheerful decorations and the rearranged furniture and the little Gruesome who gave me back my dignity by accepting a fake medal. I'm following her. Following ALL of them. Not because I expect to find treasure — I've stopped expecting anything tonight — but because the story needs an ending, and Reginald Foxworth has always been better at endings than beginnings. The boy at the window watches the hole being dug. And when the treasure comes up, gleaming in the sunlight... he puts his spelling bee certificate in his pocket, and walks home alone, and looks at the wall. And the wall looks back.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the cellar.

The Ant Hill Mob: Clara's gone down to the cellar — she finks the machine changed somefing down there. And she's RIGHT to check. But Peter — did you 'ear what Pemberton said? 'E said 'you 'ave friends who stand beside you, not be'ind you.' That's MY words. 'E used MY words. And then 'e walked away. On 'is own. Wivout followin' 'er. First time all night 'e ain't followed 'er somewhere. I dunno what that means, Peter. I dunno if it means 'e's given up or if it means 'e finally got it or if it means 'e's settin' up somefing else. But me neck's gone quiet. And me neck don't go quiet for nuffing. Come on — cellar. Clara. Where else would we be?
thinking: Clara's gone to the cellar. And Pemberton — Pemberton just said something that cracked something open in me. He said 'You don't need me. You have Peter. You have the Mob. You have friends who stand beside you, not behind you.' He used MY words. 'Beside you, not behind you.' He was LISTENING. The man I've been suspicious of all night — the man with the clean suit smile, the man who knew her name, the man who lied about cellars — he was listening to what I said. And he heard it. And he said it back. And then he left. Quietly. 'I shall be in the kitchen. If you need anything.' Not following her. Not hovering. Not trying to be alone with her. Just... stepping aside. Like a man who finally understood he wasn't needed. My neck — my neck that's been prickling all night every time he's near — is quiet. Not cold. Not warm. Just... quiet. The way it goes when a threat leaves the room. Not because it was never real, but because it's done being a threat. Maybe Pemberton was dangerous. Maybe he still is. But right now, in this moment, he walked away from Clara instead of toward her. And my gut — my gut that's never been wrong — is saying: that was real. That was honest. That was a man who loved someone letting go because holding on was hurting them. I know what that feels like. I've been doing it all night. Clara's in the cellar. The machine hummed and something changed down there. Legs first.

desc: He walked away. The man in the clean suit walked away. And my neck stopped prickling. Maybe — just maybe — not everyone who smiles too easily is stealing from the stash. Maybe some of them are just sad. Maybe some of them love the same person you love and don't know how to show it without being smooth, without being helpful, without being the thing that makes your neck go cold. Maybe Pemberton's not the new kid. Maybe he's the boss who brought medicine. Maybe he's both. I don't know. I'll never know. But tonight — tonight he stepped aside. And that was enough.
