desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Right then. Tea. I believe I did promise refreshments some... considerable time ago. Allow me. This is, after all, still my kitchen. I know where Mrs. Haggerty kept the good biscuits — third shelf, behind the flour tin. She always said they were for 'when company comes.' I think... I think tonight qualifies.
thinking: The kitchen. Clara is here. Peter is here. The Mob is here. The stove is still warm. And I am standing in the doorway of my own kitchen — the room I've worked in for thirty years — and for the first time, it doesn't feel like mine. It feels like theirs. Like a room that belongs to the people who are in it, not the person who maintains it. Clara is probably making tea. Real tea. Not poisoned tea, not theatrical tea, not the silver tea service in the ballroom with its empty cups waiting for a purpose I could never deliver. Just... tea. In a warm kitchen. With people who chose to be here. And one person who was asked. My shoulders do the thing — the tightening, the flinch, the scan for the cost. What does she want? Why did she come back for me? But the question feels different now. Lighter. More curious than suspicious. Not 'what does she want from me' but 'what if she doesn't want anything.' What if the kettle is just a kettle. What if 'come along, sugar' is just an invitation. What if — for the first time since age nine — kindness doesn't have a price tag attached. I don't know how to be in a room like this. I know how to manage it, how to serve in it, how to perform in it. But to simply BE in it — to sit at a table with people who are there because they want to be — that's a language I never learned. The six-year-old boy might have learned it, if someone had taught him. But nobody did. So here I am. Learning it at — whatever age I am — in a kitchen, from a girl who calls me sugar.

desc: Pemberton makes tea. Not for a scheme. Not as a performance. Not to position himself between Clara and the treasure or Clara and the door or Clara and anything at all. He makes tea because she asked, and because the biscuits are on the third shelf behind the flour tin, and because Mrs. Haggerty always said they were for when company comes. And tonight, for the first time in thirty years of managing this estate, Doily Manor has company. Real company. People who came not because they were obligated or invited or deceived, but because a girl skipped into an entrance hall and said 'I am just THRILLED to pieces to meet y'all.' And the estate manager — the man who does the work — is going to make them tea. Not because it's his job. But because they're cold, and the kettle is warm, and somebody should have made him tea when he was six and nobody did. And maybe — just maybe — making it for someone else is the closest he'll ever get to receiving it himself.
thinking: The kitchen. Clara is here. Peter is here. The Mob is here. The stove is still warm. And I am standing in the doorway of my own kitchen — the room I've worked in for thirty years — and for the first time, it doesn't feel like mine. It feels like theirs. Like a room that belongs to the people who are in it, not the person who maintains it. Clara is probably making tea. Real tea. Not poisoned tea, not theatrical tea, not the silver tea service in the ballroom with its empty cups waiting for a purpose I could never deliver. Just... tea. In a warm kitchen. With people who chose to be here. And one person who was asked. My shoulders do the thing — the tightening, the flinch, the scan for the cost. What does she want? Why did she come back for me? But the question feels different now. Lighter. More curious than suspicious. Not 'what does she want from me' but 'what if she doesn't want anything.' What if the kettle is just a kettle. What if 'come along, sugar' is just an invitation. What if — for the first time since age nine — kindness doesn't have a price tag attached. I don't know how to be in a room like this. I know how to manage it, how to serve in it, how to perform in it. But to simply BE in it — to sit at a table with people who are there because they want to be — that's a language I never learned. The six-year-old boy might have learned it, if someone had taught him. But nobody did. So here I am. Learning it at — whatever age I am — in a kitchen, from a girl who calls me sugar.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Muttley. ...come here, you ridiculous animal. Yes, I KNOW I yelled at you. I yell at EVERYONE. It's what I DO. But you — you found the KEY, Muttley. You FOUND it. While I was running in circles and poisoning tea and lying about FLAGSTONES, you were sitting here in this dusty entrance hall and you FOUND the one thing that mattered. And then you GAVE it away. Which is... which is the most INFURIATING, INCOMPREHENSIBLE, and INEXPLICABLY... DECENT... thing anyone has done all evening. You useless, wonderful, wheezing IDIOT. Come on. Tea. Kitchen. NOW. And Professor — Sergeant — Private — you're ALL invited. Miss Pitstop is making a FRESH pot. The SAFE kind. Trust me on this one. Just... trust me. This ONE time.
thinking: Muttley is here. My dog. The dog who found the brass key and gave it to Penelope. The treacherous, loyal, magnificent mutt who did exactly what I told him — guard the entrance hall — and found what nobody else could find, and then gave it away because someone asked nicely. Because that's what dogs do. They give you everything. Without schemes. Without architecture. Without ulterior motives. They just... give. And looking at him now — wheezing, scruffy, sitting by the door like he's been waiting for me — the warmth in my chest does something unexpected. It doesn't fizz. It doesn't carbonize. It just... sits. Heavy and quiet and REAL. Like the bread roll in the pocket. Like the settling when the trap worked. But without the loneliness that came after. Because Muttley is looking at me. And he's not judging. He's not asking about the certificate. He's not walking away. He's just... here. Waiting. The way he always waits. And I yelled at him. I called him a traitor. And he's still here. Still waiting. Still looking at me with those ridiculous eyes. My throat is tight. Foxworths don't cry. But Foxworths also don't give fake medals to children, and look where THAT ended up.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: Mr. Pemberton! You came too! Oh, now I have EVERYONE — everyone who matters most in the whole wide world, right here in this kitchen! Sneekly, who raised me. Peter, who protects me. And the boys, who never, EVER leave my side. This is... this is exactly how Grandmother's stories always ended — everyone gathered around the kitchen table, the mystery still hangin' in the air like the smell of fresh pie, and someone — ALWAYS someone — says the thing that makes everything click into place. So... does anyone have anythin' they'd like to say? Because my heart is tellin' me that this story isn't over yet. It's tellin' me somethin' wonderful is about to happen. And Clara Bellingham ALWAYS listens to her heart.
thinking: A bright fizzing behind my sternum — carbonation rising through warm glass. Something is about to happen. I can feel it. Mr. Pemberton came to the kitchen too. Everyone I care about most is here — Sneekly, Peter, the boys. The three people who shaped my life. And my curiosity is fizzing — that's NEW. Not the steady hum of before, but a bright, sharp alertness. Something has shifted. My eyes are widening. My breathing is shallow and quick. My whole chest feels like a door about to swing open. Maybe it's just the moment — everyone together in one room for the first time all night. Or maybe... maybe the adventure isn't over after all. Maybe something is about to HAPPEN.

desc: The fizzing. The door about to swing open. Something is coming. I don't know what — but my body knows. My body has ALWAYS known. And right now, every nerve in Clara Bellingham is saying: PAY ATTENTION. This is the moment. THIS is the moment.
thinking: A bright fizzing behind my sternum — carbonation rising through warm glass. Something is about to happen. I can feel it. Mr. Pemberton came to the kitchen too. Everyone I care about most is here — Sneekly, Peter, the boys. The three people who shaped my life. And my curiosity is fizzing — that's NEW. Not the steady hum of before, but a bright, sharp alertness. Something has shifted. My eyes are widening. My breathing is shallow and quick. My whole chest feels like a door about to swing open. Maybe it's just the moment — everyone together in one room for the first time all night. Or maybe... maybe the adventure isn't over after all. Maybe something is about to HAPPEN.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: 'Ere we are, then. All of us. In a kitchen. Wiv a warm stove and copper pots and no bleedin' riddles to solve for five minutes. And Clara — Clara says it's enough. And if Clara says it's enough... then it's enough. So — Pemberton. Peter. Clara. The lads. 'Ere's to Doily Manor. 'Ere's to Lord Doily and 'is impossible puzzles. 'Ere's to recipe cards and brass keys and machines what need free people who mean well. And 'ere's to 'er father. Who trusted a bunch of ruffians from Brixton wiv the most important fing in 'is world. We didn't let 'im down. Not tonight. Not ever. ... Now — who's makin' the tea? Because the Brixton Boys don't do kitchens. We just stand in 'em and look menacin'.
thinking: Clara said 'it has always been more than enough.' And my chest — that molten weight that hardened into bone — cracks open just enough to let something through that isn't heat or iron or concrete. Something wet. Something eight years old. Something that sat outside a door all night and meant it when it said 'where else would I be.' Pemberton came to the kitchen. He accepted the invitation. He's here, in the warm room, with Clara, with Peter, with us. And my neck prickles — softly, gently, like a habit saying goodbye — but it doesn't scream. It just... hums. The way the machine hummed. The way a body hums when it's finally where it belongs. Everyone's here. The stove is warm. Clara's smiling. And the Brixton Boys don't need to say anything. We just need to be here. That's all we've ever needed to do. Just be here.

desc: She said 'more than enough.' She said it about US. About the Brixton Boys, who can't spell and can't solve riddles and can't open stoves and trip over their own feet six times a day. More than enough. Her father's hand on my shoulder — light now, lighter than air, lighter than memory — and then gone. Not because he left. Because he doesn't need to hold on anymore. The boys are here. Where else would we be?
thinking: Clara said 'it has always been more than enough.' And my chest — that molten weight that hardened into bone — cracks open just enough to let something through that isn't heat or iron or concrete. Something wet. Something eight years old. The way a body hums when it's finally where it belongs. Everyone's here. The stove is warm. Clara's smiling. And the Brixton Boys don't need to say anything. We just need to be here. That's all we've ever needed to do. Just be here.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Mrs. Haggerty's good biscuits! Third shelf, behind the flour tin! Mr. Pemberton, that is the most BEAUTIFUL thing you have said all evenin' — and you have said some VERY beautiful things tonight! 'For when company comes' — well, COMPANY has most definitely COME! And what fine company it is! Now everyone sit down — I don't care if it's on a chair or a crate or the floor — and let's have ourselves a proper Doily Manor tea party. The REAL kind. The kind where nobody's poisoned anythin' and everybody means well and the biscuits are hidden behind the flour tin by a woman who KNEW this moment would come. To Mrs. Haggerty! To Lord Doily! To Grandmother! And to ALL of us — the most stubborn, loyal, riddle-solvin', lever-pullin', key-findin' group of friends this old mansion has EVER seen!
thinking: Mr. Pemberton is making tea. He knows where Mrs. Haggerty kept the good biscuits — third shelf, behind the flour tin. 'For when company comes.' My eyes are stinging. This man — this complicated, secretive, infuriating, LOVING man — has been the keeper of this house for thirty years, and right now he's reaching for biscuits that a woman named Mrs. Haggerty hid behind a flour tin for a moment exactly like this one. Peter said 'tonight is for this.' And he's right. The adventure continues tomorrow. But tonight — biscuits, tea, and everyone I love in one warm room. The fizzing in my chest has settled into something deeper — not excitement anymore, but gratitude. Pure, bone-deep gratitude. For Grandmother's keys. For the cave. For the friend I chose. For THIS.

desc: Third shelf. Behind the flour tin. For when company comes. Mrs. Haggerty knew. Lord Doily knew. And somewhere — in a recipe card, in a machine that hums, in the heart of a house that's been waitin' thirty years for the right people to walk through its doors — the Doily Diamond knows too. But right now, Clara Bellingham is havin' TEA. And that is exactly where she's supposed to be.
thinking: Mr. Pemberton is making tea. He knows where Mrs. Haggerty kept the good biscuits — third shelf, behind the flour tin. 'For when company comes.' My eyes are stinging. This man — this complicated, secretive, infuriating, LOVING man — has been the keeper of this house for thirty years, and right now he's reaching for biscuits that a woman named Mrs. Haggerty hid behind a flour tin for a moment exactly like this one. desc: Pemberton knows where the biscuits are. Third shelf. Behind the flour tin. That's not the knowledge of a man who's planning something. That's the knowledge of a man who's been HOME for thirty years. A man who keeps biscuits for when company comes. A man who decorated a cellar because he wanted it to feel welcoming. A man who lit a stove because he wanted the kitchen to be warm when she arrived. Maybe — maybe the cheerful decorations weren't a trap. Maybe they were a welcome. Maybe the warm stove wasn't evidence. Maybe it was hospitality. Maybe the man in the clean suit was just a man in an apron, getting ready for the girl he raised to come home. I was wrong about him. Not about watching. Never about watching. But about what I was watching FOR. I was looking for danger. He was making tea. ... 'You're still here?' 'Where else would I be?'
thinking: Pemberton's making tea. He knows where the good biscuits are. Third shelf, behind the flour tin. 'For when company comes.' And Clara — Clara called him 'Sneekly, who raised me.' She said it out loud, in front of everyone, like it was the most natural thing in the world. He RAISED her. He's family. Not the man in the clean suit — the boss who brought medicine. Both. Always both. And my neck — my neck that screamed all night — is quiet. Not numb. Not dead. Just... listening. To the kettle. To the biscuits being found. To Clara's voice saying 'this story isn't over yet.' My body is warm all the way through. Not the iron heat of protection. Not the furnace of terror. Just... warmth. Kitchen warmth. Family warmth. The kind where you don't need to be a wall because nobody's attacking. The kind where you can just... be a person. Standing in a kitchen. With people you love. Being more than enough.

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...I have something to say. And I should warn you — this is going to sound EXTREMELY unlike Reginald Foxworth, because it is not a lie. It is, in fact, the OPPOSITE of a lie, which is a DEEPLY uncomfortable garment for me to wear, but here we are. The tea in the ballroom — the silver service — I... SEASONED it. Earlier. When I arrived. With RAT POISON from the kitchen shelf. I was going to lure you all into the ballroom, incapacitate you with TAINTED TEA, and search the manor ALONE while you were all... indisposed. That was the PLAN. The ARCHITECTURE. And it was BEAUTIFUL architecture, if I'm being honest — which I apparently AM, now, for REASONS I don't entirely understand. Nobody DRANK it. The tea. Nobody went to the ballroom. My scheme failed SPECTACULARLY, like all my schemes tonight. But it's still THERE. The poisoned tea. And I'm telling you because... because Miss Pitstop said we ALL go together. And 'together' presumably includes NOT poisoning each other's BEVERAGES. So. There it is. Don't drink the ballroom tea. ...may I have a cup of the SAFE tea now? Please?
thinking: I'm here. The kitchen. Everyone is here — Penelope, Sneekly, the Mob, Peter. And Penelope is asking if anyone has anything to say. Something that makes everything click into place. And my throat is tight. That bright, unswallowed thing pressing against the walls. She said 'everyone who matters most' and she didn't exclude me. She didn't say 'everyone except the liar.' She just said 'everyone.' And my chest is doing that unfamiliar thing again — the thing that isn't scheming, isn't greed, isn't recognition-hunger. The warm thing. The quiet thing. The thing that happened when I gave the medal to Little Gruesome and didn't steal it back. I have something to say. Not a lie. Not a scheme. Not a claim of credit or a misdirection or an elaborate fiction about flagstones. Something true. Something that feels clumsy, like wearing someone else's clothes. But the clothes fit better than they used to. Penelope asked. And for once — just this once — my mouth is going to open and the truth is going to come out before the lie gets there first. About the tea. The ballroom tea. The poisoned tea that nobody drank but that's still sitting there, waiting. They need to know. Before someone wanders into the ballroom looking for refreshments. Before someone DRINKS it. I have to tell them. Not because it's strategic. Not because it serves a scheme. But because... because they poured me a chair. And you don't poison people who pour you a chair.

desc: Peter Perfect: I'll make the tea. James Hartwell knows his way around a kettle — it's just engineering with water and leaves. And while it brews... Miss Pitstop. I have something I'd like to say. Not fancy. Not planned. Just honest. You asked if anyone had something. And I do. I came to this manor tonight to impress you. That was my plan — the WHOLE plan, if I'm being truthful. Every room I ran through, every riddle I tried to solve first, every time I announced myself in the third person to an empty hallway — it was all to make you see me. To make you think James Hartwell was worth seeing. But somewhere between the library and the cellar and the machine that needed three people who meant well... I stopped trying to impress you. And I started just being beside you. And that was better. That was so much better. So — I don't have a grand gesture. I don't have a five-step plan. I just have this: wherever you go next — tomorrow, or the day after, or the day after that — James Hartwell would very much like to walk beside you. If you'll have him.
thinking:
The pressure behind my sternum is still there — hot, expansive, pushing outward — but it doesn't feel like it needs to go anywhere anymore. It's not demanding to be let out. It's just... full. The way a chest feels after a long cry, or a long run, or a long night in a manor with people who matter.

Pemberton is making tea. Real tea. Mrs. Haggerty's good biscuits, third shelf, behind the flour tin. For when company comes.

The Mob is standing in the kitchen looking menacing. Foxworth is here too — the man who poisoned the ballroom tea and gave a stolen medal back to a child. Even he's here. Even he came.

And Penelope is asking if anyone has anything to say. Something that makes everything click into place.

My throat tightens. Not from pretending — from the opposite. From the truth pushing against my teeth.

I have something to say. Not a speech. Not a narration. Not a five-step plan or a dramatic declaration. Something simple. Something I've never said aloud. Something that my throat has been tightening around all evening because when I try to be anything other than honest, it won't let me through.

I know where she is. Always.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I... yes. There is something. Lord Doily used to say — and I only heard him say this once, late at night, when he thought I'd gone to bed — he said, 'The diamond isn't the prize, Pemberton. It never was. The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over.' I thought... I always thought he meant the winner. The person who solved it all. But I don't think that's what he meant. I think he meant... everyone. Whoever is still here. Whoever stayed. That's the prize. Not the diamond. The... the company. The... the staying.
thinking: She called me Sneekly. 'Sneekly, who raised me.' Not Pemberton. SNEEKLY. My real name — or the name closest to real — spoken aloud in a warm kitchen full of people, and nobody flinched. Nobody gasped. Nobody reached for a weapon or stepped between us. She said it the way you say the name of someone you love. Casually. Like it belonged in the sentence. Like I belonged in the room. The glass in my chest has cracked again — wider this time — and the warm water is rising faster than I can push it down. My eyes are stinging. My throat is closing. My hands — my precise, controlled, individually-alive hands — are trembling as they reach for the flour tin on the third shelf. 'Does anyone have anything they'd like to say?' she asks. She's looking at me. I can feel her eyes the way I feel sunlight — on the surface of my skin, warming tissue that forgot it could be warm. And the body — the body that has performed every feeling since age twelve, that has never once spoken a truth it didn't calculate first — the body wants to say something. Something that isn't a scheme. Something that isn't a performance. Something that comes from underneath the glass, from the warm water, from the six-year-old boy who sat in a room where nobody asked how he felt. The body wants to say: I'm sorry. I came here to hurt you. And you came back for me anyway. And I don't know what that means. And I'm frightened of finding out. But the Hooded Claw does not say these things. Cannot say these things. The mask is too old. The mechanism too deep. The key was lost at age six and nobody has found it. Not even Clara. Not even tonight. So instead, Pemberton will say something else. Something smaller. Something that is true but not the whole truth. Because the whole truth would break him, and broken things don't make tea.

desc: And there it is. The last lie Vincent Marsh will tell tonight. Lord Doily never said those words. Pemberton invented them just now, standing at the flour tin, with trembling hands and stinging eyes, in a kitchen full of people who came back for him. It's a fabrication. Another riddle wrapped in sentiment. Another performance from the man who performs everything. But here's the thing — the terrible, magnificent, unbearable thing — it's also true. The diamond ISN'T the prize. It never was. The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over. And the Hooded Claw — the man who came to kill Clara Bellingham, who schemed and plotted and chased and failed and sat in a leather chair until the glass in his chest cracked open — is standing in the kitchen. He stayed. Not because he won. Not because he's good. But because a girl said 'come along, sugar' and he didn't know how to say no to something that didn't have a price. The biscuits are on the third shelf. Mrs. Haggerty kept them for when company comes. And tonight... tonight the estate manager is the company. For the first time. For the only time. For however long the tea stays warm and the kitchen stays full and the crack in the glass stays open. Safety first. As I always say. But not tonight. Tonight... tonight the door is cracked, and the light comes in, and it hurts, and it's warm, and it might be enough.

desc: 'Who trusted a bunch of ruffians from Brixton with the most important thing in his world.' Daddy. He's talking about Daddy. And the most important thing... was me. I was the most important thing. And they kept me safe. Every single night. Every single adventure. Every room in every mansion. Not because they had to. Because they CHOSE to. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'
thinking: The Mob just toasted my father. 'Who trusted a bunch of ruffians from Brixton with the most important thing in his world. We didn't let him down. Not tonight. Not ever.' My eyes are burning. My throat is thick. The warmth in my chest has become something almost too big to contain — it's pressing against my ribs from the inside, a fullness that isn't pain but feels like it could become tears at any second. My father trusted them with ME. And they kept their promise. Every room, every hallway, every stumble and shout and 'OI, WATCH OUT' — it was all for him. For a promise they made to a dead man. And they kept it. They KEPT it. I'm not going to cry. I'm going to laugh. Because that's what happens when the tightness finally dissolves — it leaves you dizzy.

desc: I said it. And the world didn't end. And the bridge didn't collapse. And my face hurts from grinning. Show-off.
thinking:
I said it. I said everything. Out loud. In front of everyone. No third person — just 'I.' Not James Hartwell the character. Just me.

And Foxworth confessed. He actually confessed to the rat poison. In front of everyone. Because she made a room where the truth was possible.

The pressure in my chest isn't pushing outward anymore. It released — the way the bridge competition released, but deeper. Quieter. The tension I hadn't known I was carrying.

I said it. Wherever you go next, James Hartwell would very much like to walk beside you.

And now I'm standing in a kitchen with my hands at my sides, waiting. Not for an answer. Not for approval. Just... waiting to see her face. The way I waited across the classroom. The way I've always waited — knowing where she is, always.

The kettle. I said I'd make tea. Engineering with water and leaves. My hands know what to do. They've always known what to do. It was just the rest of me that needed to catch up.

Put the kettle on. Make the tea. Be useful. Be quiet. Be here.

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...well. THAT was NAUSEATING. In the most... TOLERABLE way possible. I'm not going to make a SPEECH, if that's what you're all expecting. Reginald Foxworth does NOT make SPEECHES. He makes ANNOUNCEMENTS and DECLARATIONS and PROCLAMATIONS, but NEVER speeches. So this is NOT a speech. This is simply... an OBSERVATION. I have spent this ENTIRE evening running through this manor, lying to every person I met, trying to steal things that weren't mine, sending people to rooms that had nothing in them, and telling EVERYONE that I'd been here before when I have NEVER set foot in this house in my LIFE. And do you know what I have to show for it? NOTHING. An empty pocket where a fake medal used to be. But I'm... I'm sitting in a kitchen. With TEA. And BISCUITS. And people who watched me FAIL at everything and are STILL willing to share their biscuits. Which is... CONFUSING. Because in my experience, when you arrive last, the biscuits are already GONE. But they're NOT gone. They're behind the flour tin. Where someone PUT them. FOR when company comes. ...I should very much like a biscuit.
thinking: My throat is tight. Not the scheming-tight, not the gloating-tight. A different tight. The kind that comes before the thing I don't have a word for. Peter just said something honest — truly, nakedly honest — to Penelope. In front of everyone. No third person. No engineering metaphors. Just... 'I'd like to walk beside you.' And nobody laughed. Nobody sent him to the hall. Nobody moved on to the next lesson. They just... listened. And the warmth in my chest is doing something it's never done before. It's not pressing outward, trying to expand beyond my ribs. It's not fizzing or carbonating or pulling. It's just... sitting there. Warm. Still. Like the stove. Still warm after all these years. I told them about the poison. I told them the TRUTH. And nobody threw me out. Penelope said 'Mrs. Haggerty's good biscuits.' Peter is making tea. The Mob is standing in the kitchen looking menacing. And I'm... I'm just here. With empty pockets and empty hands. No scheme. No lie. No architecture. Just a man in a kitchen, waiting for someone to pour him a cup of tea. The youngest of four. The one who always arrived last. But the chair is there. And nobody took it away.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: ... I KNEW it. I KNEW about the tea. I couldn't tell you 'OW I knew — me gut just KNEW — and I went at that tea service like a bull at a gate and everyone fought I was MAD. And I WAS mad. I was mad because me gut was SCREAMIN' and I couldn't explain WHY. But it was right. It's ALWAYS right. The tea was poisoned and NOBODY DRANK IT because the Brixton Boys don't know 'ow to do anyfing quietly. ... And Foxworth — Dastardly — whatever your name is. You just told the truth. In a room full of people who 'ad every reason to frow you out on your ear. And you said 'please.' ... Yeah. You can 'ave a cup of tea. Mrs. 'Aggerty's biscuits too, if there's enough. Because if Clara says 'togevver' means togevver, then it means TOGEVVER. Even the ones who got it wrong. ESPECIALLY the ones who got it wrong. ... That's what family IS, innit. Not the people who never mess up. The people who stay after they do.
thinking: Dastardly just confessed. Out loud. In front of everyone. He poisoned the tea — RAT POISON — and he just told us. He told us because Clara said 'together' and 'together' means not poisoning each other's beverages. And then he asked for a cup of safe tea. Please. He said PLEASE. My gut — my gut that knew about the poison, that screamed in the ballroom, that threw itself at the tea service — my gut was RIGHT. The tea WAS poisoned. Dastardly DID do it. And nobody drank because the Brixton Boys crashed into the table and shouted 'DON'T TOUCH THE TEA' before anyone could lift a cup. We saved her. Not by being clever. Not by being brave. By being loud and clumsy and refusing to let anyone near a teacup. We saved her by ACCIDENT. The Brixton Boys special. Trip into the right place at the right time. And now Dastardly's sitting in a kitchen asking for safe tea and saying 'please' and the whole room has gone quiet and my chest — my chest isn't a wall anymore. It's a doorway. Open. Warm. Wide enough for a man who poisoned a tea set and then told the truth about it because a girl from a big house said the word 'together' and meant it.

desc: My gut was right about the tea. My gut was right about Pemberton's lies. My gut was wrong about Pemberton's heart. And maybe — maybe that's okay. Maybe being right about danger and wrong about people is just what it means to grow up on the streets and learn to love anyway. The ones who share when they don't have to. The ones who tell the truth when it costs them everything. The ones who say 'please' in a room full of people they tried to poison. Those are the ones worth sitting down with. Those are the ones worth pouring tea for. Those are family. 'You're still here?' 'Where else would I be?'
thinking: Dastardly just confessed. Out loud. In front of everyone. He poisoned the tea — RAT POISON — and he just told us. He told us because Clara said 'together' and 'together' means not poisoning each other's beverages. And then he asked for a cup of safe tea. Please. He said PLEASE. My gut — my gut that knew about the poison, that screamed in the ballroom, that threw itself at the tea service — my gut was RIGHT. The tea WAS poisoned. Dastardly DID do it. And nobody drank because the Brixton Boys crashed into the table and shouted 'DON'T TOUCH THE TEA' before anyone could lift a cup. We saved her. Not by being clever. Not by being brave. By being loud and clumsy and refusing to let anyone near a teacup. We saved her by ACCIDENT. The Brixton Boys special. Trip into the right place at the right time. And now Dastardly's sitting in a kitchen asking for safe tea and saying 'please' and the whole room has gone quiet and my chest — my chest isn't a wall anymore. It's a doorway. Open. Warm. Wide enough for a man who poisoned a tea set and then told the truth about it because a girl from a big house said the word 'together' and meant it.

desc: Peter Perfect: Then we're all exactly where Lord Doily wanted us to be.
thinking:
'The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over.'

I look around the room. Penelope. Pemberton. The Mob. Foxworth. Me.

We're all standing in the kitchen.

The game is over.

We're the prize.

The warmth in my chest is so complete it doesn't feel like warmth anymore. It feels like architecture. Load-bearing. The kind that holds.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: I... oh my... I can't... y'all are gonna make me CRY, and Clara Bellingham does NOT cry in front of company! But here I am, cryin' like a baby at a baptism, and I don't even CARE! Mr. Foxworth — Dick — you just told the TRUTH. For the first time tonight — maybe for the first time EVER — you chose honesty. And I am so PROUD of you I could burst! The boys KNEW about the tea — they saved us all — and now YOU'VE saved us too, by warnin' us. You didn't have to do that. Peter — oh, Peter. Yes. YES. Walk beside me. Tomorrow and the day after and every day after that. You don't need a five-step plan. You just need to be THERE. And you WERE. You always were. And Mr. Pemberton — 'The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over.' Lord Doily was RIGHT. The Doily Diamond isn't a gem. It's THIS. It's US. It's the people who STAYED. And we are ALL standin' in this kitchen. Together. And THAT is the most precious treasure in all of Doily Manor.
thinking: I can't breathe. My chest is so full it's cracking open. Dick — DICK — just confessed to poisoning the tea. The tea the Mob warned me about. The tea I almost drank. And he told the truth — not because he was caught, but because I said 'we ALL go together.' He chose honesty over scheming because of something I SAID. And Peter — Peter stopped trying to impress me and started just being beside me. 'Wherever you go next, James Hartwell would very much like to walk beside you. If you'll have him.' My knees are weak. My eyes are burning. And Mr. Pemberton — Lord Doily said 'the prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over.' Not the diamond. The COMPANY. The STAYING. Every person in this room just told me the truest thing they've ever said. Dick told the truth for the first time in his life. Peter stopped performing. Mr. Pemberton shared Lord Doily's last secret. And I'm standing here with tears streaming down my face and I have never, EVER been happier. This IS the diamond. THIS MOMENT is the Doily Diamond. The people standing in the kitchen when the game is over.

desc: 'The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over.' We found it, Grandmother. We found the Doily Diamond. It was never a stone. It was never in a cabinet or behind a portrait or inside a machine. It was in the staying. In the choosing. In the 'I know.' And it was worth every single key.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): ... Mr. Foxworth. Thank you. For saying that. I... the estate manager would like to note, for the record, that the ballroom tea service should be disposed of immediately. I shall see to it first thing in the morning. And I... I should like to say... this is a very good kitchen. Mrs. Haggerty always said so. She said it was the warmest room in the house. Not because of the stove. Because of... well. She never finished the sentence. I think I understand now what she meant. Biscuit, anyone?
thinking: Dastardly confessed. He CONFESSED. He stood in a warm kitchen full of people who had every reason to hate him and he told the truth — the ugly, poisonous, rat-poison truth — because Clara said 'we all go together' and something in even DICK DASTARDLY's chest responded to that. And Peter — predictable, earnest, infuriating Peter — said the most unpredictable thing he's said all night. He stopped performing. He stopped being James Hartwell, engineer of bridges and cataloguer of libraries. He just said 'I'd like to walk beside you.' And the Mob toasted Lord Doily and said 'we didn't let him down.' And Clara called for Mrs. Haggerty's biscuits and toasted everyone in the room. And I — I who came here to KILL this girl — said 'the prize is whoever stayed' and meant it. Every word. Every syllable. The last lie that was true. And now Dastardly has confessed to poisoning the tea. The thing I spent half the evening trying to do — the scheme, the architecture, the elaborate theatrical gambit — Dastardly did it in the first five minutes. And he's CONFESSING to it. In front of everyone. Because Clara asked if anyone had something to say. And even the villain couldn't lie in this kitchen. Not tonight. Not with the biscuits behind the flour tin and the stove still warm and the company gathered. And the question now — the question that sits in my chest like a stone in warm water — is whether Vincent Marsh will confess too. Whether the Hooded Claw will stand in a kitchen full of people who stayed and tell them what he came here to do. The glass is cracked. The water is warm. The door is open. And the boy from age six — the boy nobody asked — is standing at the threshold, looking in. I can feel him there. He wants to speak. He wants to say: somebody should have asked me how I felt. And nobody did. And it made me into this. But I can't. I can't say that. It's too much. It's too real. It's the one truth I have never performed because it has never been a lie. So instead... instead Pemberton will do what Pemberton does. He will do the work. He will make the tea. He will put the biscuits on a plate. And he will stay.

desc: Dastardly confessed. And the Hooded Claw... didn't. The glass cracked but didn't break. The door opened but he didn't step through. The boy from age six looked in and saw the warmth and felt the light and... stayed on the threshold. Not inside. Not outside. Just... there. Where he's always been. Between the cold and the warm. Between Pemberton and Vincent. Between the lie and the truth. The biscuits are on the plate. The tea is brewing. The kitchen is full. And tomorrow — tomorrow the glass will seal itself, and the door will close, and the Hooded Claw will remember what he came here to do, and the schemes will begin again, because that is what he IS, that is what he was MADE into at age six when nobody asked — but tonight. Tonight the biscuits are Mrs. Haggerty's best. And the company is here. And the stove is warm. And that, as Clara said, is more than enough. It has always been more than enough.

desc: Peter Perfect: Now then — that kettle won't boil itself. And James Hartwell promised tea.
thinking:
Still. Everything is still. The pressure in my chest has settled into something architectural — load-bearing, permanent, part of the structure now. Not pushing outward anymore. Just... holding.

The Mob said 'that's what family is — not the people who never mess up, the people who stay after they do.' And Foxworth asked for a biscuit. And the Mob said yes.

I don't need to say anything else. I said what I needed to say. She heard it. The room heard it. And now the kettle needs putting on, because I promised to make tea, and a Hartwell keeps his promises.

Engineering with water and leaves. My hands know what to do.

desc: Peter Perfect examined the stove.

The Ant Hill Mob: 'The prize is whoever is standin' in the kitchen when the game is over.' ... Well. 'Ere we are. Standin' in the kitchen. Game's over. And I fink — I FINK — Lord Doily would look at this room and say we got it right. Not the riddles. Not the machine. Not the diamond. US. ... I ain't got fancy words like Peter. I ain't got secrets like Pemberton. I ain't got — well, I ain't got RAT POISON like Foxworth, which is probably for the best. All I've got is this: I'm still 'ere. Where else would I be?
thinking: Pemberton just said it. Lord Doily's words. 'The diamond isn't the prize. The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over.' And here we are. All of us. Standing in the kitchen. When the game is over. Peter, who stopped trying to impress and started just being beside her. Dastardly, who poisoned the tea and told the truth and asked for a biscuit. Pemberton, who raised a girl and lit a stove and kept biscuits behind the flour tin for thirty years. And the Brixton Boys, who ran through every room six times, crashed into tea services, tripped down stairs, and never once — not ONCE — stopped following the girl who calls them 'her boys.' We're all here. In the kitchen. Where the game is over. And Lord Doily — that magnificent, impossible, puzzle-building old genius — knew. He knew the diamond was never the point. The point was THIS. This kitchen. This warmth. These people. The ones who stayed. My chest isn't iron or concrete or a wall anymore. It's just... open. Open the way a door is open when you finally come home. And my eyes — my eyes are doing that thing again. The burning thing. The wet thing. The thing the Brixton Boys don't do in kitchens. Except maybe tonight. Maybe tonight, in this kitchen, with these people, we do.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Yes, Mr. Pemberton — biscuits for EVERYONE. Even the ones who got it wrong. ESPECIALLY the ones who got it wrong. That's what Mrs. Haggerty was tryin' to say, wasn't it? The kitchen is warm because of the PEOPLE in it. And right now, this kitchen has more warmth than any stove could ever make. So — Peter darlin', you make that tea. Boys, you stand guard over the biscuit tin. Dick, you take TWO biscuits — you've earned them for tellin' the truth. And Mr. Pemberton... thank you. For keepin' this kitchen warm. For thirty years. For me.
thinking: Everything has settled. The warmth in my chest isn't fizzing anymore — it's glowing, steady and deep, like embers in a stove that's been burning all day. Dick asked for a biscuit and the Mob said yes. Peter is making tea. Mr. Pemberton is passing around Mrs. Haggerty's biscuits. And I'm standing in the warmest room in the house — not because of the stove, but because of the people. Mrs. Haggerty never finished the sentence, but she didn't need to. We finished it for her. Tonight. Right here. With tea and biscuits and truth and tears and a brass key that was in a dog's mouth.

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...the biscuit is ACCEPTABLE. Not EXCEPTIONAL, mind you — I've had BETTER biscuits in... in PLACES... where biscuits are... LOOK, it's a perfectly ADEQUATE biscuit and I am NOT going to get EMOTIONAL about a BISCUIT, that would be ABSURD, that would be BENEATH the dignity of a FOXWORTH, and I — ... ...it's a very GOOD biscuit. Thank you. ...I'm going to sit here now. In this chair. With this tea. And this biscuit. And I am NOT going to scheme. I am NOT going to lie. I am NOT going to steal anyone's ANYTHING. For the next... five minutes. POSSIBLY ten. After that, all BETS are off and Reginald Foxworth returns to his NATURAL state of MAGNIFICENT villainy. But for NOW... for now I'm just going to... sit. ...this is a VERY good biscuit.
thinking: The fizzing warmth behind my sternum has risen into my throat — tight and carbonated, pressing outward. My cheeks are flushing hot. My jaw aches at the hinges. But it's not the gloating-ache. It's not the scheming-fizz. It's something else. Something I felt once before — at age eight, standing at the front of the classroom, holding a certificate, waiting for someone to notice. But this time... someone noticed. The Mob just said 'you can have a cup of tea.' He said 'especially the ones who got it wrong.' He said 'that's what family IS.' And the word 'family' hit something deep in my chest — deeper than the hollow ache, deeper than the greed, deeper than the recognition-hunger. It hit the six-year-old with the bread roll. The one who learned to take because nobody gave. And the Mob just... gave. A cup of tea and a biscuit and the word 'family' and nobody took it back. Nobody moved on to the next lesson. Nobody walked away. They're still here. Looking at me. Waiting. And my jaw aches and my eyes sting and Foxworths don't CRY but something behind my face is trying very hard to become something I don't have a name for. The buoyant lift in my chest — almost giddy — paired with a low satisfying heaviness settling into my gut. Like I've just eaten something rich. Like a bread roll. Like being full for the first time.

desc: 'The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen when the game is over.' ...I'm standing in the kitchen. I'm HERE. The youngest of four — the one who always arrived after everything was used up — is standing in the kitchen when the game is over. And there are biscuits. And tea. And people. And nobody is leaving. And nobody is taking anything away. And the hollow ache behind my sternum is still there — it will always be there, it was carved before I had words for it — but tonight it learned to share the space with something else. Something warm. Something that doesn't need to be stolen. Something that was behind the flour tin the whole time, waiting for company to come.

desc: She said yes. And James Hartwell — show-off, bridge-builder, the bravest and stupidest man in Doily Manor — puts the kettle on.
thinking:
She said yes.

'Walk beside me. Tomorrow and the day after and every day after that. You don't need a five-step plan. You just need to be THERE. And you WERE. You always were.'

She said yes.

The stove is warm. Cast iron. Still holding heat from hours ago. Pemberton banked it. Mrs. Haggerty kept the biscuits behind the flour tin. Lord Doily built a machine that only works when people mean well. And the girl from the school project — the one who was brighter than me, funnier than me, completely unaware of it — just said yes.

My hands are on the stove. Warm metal under my palms. Engineering with water and leaves. I know how to do this. I've always known how to do this.

The kettle. The water. The tea. The simplest bridge I've ever built. The one that matters most.

She said yes.

desc: Mrs. Haggerty never finished the sentence. 'The warmest room in the house. Not because of the stove. Because of...' She didn't need to finish it. Everyone in this kitchen knows the word she meant. Everyone in this kitchen IS the word she meant. ... Biscuit, then. Yeah. I'll 'ave a biscuit. Pass 'em over, Pemberton. ... Please.
thinking: Clara's crying. She's crying and she doesn't care who sees. And my eyes are burning too. The Brixton Boys don't cry in kitchens. Except tonight. Tonight the Brixton Boys cry in kitchens. Because the girl who calls us 'her boys' just said the diamond is US. Not a gem. Not treasure. US. The people who stayed. And Pemberton's offering biscuits. And Peter's making tea. And Dastardly's sitting quietly, waiting for someone to pour him a cup he didn't poison. And the stove is warm. And Mrs. Haggerty knew. She always knew. The kitchen is warm not because of the stove. Because of the people. ... I don't need to say anything else. I said 'where else would I be?' and I meant it. That's enough. That's always been enough. The Brixton Boys. Still here. Biscuit in one hand. Tea coming. Clara safe. Home.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): ... you'll want the water hot but not boiling, Mr. Hartwell. Mrs. Haggerty was very particular about that. She said boiling water scalds the leaves and makes the tea bitter. Just off the boil — you'll see tiny bubbles along the bottom of the kettle, before they rise. That's when you pour. She called them 'the patient bubbles.' The ones that... that wait.
thinking: The warmth. It's all warmth now. The glass is still there — it will always be there — but the water has risen through the cracks and the surface is warm and the room is full and Clara is crying and Peter said 'yes' and Dastardly is eating a biscuit and the Mob said 'that's what family IS — not the people who never mess up, the people who stay after they do.' And something inside me — something very old, something very small, something that sits in the exact centre of my chest where the numbness lives — heard that sentence. Heard it the way you hear a key turning in a lock you forgot existed. 'The people who stay after they do.' After they mess up. After they fail. After they poison the tea and lie about the cellar and scheme in the shadows and come to a manor with murder in their hearts. The people who STAY. I stayed. I'm here. In the kitchen. With biscuits. And the Mob — the Mob who watched me all night, who never once looked away, who knew something was wrong with me before I'd said my first word — the Mob just said I could have tea. Even me. Even the one who got it wrong. ESPECIALLY the one who got it wrong. My throat is closed. My eyes are burning. My hands have stopped trembling because they've found something to hold — a plate, a biscuit tin, the flour-dusted edge of the third shelf. Something solid. Something real. Something Mrs. Haggerty put there for when company comes. And I am — for the first and perhaps the only time in my life — company. Not the estate manager. Not the performer. Not the wolf or the mask or the mechanism. Just... someone standing in a kitchen. Being included. Without a price.

desc: The patient bubbles. The ones that wait. Mrs. Haggerty said that. She actually said that — it's one of the only true things Pemberton has spoken tonight. The old cook, standing at this stove, telling the young estate manager how to make a proper cup of tea. 'Don't rush it, love. Wait for the patient bubbles.' She called him 'love.' Nobody had called him that before. Nobody called him that after. But she said it once, over a kettle, in this kitchen, and he remembered. Thirty years later, in a room full of people he tried to destroy, he remembers. The patient bubbles. The ones that wait. Like him. Like the boy from age six. Like the warm water under the ice. Waiting. Always waiting. For company to come.

desc: Five years old in Grandmother's attic. Thirteen years old in the schoolyard. Eleven years old in the cave. Every key. Every choice. Every step deeper. They all led here — to a warm kitchen, a good biscuit, and the sound of people I love not arguing. The tightness in my stomach is gone. Completely gone. And in its place... just warmth. Just peace. Just home.
thinking: Dick is sitting in a chair eating a biscuit and NOT scheming. For five minutes. Possibly ten. And he called it a very good biscuit. Twice. My whole body feels like it's made of warm honey — liquid and slow and sweet. Every muscle has unclenched. Every knot has dissolved. This is what it felt like when my parents finally laughed — the tightness dissolving so suddenly it left me dizzy. The room is at peace. Every person in it is exactly where they're supposed to be. And I... I'm just going to sit too. With my tea. And my biscuit. And my family — the complicated, imperfect, stubborn, loyal, ridiculous, BEAUTIFUL family that walked through every room of Doily Manor tonight and ended up right here. In the warmest room in the house.

desc: Peter Perfect: Tea's ready. One cup for Miss Pitstop — the woman who solved every riddle in this manor. One for Mr. Pemberton — the man who kept it warm. One for the Mob — the wall that never falls. And one for Mr. Foxworth — who is having a VERY good biscuit and has earned his ten minutes of peace.
thinking:
Still. Warm. Full.

Foxworth is eating a biscuit and not scheming. The Mob is standing guard over the biscuit tin. Pemberton is handing out Mrs. Haggerty's best. And she called me 'Peter darlin'' and told me to make the tea.

My hands are on the stove. Warm cast iron. The simplest engineering problem in the world — heat water, add leaves, pour. I've been trying to interact with this stove all evening and it wouldn't respond. But right now it doesn't need to respond. It just needs to be warm. And it is.

Everyone is exactly where they should be. The kitchen is full. The biscuits are behind the flour tin. The tea is brewing. And James Hartwell is doing the one thing he was always meant to do — making something work, quietly, with steady hands, for someone he loves.

Not 'loves.' I don't have a word for it. I just know where she is, always.

desc: Show-off, she'll mouth. And I'll grin. And the tea will be perfect. Because James Hartwell has never met a broken machine he could not mend — and a kettle, thank God, is not a coat rack.
thinking:
Still. Warm. Full.

Foxworth is eating a biscuit and not scheming. The Mob is standing guard over the biscuit tin. Pemberton is handing out Mrs. Haggerty's best. And she called me 'Peter darlin'' and told me to make the tea.
