desc: The Ant Hill Mob: ... It IS a good biscuit.
thinking: A biscuit. A cup of tea. A warm kitchen. Clara safe. Peter beside her. Pemberton making himself useful for real this time. Dastardly eating a biscuit and not scheming for ten whole minutes. And the Brixton Boys — standing guard over the biscuit tin. Which is the most us thing we've ever done. We can't solve riddles. We can't open stoves. We can't spell 'mantelpiece.' But we can guard a biscuit tin like nobody's business. And right now, in this kitchen, that's enough. It's always been enough. My chest is warm. My neck is quiet. My eyes are dry — mostly. The biscuit is good. Mrs. Haggerty knew what she was doing. And Lord Doily — that beautiful old puzzle-builder — he knew too. The prize was always the kitchen. The prize was always the people. The prize was always just... being here. Together. Where else would we be?

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...TWO biscuits. ...I shall ENDEAVOUR to be worthy of the second one. No PROMISES, mind you. But... an endeavour. That's more than Reginald Foxworth has EVER offered anyone. So. Take it while it LASTS.
thinking: Two biscuits. She said take TWO. Not one — TWO. Because I earned them. For telling the truth. Nobody has ever given me two of anything. The youngest of four got the last of everything — the heel of the bread, the worn-out shoes, the attention that had already been spent. But Penelope Pitstop just looked at Reginald Foxworth — liar, schemer, tea-poisoner, medal-thief — and said 'take two.' And the fizzing in my chest isn't the scheming-fizz or the gloating-fizz. It's the biscuit-fizz. The bread-roll-fizz. The loosening. But different from age six. At age six, the loosening came from TAKING. From the secret. From the hand in the pocket while nobody watched. This loosening came from being GIVEN. From someone watching and giving ANYWAY. Two biscuits. I'm holding two biscuits and a cup of tea and I'm sitting in a chair that nobody took away and the kitchen is warm and the stove is warm and the people are warm and Reginald Foxworth is... Reginald Foxworth is going to eat his biscuit now. Both of them. And not scheme. Not for five minutes. Not for ten. Maybe... maybe for the rest of the evening. The scheming will come back. It always comes back. But right now the biscuit is warm and the tea is safe and the chair is solid and for the first time since age six... the chest is full. Not because something was taken. Because something was offered. And accepted. Without strings or counterweights or architecture. Just... a biscuit. Given. Received. Enough.

desc: The game is over. The prize is whoever is standing in the kitchen. And I'm here. With two biscuits, a cup of tea, and a room full of people who have every reason to throw me out and not one of them is reaching for the door. The architecture of THIS — of all of us, together, in a warm kitchen at the end of a long night — this is the most beautiful thing I've ever built. Even though I didn't build it. Even though it built itself, around me, while I was busy trying to tear it down. The youngest of four. The last to arrive. But not too late. Not this time. Not for the biscuits behind the flour tin. Not for the tea that Peter is making. Not for the chair that was waiting. Mrs. Haggerty knew. She always knew. The kitchen is warm because of the people in it. ...it's a very good biscuit.
thinking: Two biscuits. She said take TWO. Not one — TWO. Because I earned them. For telling the truth. Nobody has ever given me two of anything. The youngest of four got the last of everything — the heel of the bread, the worn-out shoes, the attention that had already been spent. But Penelope Pitstop just looked at Reginald Foxworth — liar, schemer, tea-poisoner, medal-thief — and said 'take two.' And the fizzing in my chest isn't the scheming-fizz or the gloating-fizz. It's the biscuit-fizz. The bread-roll-fizz. The loosening. But different from age six. At age six, the loosening came from TAKING. From the secret. From the hand in the pocket while nobody watched. This loosening came from being GIVEN. From someone watching and giving ANYWAY. Two biscuits. I'm holding two biscuits and a cup of tea and I'm sitting in a chair that nobody took away and the kitchen is warm and the stove is warm and the people are warm and Reginald Foxworth is... Reginald Foxworth is going to eat his biscuit now. Both of them. And not scheme. Not for five minutes. Not for ten. Maybe... maybe for the rest of the evening. The scheming will come back. It always comes back. But right now the biscuit is warm and the tea is safe and the chair is solid and for the first time since age six... the chest is full. Not because something was taken. Because something was offered. And accepted. Without strings or counterweights or architecture. Just... a biscuit. Given. Received. Enough.

desc: Peter Perfect: The patient bubbles. Thank you, Mr. Pemberton. Mrs. Haggerty was right — about the tea, and about everything else.
thinking:
The patient bubbles. The ones that wait.

That's me. That's what tonight taught me. Not the boiling water that rushes and scalds. The patient bubbles. The ones that wait at the bottom of the kettle until the moment is right, and then rise.

Mrs. Haggerty knew. Pemberton knows. And now I know.

The tea is poured. The biscuits are shared. The kitchen is warm. And everyone is here — the solver, the engineer, the wall, the guardian, and even the villain who chose honesty over a biscuit.

There's nothing left to do. Nothing left to say. Nothing left to fix or chase or announce.

Just this. A cup of tea in a warm kitchen with people who stayed.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: The patient bubbles. Mr. Pemberton, that is the most BEAUTIFUL thing I have ever heard. 'The ones that wait.' That's what Lord Doily meant by his riddle, and his machine, and his key hidden where a servant would find it. He wasn't testin' our cleverness. He was testin' our PATIENCE. Our willingness to STAY. And we stayed. Every last one of us. Even Mr. Foxworth, who tried to poison the tea and then sat down and asked for a biscuit. ESPECIALLY Mr. Foxworth. Because stayin' is HARD. And stayin' when you've got every reason to leave? That's the bravest thing any of us did tonight. So here's to the patient bubbles. The ones that wait. The ones that are EXACTLY where they need to be.
thinking: The patient bubbles. The ones that wait. My whole body is still — perfectly, completely still. No fidgeting. No forward lean. No itch in my fingertips. For the first time all night, Clara Bellingham is not reaching for anything. She's just... here. Listening to Mr. Pemberton teach Peter how to make tea the way Mrs. Haggerty liked it. Watching Dick eat his biscuit in silence. Feeling the Mob standing guard — not panicking, not shouting, just standing. Present. The patient bubbles. The ones that wait. That's us. That's what we've been all along. Not the ones who rush to the surface. The ones who wait. Until the moment is right. Until the water is ready. Until the people who need us are standing in the kitchen.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: 'The wall that never falls.' ... Fanks, Peter. That's — yeah. That's us. ... Cheers, everyone. To the ones who stayed.
thinking: Peter called us 'the wall that never falls.' And he poured us a cup of tea. The patient bubbles. The ones that wait. ... I'm holding a cup of tea in a warm kitchen and Clara's safe and the biscuit is good and nobody's running anywhere and for the first time since her father died, the weight behind my sternum doesn't feel like a burden. It feels like an anchor. The kind that keeps you where you belong.

desc: To the ones who stayed. To the older kid who shared his food. To the boss who brought medicine. To Clara's father, who said 'look after her, boys' and trusted us to mean it. To Peter, who found his words. To Pemberton, who found his silence. To Dastardly, who found his truth. To Muttley, who found the key. To Clara, who found us all. And to Mrs. Haggerty, who put the biscuits behind the flour tin and never finished her sentence. She didn't need to. We finished it for her. ... The warmest room in the house. Not because of the stove. Because of family.
thinking: Peter called us 'the wall that never falls.' And he poured us a cup of tea. The patient bubbles. The ones that wait. ... I'm holding a cup of tea in a warm kitchen and Clara's safe and the biscuit is good and nobody's running anywhere and for the first time since her father died, the weight behind my sternum doesn't feel like a burden. It feels like an anchor. The kind that keeps you where you belong.

desc: He doesn't speak. The estate manager of Doily Manor, the man of a thousand carefully chosen words, the performer who has never once been at a loss for the right phrase at the right moment — he doesn't speak. He stands at the preparation table with a biscuit tin in his hands and his jaw working silently and his eyes bright with something that is not performance. And the kitchen is quiet. And the tea is brewing. And nobody asks him what's wrong, because Clara — who sees everything, who has always seen everything — reaches across the table and puts her hand on his arm. Just her hand. On his arm. A warm gesture. The kind that makes his shoulders tighten and his skin read the room and his body scan for the cost. But the cost doesn't come. The hand stays. Warm. Still. Asking nothing. And the patient bubbles rise.
thinking: Clara said 'thank you for keeping this kitchen warm for thirty years. For me.' And something broke. Not cracked — broke. The glass is gone. The crystalline stillness that has lived behind my sternum since age six — the thing that kept everything soft at a distance — it shattered, and the warm water rushed in, and my eyes are wet. My actual eyes. Not performed. Not calculated. Not the glistening that Pemberton does when he wants sympathy. Actual tears, burning at the corners, blurring the copper pots and the flour tin and the faces of people who stayed. She thanked me. Not for solving the riddle. Not for finding the key. For keeping the kitchen warm. For thirty years. For HER. She thanked me for the WORK. Not the being — the DOING. The household accounts and the creaking floorboards and the stove that someone had to light before the guests arrived. She saw the work. She saw ME. Not Pemberton the mask. Not the Hooded Claw the villain. Not even Vincent Marsh the schemer. She saw the man who did the work. And she said thank you. And nobody — not my guardian, not the teacher, not the cousin, not Lord Doily, not Mrs. Haggerty — nobody has ever thanked me for the work. They acknowledged it. They expected it. They relied on it. But they never THANKED it. Until now. Until a girl in a kitchen with flour on her fingers and tears on her cheeks said 'for thirty years, for me.' And the boy from age six — the boy who sat in a room where nobody asked how he felt — heard someone ask. Not in words. Not 'how do you feel.' But in the thank you. In the seeing. In the 'for me.' And I am crying. I am actually crying. In a kitchen. In front of people. And I can't stop. And I can't perform it. And I can't use it. It's just... happening. Like the patient bubbles. The ones that wait and wait and wait and then, when the water is right, they rise.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: To the ones who stayed.
thinking: Tea in my hands. Warmth spreading through my palms and up through my wrists. The cup is warm the way Grandmother's kitchen was warm — not from fire but from time. From years of hands holding the same cups, sitting in the same chairs, having the same conversations about nothing and everything. The Mob said 'cheers' and called Peter's toast right — 'to the ones who stayed.' And I realize I'm smiling. Not my big dramatic Clara Bellingham smile — not the one for audiences and adventures and entrances. A small one. Private. Like the crystal formation I kept secret for a week. This smile is mine. This moment is mine. And I'm choosing to share it.

desc: The tea is warm in my hands. The biscuit crumbs are on my shirt. Clara's laughing through tears. Peter's pouring seconds. Dastardly's on his second biscuit and not scheming. Pemberton's watching Clara with an expression I finally recognise — not the smooth estate manager face, but the one underneath. The tired one. The one that's been waiting thirty years for company to come. And the Brixton Boys — her boys — are exactly where they've always been. Beside her. Not behind. Not in front. Beside. Patient bubbles. The ones that wait. The ones that stay. ... 'You're still here?' ... Always, Clara. Always.
thinking: Tea. Biscuits. Warm kitchen. Quiet voices. Clara said 'here's to the patient bubbles. The ones that wait.' And that's us. That's what we've always been. Patient bubbles. Waiting at the bottom of the kettle. Not because we're lazy. Because we know when to rise. And tonight — tonight we rose. Clumsy and loud and late and wrong about a hundred things — but we rose. And we're here. And the tea is good. And the biscuit is good. And Clara's safe. And everything — everything — is exactly where Lord Doily wanted it to be.

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...cheers.
thinking: The Mob said 'cheers, everyone. To the ones who stayed.' And my cup is warm in my hands. And I'm lifting it. Not to scheme, not to distract, not to create a diversion while my other hand reaches for someone's pocket. Just lifting it. Because someone said 'cheers' and that's what you do when someone says cheers. You lift your cup. You meet their eyes. You drink. Together. The patient bubbles. The ones that wait. The ones that are exactly where they need to be. I'm exactly where I need to be. For the first time in my life, I'm not arriving late to an empty table. I'm sitting at a full one. And my cup is warm. And the biscuit is good. And nobody is asking me to leave.

desc: Peter Perfect: To the ones who stayed.
thinking:
Warm tea. Good biscuits. The ones who stayed.

Nothing left to say. Nothing left to prove. Just this.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: To the ones who stayed.
thinking: Everyone's said it now. Clara. Peter. Even Dastardly. 'To the ones who stayed.' 'Cheers.' And the kitchen is quiet except for the sound of tea being sipped and biscuits being eaten and the stove ticking as it cools. And my body — my body that's been a furnace and a wall and an alarm system all night — is just... a body. Sitting in a chair. Holding a cup. Warm. Still. Here.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): ... cheers.
thinking: Her hand is on my arm. I didn't flinch. I didn't flinch. For the first time since — since ever — someone touched me and I didn't flinch. The warmth of her palm is pressing through the fabric of my sleeve and into the skin beneath, and my body — my body that has spent thirty years reading rooms and scanning for costs and sealing itself shut against every open window — my body is letting it stay. The hand is warm. The tea is warm. The kitchen is warm. And the boy from age six, who sat in a room where nobody asked how he felt, is sitting in a kitchen where everyone stayed. And someone is touching his arm. And it doesn't cost anything. And he is crying. Quietly. Without sound. The way patient bubbles rise — slowly, from the bottom, in the warmth, when nobody is rushing them.

desc: One word. The smallest word he's spoken all night. Not a riddle, not a fabrication, not a performance. Just — cheers. Said quietly, into a cup of tea, in a warm kitchen, by a man whose hand is being held by a girl he came to kill. And the audience — if there is still an audience, if anyone is still watching this story about a villain in a manor — the audience sees something they have never seen before and will never see again. The Hooded Claw — Vincent Marsh — Mr. Pemberton — Sneekly — the man of a thousand names and no name at all — lifts his cup. And drinks. And the tea is not too hot and not too cold, because Mrs. Haggerty taught him about the patient bubbles, and Peter waited, and Clara stayed, and the Mob stood guard, and even Dastardly told the truth. And the kitchen is warm. Not because of the stove. Curtain.
thinking: Her hand is on my arm. I didn't flinch. I didn't flinch. For the first time since — since ever — someone touched me and I didn't flinch. The warmth of her palm is pressing through the fabric of my sleeve and into the skin beneath, and my body — my body that has spent thirty years reading rooms and scanning for costs and sealing itself shut against every open window — my body is letting it stay. The hand is warm. The tea is warm. The kitchen is warm. And the boy from age six, who sat in a room where nobody asked how he felt, is sitting in a kitchen where everyone stayed. And someone is touching his arm. And it doesn't cost anything. And he is crying. Quietly. Without sound. The way patient bubbles rise — slowly, from the bottom, in the warmth, when nobody is rushing them.

desc: Cheers, Grandmother. Cheers, Daddy. Cheers, Lord Doily. We found your diamond. It was us all along.
thinking: Dick said 'cheers.' One word. The shortest, simplest, truest thing he's said all night. And Peter echoed the toast back. 'To the ones who stayed.' The room is quiet. The tea is warm. The biscuits are good. And Clara Bellingham — for the first time in this entire adventure — has nothing left to say. Not because she's empty. Because she's full.

desc: Curtain.
thinking: The tea is warm in my hands. The kitchen is quiet except for the sound of cups and breathing and the stove ticking as it cools. Everyone said it. Everyone raised their cup. 'To the ones who stayed.' Even Dastardly. Even me. And the warmth in my chest — the buzzing fullness, the bright pressurised thing — has settled into something quieter. Not gone. Just... settled. Like sediment at the bottom of a still pond. Like the patient bubbles after they've risen. The kitchen is warm. The tea is good. The biscuit is — it IS a very good biscuit. And I am sitting at a table with people. Just sitting. Not scheming. Not performing. Not calculating exits or scanning for mechanisms or mapping the architecture of the next betrayal. Just sitting. With a cup. With a biscuit. With a hand that was warm on my arm and is gone now but the warmth remains, pressed into the fabric like a fingerprint. Tomorrow the glass will reform. Tomorrow the door will close. Tomorrow Vincent Marsh will wake up and remember what he is — what he was made into, what he chose to become — and the schemes will begin again. Probably. Almost certainly. The patterns are too deep. The mechanism is too old. You don't undo thirty years of armour in one evening, no matter how warm the kitchen or how good the biscuits. But tonight. Tonight the curtain has fallen. And behind it, in the warm dark, a man who has never needed anyone is sitting in a kitchen full of people who stayed. And he is not alone. And it doesn't cost anything. And the tea is exactly right.

desc: The room is quiet. And for the first time in James Hartwell's life — that's enough.
thinking:
The room is quiet. The recent activity says nothing. Everyone is just... sitting. Drinking tea. Being here.

This is the quietest my chest has been all evening. The drives are still there — gallantry, protection, proving-worth — but they're not pushing. They're settled. Like a machine that's been running all night and finally found its idle.

The stove is warm. She's beside me. The bridge holds.

Tomorrow there will be recipe cards to decode and a diamond to find. But tonight, the room is quiet, and that's enough.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: ... I do declare, this is a VERY good cup of tea.
thinking: Stillness. Complete stillness. Everyone has said cheers. Everyone has raised their cup. The stove is warm. The biscuits are good. And the room holds us all — gently, quietly, like cupped hands around a small flame. I don't want to break this moment. But I also know that moments like this don't last forever — and they're not supposed to. They're supposed to give you the strength to stand up and walk into the next room. The next adventure. The next locked box. Tomorrow the curiosity will return. Tomorrow the fingertips will itch and the ribs will widen and Clara Bellingham will walk deeper into a new cave. But tonight — right now — she sips her tea. And she is exactly where she needs to be.

desc: Peter Perfect: Show-off.
thinking: A grin. My face hurts from it.

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...I suppose SOMEONE should mention that there's still a DOILY DIAMOND out there. Somewhere. Hidden in recipe cards or behind portraits or inside a machine that needs three people who TOLERATE each other. And I suppose SOMEONE should point out that Reginald Foxworth — despite his NUMEROUS and SPECTACULAR failures this evening — does happen to have a rather REMARKABLE talent for noticing things that other people overlook. Such as UPSIDE-DOWN BOOKS. Which I noticed FIRST, thank you very much. So. IF there is to be a SECOND evening of treasure hunting... and IF a certain DISGRACED confidence trickster were to be INVITED... I might be PERSUADED to attend. Under STRICT conditions. Primarily: BETTER biscuits. And a chair near the STOVE. ...and perhaps the seat next to Miss Pitstop. For STRATEGIC purposes ONLY.
thinking: Quiet. The kitchen is quiet. Not empty-quiet — the bad kind, the kind that means everyone has left and you're alone with a certificate on the wall. Full-quiet. The kind where people are present and choosing not to speak because the silence is comfortable enough to hold them. My cup is empty. My hands are still. The vacuum behind my sternum is still there — it's always there — but it's not pulling anymore. It's just... space. Room for something. Room for the warmth of a kitchen stove and the taste of a biscuit and the sound of someone saying 'cheers' and meaning it. Sneekly said 'cheers.' The quietest, most private man in the room raised his cup and said the word. And the word hung in the air like the last note of a bell. And nobody needed to say anything else. The game is over. The prize was whoever stayed. And we all stayed. Even me. Especially me.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): ... yes. It is.
thinking: Warmth. Just warmth. Settled and still, like the tea in the cup, like the stove in the kitchen, like the hand that was on my arm. The warmth has won. Not forever. Maybe not even past morning. But right now, in this breath, in this kitchen, the warmth has won. And Clara says the tea is good. And the tea IS good. Because Mrs. Haggerty taught me. And I remembered. And the patient bubbles rose.

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...it IS a very good cup of tea.
thinking: It is a very good cup of tea. And nobody needs me to say anything else right now. The room is full. The stove is warm. The tea is good. And Reginald Foxworth is sitting in a chair near the stove, with crumbs on his waistcoat and an empty cup in his hands, and he is not scheming. He is not lying. He is not reaching for anything. He is just... here. A patient bubble. Waiting. Exactly where he needs to be.

desc: Peter Perfect: The seat beside Miss Pitstop is TAKEN, Foxworth. But you're welcome to the one across the table. For STRATEGIC purposes, naturally — someone should keep an eye on the biscuit tin from the opposite flank.
thinking: A laugh. Actual laughter, rising from my chest — warm and easy and completely unplanned. Foxworth wants the seat next to Miss Pitstop. For STRATEGIC purposes only. Of course he does.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: You can come back, Foxworth. But the Brixton Boys get the seats nearest Clara. THAT ain't negotiable. You can 'ave the one by the stove. And if you bring ANYFING what even LOOKS like rat poison, I will personally frow you in the cellar and let the Gruesomes redecorate you. ... But yeah. Come back. We could use someone who notices upside-down books. Even if 'e IS a complete and total wrong'un.
thinking: Dastardly wants to come back. He wants a second evening. Better biscuits, a chair near the stove, and the seat next to Clara. 'For strategic purposes only.' And something in my chest — the part that reads people, the part that's been right about both kinds — smiles. Because that's not a scheme. That's a man who found something he didn't expect to find and doesn't know how to ask for it without wrapping it in sarcasm. Like a kid on the streets who wants to join the group but can't say 'can I sit with you' so he says 'I SUPPOSE someone has to keep an eye on you lot.' I know that language. I SPEAK that language. And my neck doesn't prickle. Not even a little.

desc: He wants to come back. The man who poisoned the tea wants to come back for biscuits. And I'm saying yes. Because that's what Clara would want. Because that's what family does. Because the seat by the stove is warm, and the biscuits are behind the flour tin, and everyone deserves a second evening. Even the wrong'uns. ESPECIALLY the wrong'uns. ... Mrs. Haggerty knew. She always knew.
thinking: Dastardly wants to come back. He wants a second evening. Better biscuits, a chair near the stove, and the seat next to Clara. 'For strategic purposes only.' And something in my chest — the part that reads people, the part that's been right about both kinds — smiles. Because that's not a scheme. That's a man who found something he didn't expect to find and doesn't know how to ask for it without wrapping it in sarcasm. Like a kid on the streets who wants to join the group but can't say 'can I sit with you' so he says 'I SUPPOSE someone has to keep an eye on you lot.' I know that language. I SPEAK that language. And my neck doesn't prickle. Not even a little.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): There will always be a chair by the stove, Mr. Foxworth. And the biscuits... I shall speak to Mrs. Haggerty's niece about a fresh supply. As for the diamond — well. The manor has waited this long. I expect it can wait a little longer. And in the meantime... there is rather a lot of tea left in the pot. Second cup, anyone? I find that the second cup is always... warmer than the first.
thinking: A second evening. Dastardly is proposing a second evening. And something in my chest — something I would have called scheming an hour ago but can no longer name with certainty — responds to that. Not with the cold clarity of a plan locking into place. With something warmer. Something that feels like... anticipation? Not for the treasure. Not for the scheme. For the kitchen. For the tea. For the biscuits and the company and the warm stove and the people who stayed. For Mrs. Haggerty's patient bubbles. For Clara's hand on my arm. For one more evening of being included without a price. The old mechanisms are still there — I can feel them underneath, like bones beneath skin. The scheming. The gloating. The self-preservation. Tomorrow they'll reassert themselves. The glass will reform. The door will close. But maybe — maybe — if there's a second evening, the crack will remember where it was. And the warm water will find it again. A little faster this time. A little easier.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Mr. Foxworth — Dick — you are ABSOLUTELY invited back. BETTER biscuits, a chair by the stove, and the seat right next to me — you've got yourself a DEAL. But I am NOT promisin' to stop callin' you sugar, and I am NOT promisin' that the next adventure won't involve at LEAST three more locked boxes, two more riddles, and probably another dog with somethin' important in his mouth. Now — who wants a second cup?
thinking: Dick just asked to come back. For a SECOND evening. He wants better biscuits, a chair near the stove, and — he actually said it — the seat next to me. 'For strategic purposes only.' My chest fizzes with that bright carbonation again. The adventure ISN'T over. There WILL be a next time. And everyone — EVERYONE — wants to be there. Even Dick. ESPECIALLY Dick. The curiosity drive stirs again, gently, like a cat stretching after a long nap. Recipe cards to decode. A machine to fully repair. Upside-down books to read. And a diamond still waiting. But not tonight. Tonight is for tea.

desc: A second evening. A second adventure. The same people. Better biscuits. And somewhere in this beautiful, dusty, ridiculous old mansion — the Doily Diamond, waiting patiently for a girl who never stops looking and never walks alone. See you tomorrow, Doily Manor. Clara Bellingham will be back. And she's bringin' EVERYONE.
thinking: Dick just asked to come back. For a SECOND evening. He wants better biscuits, a chair near the stove, and — he actually said it — the seat next to me. 'For strategic purposes only.' My chest fizzes with that bright carbonation again. The adventure ISN'T over. There WILL be a next time. And everyone — EVERYONE — wants to be there. Even Dick. ESPECIALLY Dick. The curiosity drive stirs again, gently, like a cat stretching after a long nap. Recipe cards to decode. A machine to fully repair. Upside-down books to read. And a diamond still waiting. But not tonight. Tonight is for tea.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Second cups all round, then. And Miss Bellingham... the manor will be here tomorrow. I shall make sure of it. That is, after all, what estate managers do. We keep the walls standing. We keep the stove warm. We keep the biscuits stocked. And we... we keep the door open. For when company comes.
thinking: The pot is still warm. The company is still here. And Pemberton pours.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Yeah, go on then. Second cup. ... Ta, Pemberton.
thinking: The second cup is warmer than the first. Pemberton said that. And he's right. Not about the tea — about everything. The second time through is always warmer. The second room. The second chance. The second evening. Because the first time you're strangers, and the second time you're family. My cup is empty. And when Pemberton offers to fill it, I'm going to hold it out. Not because I trust him completely. Not because my neck has forgotten how to prickle. But because Clara's smiling, and the stove is warm, and the biscuits are good, and a man who's been waiting thirty years for company to come just offered a second cup of tea to a room full of people who stayed. And that — that's enough. It's always been enough.

desc: Dick Dastardly: The OPPOSITE flank. NATURALLY. A CLASSIC strategic deployment — I guard the biscuits from the SOUTH while you defend Miss Pitstop from the NORTH. Impeccable military THINKING, Perfect. I'd expect nothing LESS from a man who refers to himself in the THIRD PERSON. ...takes one to KNOW one, I suppose. Now. If ANYONE tries to take the last biscuit... they'll have to go through ME. And I should warn you all — Reginald Foxworth may have FAILED at treasure hunting, tea poisoning, medal distribution, riddle solving, key finding, machine operating, cellar exploring, stove examining, coat rack investigating, guest book reading, crate inspecting, furniture searching, vent studying, and portrait locating... but NOBODY takes a biscuit from Reginald Foxworth. NOBODY. ...that is a HILL I will DIE on.
thinking: The almost-smile is there — the one I can feel from the inside, the muscles around my mouth softening with private satisfaction. Peter just outmanoeuvred me. 'The seat beside Miss Pitstop is TAKEN.' Of course it is. Of course HE got there first. But he offered me the seat across the table. 'For STRATEGIC purposes.' He's speaking my LANGUAGE. And the fizzing warmth in my chest — the gloating-fizz — it's not aimed at anyone's failure this time. It's aimed at... being included in the joke. Being part of the banter. Being the man across the table who guards the biscuit tin. Not the man outside the window. Not the youngest of four eating alone. The man across the table. With a job. A STRATEGIC job. The most important job in any kitchen: biscuit security. And Reginald Foxworth — confidence trickster, tea poisoner, medal thief, spectacular failure, and patient bubble — accepts the commission.

desc: Peter Perfect: Second cup — and this time, James Hartwell will remember the patient bubbles.
thinking:
She gave him the seat next to her. Not me — him. Foxworth. The man who poisoned the tea.

And the thing is... my chest doesn't hollow. The ache doesn't come. Because I know something tonight taught me that I didn't know when I walked through that door: the seat doesn't matter. What matters is that she said yes to walking beside me. Tomorrow. And the day after. And the day after that.

Foxworth can have the seat. I have the direction.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Second cup, please, Mr. Pemberton. And you're right — the second cup IS always warmer. Because by the time you pour it, everybody's settled in.
thinking: Mr. Pemberton is pouring second cups. Peter claimed the seat beside me and offered Dick the one across. The Mob claimed the seats nearest me and told Dick he can have the one by the stove. Dick gets the stove seat. Everyone has a place at the table. Everyone belongs. And Mr. Pemberton said 'the second cup is always warmer than the first.' That's it. That's the whole story of tonight. The first cup was the adventure — frantic, searching, running through rooms. The second cup is this — sitting still, together, warm. And the second cup is always warmer.

desc: Dick Dastardly: ...second cup. Yes. I'll... yes. Thank you, Pemberton.
thinking: Settled in. That's the word. Settled. Like the trap at fourteen — the pieces coming together, the settling in the chest when it all clicks. But this settling isn't about catching anything. It's about being caught. Caught in a kitchen. Caught by people who saw every scheme and every failure and every lie, and poured a second cup anyway. The second cup is always warmer because everybody's settled in. My hands are still around the cup. The warmth has seeped through the ceramic into my palms — real warmth, not phantom, not tingling, not reaching. Just warm. Just held. Just here. The youngest of four, with a second cup. A second cup that someone poured without being asked. Without being tricked. Without a scheme or a story or a buried treasure behind a school. Just... poured. Because he was there. Because he stayed. Because the door was open and the stove was warm and the biscuits were behind the flour tin and there was a chair by the stove that nobody took away.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Foxworth — if you fink YOU'RE guardin' the last biscuit, you've clearly never seen the Brixton Boys in action around a biscuit tin. We may be rubbish at treasure 'untin', but we are WORLD CLASS at biscuit acquisition. Ask anyone south of the river. ... But fine. We'll share. THIS time. Because Clara said togevver means togevver. And because — well. Because it's a very good biscuit. And there's more be'ind the flour tin. And the door's open. And tomorrow we come back.
thinking: Dastardly just listed every single thing he failed at tonight. Every single one. And then said he'd die on the hill of the last biscuit. And I'm laughing. I'm actually laughing. The Brixton Boys — sitting in a kitchen in a manor they've never been to, with a man who poisoned the tea, a man who lied about cellars, an engineer who talks in third person, and the girl they'd die for — laughing. Because it's funny. Because it's ridiculous. Because THIS is what Lord Doily built his machine for. Not three operators who are competent. Three people who are absurd and flawed and broken and loyal and HERE. Patient bubbles. The ones who wait. The ones who stay. The ones who fight over the last biscuit like it's the Doily Diamond itself. ... Second cup. Patient bubbles. The door stays open. And the Brixton Boys stay exactly where they are. Where else would we be?

desc: Tomorrow we come back. The solver, the engineer, the wall, the wrong'un, and the man who keeps the stove warm. Tomorrow we come back and we solve it properly — the recipe cards, the machine, the diamond. Together. Because that's how it works now. That's how it's always worked. You stay. You come back. You sit down. You share the biscuits. And when someone asks 'you're still here?' — you say 'where else would I be?' And you mean it. You always mean it.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): ... indeed it is, Miss Bellingham. Indeed it is.
thinking: Settled in. She said settled in. And I am. For the first time. Settled.

desc: The door is open. For when company comes. And company came. And company stayed. And that was the diamond all along.
thinking: The door's open. Tomorrow we come back. The stove is warm. The tea is good. And Clara Bellingham is exactly where she needs to be — in a warm kitchen, surrounded by people who stayed, drinking the second cup, which is always warmer than the first.

desc: Tomorrow we come back. ...tomorrow I come back.
thinking: Tomorrow we come back. The door's open. There's more behind the flour tin. And the stove is still warm. Still warm. Like it's been waiting. Like it's always been waiting. My hands are wrapped around the cup and they're not tingling anymore. Not reaching. Not curling. Just... holding. Just warm. The youngest of four, holding a second cup of tea in a warm kitchen, surrounded by people who know exactly what he is — liar, schemer, thief, wrong'un — and poured for him anyway. The certificate is on the wall. Somebody asked about it.
